6169: The petitioner, a social worker of the State of Jammu & Kashmir, was appointed as a member of the Advisory Board on October 1, 1973. He was placed under suspension from service by the Government of India in terms of section 3(1) of the . On November 30, 1974, he was served with a notice requiring him to show cause why his services should not be terminated for having committed misconduct and negligence in discharge of his duties. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the said notice. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice had been issued after the expiry of the period of six weeks prescribed in section 3(2) of the , and that the petitioner could have no grievance if the notice was not served within the time prescribed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The Board is an independent body constituted under the Act and it has to act independently and follow the scheme laid down by the Act. It is open to the State Government to make small variations depending upon the requirements of any particular State. [766C] (ii) The Board has to function as a representative body and it cannot be expected to act independently or through its members. The Board must be set up within six weeks from today and report compliance shah be filed with the Registry of this Court within eight weeks. The first meeting of the Board should be within four weeks of its constitution and every such Board is directed to send its second proceeding to the Registry. The Board shall also indicate as to who would be the Chairman and Secretary respectively of the Board. The Board will thereafter submit its report to the Government within two weeks. The Government may take appropriate action against the Board either suo motu or on receipt of the report. [767B C]
5386: The petitioner was a tenant of the premises in question. He filed an application for release of the premises on the ground that he had been allotted a house in the same locality and that he was not allowed to live with him in another house belonging to his son. The Government rejected the said application on the ground, inter alia, that the petitioner was not entitled to stay in the premises as he was in service and that he could not be permitted to live with his son in another house. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the order of release was bad because the authorised officer had no power to review the previous order nor he had the power to release the premises without even giving an opportunity to the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of release is not vitiated because the petitioner was never given an opportunity to show cause against the order of detention. [801F] 2.1 It is well settled law that in case of bona fide need subsequent events must be taken into consideration if they are relevant on the question of release or possession of the premises. [802A] 2.2 The High Court has rightly held that the Government cannot review its own order. [803B] 2.3 The High Court was right in holding that the Government could review the order only when there was some material on record which would justify the exercise of the power under section 48(3) of the Act. [804C]
6517: The appellant, a lessee of a Petrol Pump, was granted a licence to run a Petrol Tank for the purpose of carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The licence was renewed from time to time and the appellant was given a licence to operate the said Tank for the period ending 31st March, 1979. On the expiry of the licence, the appellant applied for renewal of his licence. The District Authority cancelled the licence. The appellant filed an appeal before the Commissioner, Dehradun. The Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant had ceased to have any right to use the site for storing petrol. The appellant challenged the order by way of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the District Authority under Rule 151 could cancel the licence only when the licensee ceases to have any fight to use the land for storing petrol and that right could be lost by a licensee either by his tenancy or right to the use of the site coming to an end or for any other reason where by, in law, the right to use site came to an end. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The District Authority under rule 151 can cancel the licence if the licensee ceases lo have any right of use the site. [850F] 1.2 In the instant case, the District Authority has not cancelled the licence of the appellant. The District Magistrate has no power to cancel the licence of a licensee. The District Officer is not competent to cancel the license of a licensee as he does not possess any right to do so. [851G H] 1.3 The District Magistrate cannot cancel the licence merely because he has taken into consideration the relevant facts. He must take into account the fact that the licensee has ceased to have a right to use his site for storing petroleum. [852A B] 1.4 The District Magistrate is not competent under section 4(a) of the Petroleum Act to cancel the licences of a licensee who has ceased to be in possession of any right to the user of the site for storage of petrol. [853C] 1.5 The District Magistrate can cancel the licences only when the licence ceases to have the right to the licensee either by its tenancy or right of the use of site
4865: The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge, Bhilwara under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code. He was acquitted on the ground that the evidence of the eye witnesses did not inspire confidence and that the High Court had set aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial court in favour of the appellant. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellant and convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. The High 'Court set aside the conviction of the appellant on the ground: (1) that the evidence was not properly appreciated; (2) that the High 'Court had failed to take into consideration the fact that the incident out of which the prosecution arose happened at about 8 p.m. On September 29, 1970, when the deceased Gyanchand was returning home after attending a marriage ceremony, he was attacked by the appellant and the co accused who were charged under section 302/34 I.P.,C. The prosecution examined three eye witnesses, namely, Bodu Lal, the brother of the deceased and Ram Niwas, the brother-inlaw of the deceased. The trial court acquitted the appellant but the High Court confirmed the acquittal of Bodu lal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in setting aside the acquittal and that the judgment of the trial court was vitiated by reason of its failure to consider the relevant circumstances and the reasons given by the trial judge for acquitting the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the evidence is not reliable and the High Court was justified in reversing the order of the trial Court. [862B] 2. There is no substance in the contention that the High. Court should have considered the evidence of two independent witnesses. The High. Court has also taken into consideration the evidence of other witnesses. The evidence of the two eye witnesses is corroborated by the discovery of blood stained baniyan and knife. The recovery of blood stained clothes of the appellant from his house is proved by the evidence of P.W. 3, the brother and the recovery of blood stains from the house of the appellant, which are sufficient to establish the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt
4923: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Madhya Pradesh. They transferred them to the respondent, who was the State Government. The transferees filed applications before the Collector under the Abolition Act for a declaration that they had no right to transfer the land and that the transferees were entitled to retain possession of the land. The Collector rejected the application on the ground that he had no power to revise the order of the Collector. The Commissioner and the Board of Revenue held that the transferors had no right or title to transfer the lands. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the Revenue Officers could not exercise powers as Revenue Officers but as a persona designata under the Abolition act. HELD: (i) Under the Abolition Act as also the Code there is a right of appeal provided against all orders passed by the Collector. Section 84 of the Abolition Act does not confer any jurisdiction upon the Commissioner or the Board of Revising Authority to revise an order of the Revenue Officer. [804 E] (ii) The provisions of the Abolition act are not applicable to the proceedings before the Collector. [805 F] (iii) The Revenue Officers have been invested with powers which are vested in the Collector under section 84 of the Act. The Collector has no power to review his own order. [806 A B] (iv) The Revenue officers while exercising powers under the Abolition Acts are not exercising the powers as Revenue officers but as a personsa designata. [807 C D]
3809: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed an appeal before the High Court which confirmed the death sentence awarded by the Sessions Judge. The High Court, however, reduced the sentence of life imprisonment to one year. In this appeal, it is contended that the High Court erred in confirming the death sentence as well as the conviction and sentence of life sentence imposed on the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the provision is to give a fresh such circumstances as may help the court in awarding appropriate sentence having regard to the personal, social and other circumstances of the case. [713B] 2. The object underlying the provision is not to provide an opportunity to the prosecution and the accused to place before the court facts and materials relating to the various factors bearing on the question of sentence and if they are contested by either side, then to produce evidence for the purpose of establishing the same. But the legislature has made no change in the previous law, but the courts have been given greater powers to consider the question of sentencing in a manner which will be just and fair. [714E F] 3. The object behind the provision is that the accused should be given an opportunity to place his case before the court and the court must take into account all relevant factors including the nature and stage of the trial, the stage of the case, the interest of justice and the like. It is only when the ends of justice are met that the court can exercise its power under section 235(2) Cr. P.C. [715D E] 4. The object and scope of the provision are two fold; (1) to enable the appellate court to give an opportunity to both sides to place their respective cases before the court, and (2) to afford an opportunity to adduce the entire evidence and to lead the necessary material. The provision is intended to give an additional opportunity to the accused to produce his own witnesses and also to examine himself or any other witness. If the accused does not avail of the opportunity granted to him under section 235, the court cannot be said to have committed any error in convicting him. [716F G]
3351: The respondent was a broker of foreign machinery parts. He had agreed to purchase the goods from Ram Avtar and promised to supply them on the following day. On November 8, 1967 Shanker Lal, representing himself to be a broker of Indian currency, handed over the formal order to Ram Avtars who were told that he would arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The respondent 's case is that on November 8, the appellant had taken away the documents of the foreign goods and had sold them to him. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 420 read with section 511 I.P.C. before the Presidency Magistrate. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and committed the case to the Court of Sessions. The appellant contended that the charge against him was not sustainable as he was not present at the time when the cheques were given by the respondent to Ram Arogar. The Magistrate held that the charge was not proved. The High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and convicted the appellant under sections 420 read with s.511 I. P. C. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The charge against the appellant was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [279E] (ii) The charge was not established. The evidence showed that the appellant had been present at the relevant time when the cheque was given to Ram Arya. There was no reason why the appellant should have been shown to have been present at that time. [280F] (iii) The charge could not be said to have been proved because the appellant did not appear to be present at the place where the cheque was issued. [281G]

The petitioner, who was the husband of the deceased, filed an application for committing the case to the Court of Session for trial for an offence under section 304 B I.P.C. which was inserted in the Indian Penal Code by Act No. 43 of 1986 w.e.f. 19.11.1986. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that this amendment being prospec tive was inapplicable to a death which occurred on 13.8.1986, prior to the amendment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 498 A and section 113A of the Indian Penal Cod e are not attracted to the present case. [766B] 2.1. Section 498 A is added in the Indian penal Code by Act 43 of 1986 and incorporated in the Code of Criminal Procedure. The new section reads as follows: "490. Dowry death. Explanation : For the purpose of this sub section, 'dowry' shall have the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. Explanation : In this sub section 'Dowry' shall include 'dowry'.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a woman who has been married or adopt ed before the commencement of this Act shall be deemed to have gifted to her free will. Explanation : A woman who has already been divorced by a court or a company by which she has obtained a divorce shall be deemed not to have greed her second wife 's life for the former expression. Explanation : The term 'wife ' includes husband and wife 's legitimate children. Explanation : This section applies also to cases of dowry deaths. [767E F
5094: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. He was carrying on business in the name of Khushi Ram Rangi Lal. On October 10, 1961, there was a partial partition in the family by which the business was divided between the father and the son, and thereafter, it was carried on by a partnership consisting of the two. For the assessment year 1966 67, the assessee filed his wealth tax return for the assessment year 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included the property of the assessee in his net wealth. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Wealth Tax Officer. In appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that in view of section 6 of the Wealth tax Act, 1957, the income from assets inherited by a son from his father from whom he had separated by partition could not be assessed as the income of the Hindu undivided family of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the reference. Hence the appeal by the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The decision of the High Court is based on its own interpretation of section 6(2) of the Wealth 'Tax Act, 1957. [766C] 1.2. Section 6(2)(a) of the Act provides that where a person has been succeeded by another person or persons, the value of the assets of the former person shall be deemed to be the aggregate of the amounts of debts due by such person or persons. [765D] 1.3. In the instant case, the assessee was succeeded by his brother, who was a Hindu Undivided Family. The assessee was the owner of the business carried on by his father. His brother died leaving behind him his wife and children. The assessee had no other joint family with his brother. The assessee did not have any other joint family. The assessee, therefore, cannot be said to be a separate legal entity. [764E F] 1.4. In the present case, the property of a Hindu undivided Family is not an asset of the assessee but is a joint family property. It is a joint Hindu family. The property of the Hindu Undivided family is not an individual property of the individual. The assessee has not been able to show that the property of his father was not his individual
3366: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants on the ground that the dying declarations made by the deceased were not reliable, because they did not bear any enmity or hostility to the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the oral statement which Bahadur Singh made could not be relied upon as a dying declaration because he had no reason to implicate the appellants falsely. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The dying declaration is admissible in evidence under section 32(1) of the Evidence Act. [768E] (2) The dying declarations are admissible under section 32 of the Evidence act. [769A] (a) The dying statements are admissible under Section 32(1). But if the dying declaration is recorded by a police officer in writing, the same cannot be treated as substantive evidence. It is only when such statement is recorded by an Executive Magistrate and is signed by the person making it that it can be used as evidence against the accused. [770B C] (b) The dying statement is admissible under section 33 of the Evidence. [771C D] (c) The dying declartions are admissible under s.32(1) and not under s.33 of the Evidence, but under section 32 (3), where the statement is recorded in writing by a police official and is signed and attested by witnesses, the statement would fall within the mischief of section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [772D E] (d) The dying Declaration is admissible under s 32(1), but if it is recorded by the police officer in his pen and signature, it will be admissible under section 162 of Criminal Procedure Code, even though it is recorded in the pen and signature by a police Officer. [773F G] (e) The dyingdeclaration is admissible under Section 33 of the Indian Evidence Act. The dying declaration must be made before the Magistrate who records it. If the Magistrate does not record the dying declaration, the dying declaration becomes inadmissible under Section 32 of the Indian Indian Evidence Act, because the statement is not recorded in the presence of the Magistrate. [775G H; 7
5825: The appellant Laisal Haque was charged along with other accused persons under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, for causing death of Gulam Rabbani and injure others. He pleaded not guilty to the charge framed against him and his case was that he had been falsely implicated in the case by the police. The Additional Sessions Judge convicted the accused persons under sections 302 read with Section 149 of the I.P.C., and under section 147 I.P,.C. and under section 148 I.P.,C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that (1) it was a case of common object of the unlawful assembly being to murder Gulam Rabani and injuring others, all the rioters committed the murder of Gulam Rasuldin and injure him; (2) the charge framed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge as against the respondent Laisal Haqr was substantially defective inasmuch as it was a rolled up charge, the common object of unlawful assembly was to murder Gulambrani and injures others. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) It is clear from the language employed in section 218 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that the charge framed must be one which is intended to be tried separately or at different stages. [887B] (2) The charge framed by an Additional Sessions Judge was not a mere irregularity but was a complete compliance with the provisions of section 220(3) of the Code. [888D] (3) The charge was not a composite charge but a separate charge. [889E] (4) The charge did not contain any specific allegation against the accused persons. The charge was therefore defective. [885F] (5) The charge could not have been split up into two parts. One part was a charge of conspiracy and the second part was a separate charge of murder. [886G]
4503: The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the Sessions Judge ignored the provision contained in section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which provides, in so far as is relevant, that when the accused was asked on the question of sentence, he did not say anything. In the first place, the Sessions Judge overlooked this provision, contained in section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and committed a serious error by putting a formal question to the accused as to what he had to say on the question. The High Court also overlooked the provisions contained in section 359(1) of the Cr. P.C., 1973, which provide, in so many words, that when a person is brought before the Court for trial, whether with or without sufficient reason, he shall be put to an end to his life, if there is no reasonable chance of his absconding. The High court also overlooked the provision contained under section 384(1) Cr. P,.C. 1973, which provided that when the Court has made a finding that the accused has committed an offence punishable with death, the Court may, instead of sentencing him to imprisonment, direct that the accused should be released on probation of good conduct under section 360 of the Criminal procedure Code. The High 'Court also overlooked the fact that the appellant was not on good terms with the Sub Inspector and, therefore, the former made a false entry that the latter was present at the police station, which according to the High Court, was a serious matter. The High. Court also ignored the provisions contained under section 354(1) and the answers which the appellant made to those questions were beyond the narrow constraints of the Evidence Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have been adopting a very technical approach in dealing with cases of murder and other offences where they are called upon to decide the question of guilt. [766A] 2. The High courts must be slow to interfere with the discretion exercised by the Sessions Judges in the matter of sentence. [767B] 3. The High Cour t erred in exercising its
3405: The appellant Bank claimed bonus for the accounting year 1966, however, could not be settled between the parties and, though the Bank paid 18% of the wage or salary earned by the workmen during that accounting year as bonus, the workmen were not satisfied and the industrial dispute arising from their claim had to be referred for adjudication. The Industrial Tribunal held that the claim for bonus was not tenable and directed the payment of bonus at the rate of 15 per cent of the wage/ salary earned by each workman. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that: (i) the claim for the accounting years 1966, 1966 and 1967 were barred by limitation; (ii) the claim made in the application for clarification was beyond time; (iii) the claim was barred by limitation because the claim for deduction under section 10(2)(vi) of the Act was made after a period of three years from the date of the award and therefore, the claim should have been rejected; (iv) the claim of the Bank was barred by res judicata; (v) the claim related to the year 1964 and the claim was made in the year 1965; (vi) the claim relating to the year 1965 was barred by constructive res judicata; and (vii) the claim relates to the year 1966 and the claim is barred by res judciation. HELD : (1) The claim for the year 1965 is barred by constructive Res Judicata. [166 D] (2) The claim of the appellant was barred by the principle of constructive res judicata. [165 E] (3) The claim was barred under section 11 of the Act. The claim was made after the award was passed and the award became enforceable. It was open to the appellant Bank to raise the plea of res judicata before the Tribunal. [168 F] (4) The claim made in regard to the year 1963 was barred by bar of res judicata. The claim made by the appellant Bank in the year 1964 was barred by delay and laches. [169 G H]
7035: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of PW3, who had accompanied the deceased to the place of occurrence, is not reliable and his testimony should be discarded as he did not see the accused assaulting the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that a witness may lie but not the circumstances in which it is made. [398B] 1.2 If the court finds that the evidence given by the eyewitness is credible and trustworthy, then there can be no legal impediment in convicting the accused. [399A] 1.3 In the instant case, the evidence of PWs 3, 4 and 5 does not inspire confidence. They are closely related to the deceased. Their presence at the time of the incident cannot be doubted. They have seen the accused assaultting the deceased with the crowbar. The fact that they were armed with the crowar does not affect their credibility. [400D E] 1.4 There is no reason why the evidence of these two witnesses should be rejected. [407E] 1.5 The evidence of PW 3, who has been declared hostile, is not worthy of credence. He has stated that he saw the accused assault the deceased. This statement is not corroborated either by any independent or corroborative evidence. [406F] 1.6 The evidence of PWs 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 is not worth reliance because they are closely related. The evidence of these witnesses is not worth relying because they are close relatives of the deceased. [405G H] 1.7 The evidence of the other two eye witnesses is not reliable. [404H; 405A B] 1.8 The evidence of P.W.3, who is an injured witness, is not trustworthy. 5086: The assessees, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, were carrying on business in the State of Kerala. They owned an estate from which they derived agricultural income liable to be assessed in the year 1963 64. In assessment proceedings for the year 1963 65, the assessees claimed a deduction of Rs.33,747.09 from their agricultural income on the ground that it was payable towards interest on a loan of Rs.4,00,000 taken by them from M/s. Associated Planters Ltd.,waived payment of interest to the extent of Rs.3,00,00, 000. The assessing authority held that the amount of interest paid was not agricultural income and accordingly the amount was credited to revenue accounts of the assessees. 2428: The appellants were the owners of a plot of land in the District of Patna. The lease was granted to them by the State of Bihar for agricultural purposes. The appellants challenged the validity of the lease on the ground that it had not been brought in accordance with the provisions of the Act and hence not maintainable. The High Court held that the lease was invalid as it did not conform to the provisions of section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act and therefore they were entitled to evict the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 117 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [766A] (2) The High Court was right in holding that the lease in favour of the appellants was governed by section 117 of that Act. [767B] (3) The High Courts of Patna and Calcutta have consistently followed the decisions of the Calcutta High Court. [768C] (4) The High courts of Patna and Madras are bound by the decision of the Calcutta high Court. [776D] (5) The High court has rightly decided that the lease is not governed by section 6 of the Bengal Rent Control Act. [777E] (6) The High Cour t erred in reopening the question. [779F] (7) The High 'Court was wrong in remitting the matter to the trial court for fresh disposal. [778G]
5543: The appellant was employed by the respondent Bank as a clerk in the erstwhile Narang Bank of India Ltd. The terms and conditions of his service were governed by the terms of the agreement dated October 10, 1956 entered into between the appellant and the said Bank. Clause 20 of the said agreement provided that "the services of the staff of the erstwhile Narag Bank of India Limited shall be taken over by the United Bank of India, New Delhi on or after the 10th February, 1975 and their pay and allowances shall be determined in accordance with the rules applicable to them." Clause 20 of this agreement provided that the services of the employees of the erstwhile Bank would not be terminated except for good cause and without notice and without assigning any reason. The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent Bank on July 11, 1973. He was transferred from the said post to the new post of Senior Manager in the year 1976. On August 25, 1976 he was served with a charge sheet alleging that he had committed certain acts of misconduct while working as Senior Manager in his capacity as Senior Manager. The charges were denied by him. The enquiry officer submitted his report holding that the charges were proved against the appellant. The disciplinary authority accepted the findings of the enquiry officer and dismissed the appellant from service. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which was rejected. Thereafter the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The Single Judge held that the appellant should be deemed to be in continuous service of the Narang Bank on and after the 10 th February, 1975, and consequently of the United Bank Of India, on the date of award. The Division Bench set aside the judgment of the Single Judge and allowed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the appellant was not given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses whose evidence had been recorded earlier. The principles of natural justice require that he should be given an opportunity of cross examining those witnesses whose evidence has been recorded earlier and since the Tribunal had declined to grant permission to the United Bank to cross examine those witnesses whose statements had been recorded later on, the award was liable to be quashed. [880C D] 1.

The income from the hospital was received by it in the year of account ending March 31, 1948, but the income was not included in the total income of the assessee. 2907: The respondent, a member of a scheduled tribe, applied for settlement of the quarry in question. He was not paid the amount due under the contract. The Divisional Forest Officer accepted the tender and issued a notice to the respondent calling upon him to pay the amount within 15 days. The respondent 's appeal against the order of the Divisional Forest Officer accepting the tender was dismissed by the Conservator of Forests. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the amount claimed was not recoverable under the provisions of the Assam Forest Regulation VII of 1891 and quashed the proceeding for recovery. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amount was not recoverable as the respondent had failed to carry out the obligations of the tender and that the amount could be recovered only under section 75 of the Assam forest Regulation VII of 1918. HELD: (i) Section 75 of the Act does not apply to proceedings under the Assam Forest Regulations, 1891. It is only the mode of recovery provided by section 75 of that Regulation which is applicable to proceedings under that Regulation. [839 E] (ii) The amount claimed is not due from the respondent but is payable in execution of the contract. [840 F] (iii) The respondent 'was entitled to recover the amount claimed under the Assam forest regulation VII of 189 1. [841 A] (iv) The respondent was entitled to recover his dues under the Assam Forests Regulation, 1891, and the High Court was right in quashing the proceeding for recovering the amount alleged to be due from the appellant. [842 B]

4832: The Appellants, who were publishers of books for general reading to be kept in school and college libraries, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the State Government 's decision regarding the assessment, selection, purchase and distribution of books out of the cyclone and flood relief grant made by the Central Government inter alia on the ground that the procedure followed by the State Government in setting up a committee for the selection of books was not fair and just. The proviso only makes it clear that the conditions mentioned therein are subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. 826: The appellant company was a public limited company. The respondent company had its registered office at Bombay and its head office was at Bombay. The company claimed that the reserves of the company were not utilised as working capital, but they were used only for the purpose of rehabilitation and that the said reserves should be deducted from the rehabilitation amount. The Industrial Court held that the reserves were used as working capital and that the company was entitled to deduct the said amounts from the rehabilitation payment made by it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The items of rehabilitation are not necessarily related to the working capital of the company. They are merely incidental to the working of the company and do not form part of the working capital. [801 B] (ii) The item of rehabilitation is generally a major item that enters into the calculation of the surplus and that the amount required for rehabilitation must be ascertained on a correct basis. The item of Rehabilitation is usually a major item which enter into the calculation for the purpose. [802 C D] (iii) The item in question does not fall within the definition of "working capital" given in section 2(5) of the Act. It is an inclusive one. It is a term of art. It has been defined in the Act to mean "any word, letter or expression in, which is used in relation to the employment, salary, wages, hours of work, privileges, rights or duties of employers and includes any process of promotion or development thereof." [803 A B] (iv) The item does not come under the definition of the word "working" in section 2 (5). The item is a general description of the various kinds of activities which the employer may choose to undertake. The item is not exhaustive of the objects of the Act and is not intended to cover all possible activities of the employer like the construction of buildings, roads etc., but is intended to cover the whole of the undertaking. [804 E F] (v) The item is an inclusive item. It is not exhaustive. It is exhaustive. 2383: The appellants were the owners of certain goods manufactured by them. They sold to various parties, their depots outside the Province of Uttar Pradesh, for example, at Calcutta in the State of West Bengal before any contract of sale was made. The sales tax authorities assessed the outside sales of all the appellants to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1954, and the Sales Tax Officers of Uttar Pradesh assessed the outside sale of the appellants to tax. The appellants filed appeals under section 9 of the Act against the assessments but they failed. In the meantime, the Sales Tax Officer of Uttar Pradesh levied a penalty on the appellants under section 10(1) of the Act. The appellants challenged the imposition of the penalty by way of an appeal under section 9. The High Court held that the out of State sales would be taxable (1) if the goods were in existence in the Province of U.P., at the time when the contracts for sale were made, and (2) if the contracts were entered into after the goods had been exported out of the Province of UP, they would not be liable to pay the tax. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Explanation II to section 2(h) of the U. P. Sales Tax act, 1954, which came into force on April 1, 1954, was intra vires as being beyond the legislative competence of the State Legislature. The Explanation II to s. 2(h), therefore, did not apply to the present case.
886: The appellant was charged with having committed offences under section 147 and section 452 of the Code. He pleaded that he had been falsely implicated in the case by the police, and that the First Information Report lodged by him was a result of an after thought. Held, that the Magistrate before whom the police report has been filed under section 173 of the Code should have applied his mind to the merits of the said report and it could not be assumed that the case started against him by the First Information Officer was still pending with the police. The Magistrate did not apply his mind to any material on which the police report could be quashed. The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings initiated by the First information Report. The Magistrate was bound to consider all the evidence adduced during the course of the investigation and come to his own conclusion whether or not the prosecution case was true. The Magistrate could not take into consideration the statements of witnesses recorded during the courseof investigation. The Magistrate 's order was without jurisdiction. The Magistrate erred in taking cognizance of the offence.

2126: The plaintiff alleged that the properties described in Schedule Ka were his personal properties, that they were gifted to or purchased by him or his ancestors and that they were wrongly recorded as marfatdars of Lord Jagannath. Sub section(12) of section 6 defined 'religious endowment ' or 'endowment ' as meaning: " all property belonging to, or given or endowed for the support of maths or temples or for the performance of any service or charity connected therewith whether or not such math or temple or gurudwara is discontinued either temporarily or permanently." The defendant contended that the institution was a public religious institution and that the properties belonged to the Math. Held, (1) that the Emar Math was a private trust and the properties belonged exclusively to the Math; that the institution had been acquired by the Math for the benefit of the Math and that the Math was not a private one. The property was not a public trust but a private one and that the property was not dedicated to the Math for its own use. The property did not belong to the Math but to the Math and it was not a trust property. The property belonged to the math and the Math was a public trust. The property had been acquired for the benefit and benefit of the math. The Math was not an institution of a public nature within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. The property must be held to be a public trust property. (2) that the properties were not gifted by the Math to the Math nor were they ever appropriated by the Math. The property in question was not a religious trust but a public trust and the property was never dedicated to the maths. (3) that the Math being a public trust, the property was a public property and the Math could not claim any right over the same. (4) that the property had been gifted only to the Math, and not to the Math itself. (5) that the institution being a public religious trust, the properties were rightly held to be not a public charitable trust.
1851: The respondent, one of the candidates in the election to the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly filed an election petition under section 8 1 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election of the appellant on various grounds. The appellant was declared elected. The respondent challenged the election on several grounds including the corrupt practice of bribery and undue influence. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondent had failed to establish his case. In appeal by special leave it was contended before this Court: (i) that the poster is not hit by the provisions of section 123(4) of the Act; (ii) that the election petition should have been dismissed on the ground that it had not impeded Hariram, another duly nominated candidate who withdrew his candidature before the election and against whom allegations of corrupt practice were made; (iii) that the allegation of corrupt practice was vague and general in nature and could not be taken into account; (iv) that the statement of fact about the personal character or conduct of Ramchander Chowdhary, one of his candidates in the Election Petition, was a mere statement of fact regarding his personal character and conduct which did not make it any the less a statement in relation to his personal character or that of his political or public activities and policies. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (i) The poster was not hit by section 123(1)(b) of the Representation Act. It was not so hit because it contained a statement of fact relating to the personal character and/or conduct of Ram chandra Chowdhary. [801 B] (ii) The posters are not defamatory of any person. They do not contain any imputation of personal character or of any particular political party. The poster does not contain any such imputation. The posters do not contain anything which would indicate that the posters were intended to convey the idea that Ramchander Choudhary misappropriated the cement of the Rajasthan Canal. [802 C D] (iii) The postter was not published as required by section 123 (4). The poster did not contain any reference to any matter other than what was stated in the poster. The postter did not contain anything in respect of the poster

2800: The appellant, a tenant in respect of a plot of land, filed an application under section 6(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for fixation of standard rent. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the question whether to an open piece of land let for the purpose of constructing buildings for residence or educational purposes only after a structure was built thereon, did not fall within the purview of section 6(2) of the Act. The High Court held that the question as to whether to an existing building or a building for residence or education was a mixed issue of law and fact and that it had been finally decided by the Rent Controller. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The decision of the Rent Controller on the question of the standard rent is final and binding on the parties. [833 G] (ii) The decision on the question whether the building should be fixed at a particular rate or standard rent depends upon the terms of the lease deed and not upon the question of construction of the building. [834 B] (iii) The decision cannot operate as res judicata in a subsequent proceeding between the same parties if the cause of action is different from the one which has led to the earlier decision. [835 D]
544: The appellants, who were the members of a religious denomination, filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to the protection of article 26 (b) of the Constitution and for an injunction restraining the State from interfering with their right to worship in a temple. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the provisions of section 3 of the Act were not applicable to the suit as it was not a matter of religion as to which the appellants had to be determined solely with reference to article 26(b). On appeal by special leave: Held, that the provisions contained in section 3 of Act V of 1947 were not applicable because the temple was not a denominational one and the provisions of the Act did not apply to it. The definition of 'temple ' as it then stood, took in only institutions which were dedicated to or for the benefit of the Hindu community in general as to which they were entitled, and that section 3 of this Act was not invalid merely because it was not enacted in respect of any institution which were dedicated exclusively to or for any of the Hindu religion.
903: The assessee was a private limited company with its registered office at Bombay. In the year 1947, Mafatlal Gagalbhai & Co., Ltd., was incorporated in Bombay. The assessee was also a private limited Company with its registered address at Bombay. The Income tax Officer, Ward 'A', Bombay, assessed the assessee under section 23(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and issued a notice to the assessee under sub section (1) of section 22 of the Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question referred by the Tribunal holding that the income had accrued to the assessee in the former State. The assessee appealed to this Court. [249 F] (ii) The Tribunal could have decided the question whether it was income accruing or deemed to have accrued to the appellant in the latter State. The Tribunal had decided that the income does not accrue to the assessee, in the former Baroda State, or in the latter part of the country. The Tribunal should have decided the matter on merits. [250 B C] (iii) The Tribunal has wrongly assumed that the income arose to the assessee from the Baroda territory. The Tribunal has not given any reason for coming to the conclusion that the income was not accrued to the Baroda. [251 D]

On November 17, 1952, a report was submitted by the Sub Divisional Inspector to the Superintendent, of Police, stating that the respondent was guilty of misconduct under para. 486 of the Police Regulations.
