7070: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission, a statutory body constituted under the Jammu and Kashmir State Universities Act, 1979, was established in the year 1984. The Government of Jammu and Kashmir issued a notification on May 28, 1984 inviting applications for appointment to the post of munsifs and requested the public service commission to select twenty candidates in the place of ten. The Public Service Commission sent three names containing twenty candidates, the remaining nine candidates were recommended by the High Court. On March 11, 1985, the High Court intimated the Government of Jammu & Kashmir that the government had decided to recommend five candidates in the waiting list. The Government, however, did not approve the list as it was not prepared in accordance with the Rules of 1967 and the Government, therefore, wrote to the Public Service Commission to select twenty five candidates in place of ten and the Government also directed the Public Service commission to select thirty candidates. The Government again sent three names along with the waiting list and the Public ServiceCommission accepted the list. The appellants challenged the validity of the selection process before the High Court contending that the government having approved the list, the government cannot sit in judgment over it. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The government is entitled to scrutinise the list prepared by the Public Service Commissioiner. The list of selected candidates after it is approved shall be published by the Government Gazette and a copy thereof shall be sent to the court along with the Waiting List, if any furnished by the Commission for record in their office. [407B] 1.2. The government has no power to sit in judgment or disapprove or cancel the select list. The government can always disapprove or disapprove the select list but it does not have any power to act arbitrarily or capriciously or to make appointments without following the procedure prescribed. [408C D] 1.3. The government being the appointing authority, is entitled to scrutiny and look into the list prepared and take appropriate decision. If it decides to disapprove or to cancel the select lec tion, then it must record reasons for doing so. [409D E] 1.4. The government may accept the list even though it is not prepared in the prescribed manner.
4282: The assessee was a non resident company. During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1962 63, the statutory agent purchased tobacco in India and exported it to Japan. The assessee received commission on sale of tobacco in Japan and credited it in his books of account. The commission amount was remitted wholly to the statutory agent who debited his commission account with the amount of commission payable to the assessee and credited the same in the account of the assessee. The assessee 's case was that the commission paid by him to the statutory agents was not taxable in view of section 5(2) of the Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim for deduction under section 80HHC of the Act holding that the commission was not taxable as it was not received in India. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the commission received by the assessee was not taxable. The High Court dismissed the reference. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the commission is not taxable because it is received in India and therefore the commission cannot be taxed in India. HELD: (1) Section 5(2)(b) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that subject to the provisions of the Act, the total income of any previous year of a person who is a non resident includes all income from whatever source derived which is received or is deemed to be received in India in such year by or on behalf of such person. The Explanation to section 80H HC provides that in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed under this clause to accrue or arise in India during such year shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operation carried out in the business. [780G] (2) The Explanation to sub section (2) of section 80HD clearly indicates that the profits and gains arising from the business of the assessee should be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 48 and not in accordance with section 48. [790A]
569: The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had two units in its name and one unit in the State of Bihar. In respect of sales tax assessment orders made against the appellant company for the years 1952 53 and 1953 54, the Sales Tax Officer held that the said transactions were not liable to be taxed at the hands of the appellant company. On appeal by the appellant company, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Sales Tax officer but on further revision petitions filed by it, he held that the sales tax authorities could not levy sales tax on the appellant company as they were not taxable under the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant company then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the orders passed by the Sales Tax Officers. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the sales of goods in question were not exigible to sales tax. The appellant appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Court. Held: (i) The expression " sale " occurring in section 100(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, means a transfer of property in goods from one person to another; (ii) the word " sale " in entry 48 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of Indian Act, 1935 includes a sale in the course of interState trade or commerce, and (iii) the word 'sale ' in entry 48 of List II of Seventh Schedule to that Act does not include a sale in course of inter-State trade or export. The word " sale" in entry 48 is used in entry 54 in List II in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution and it has been defined in section 2(g) of the Act to mean " any transfer otherwise than in pursuance of a contract, and includes also a mortgage, charge, lien or ejection."
2406: The appellants, who were the owners of the land in dispute, executed two mortgage deeds in favour of the respondent. In the year 1939, the proprietary rights of the respondent were purchased by one Vinayakrao, who had two sons, and Wamanrao, who died in 1939. The respondent filed a suit for possession against the appellants on the ground that he was the owner of the property and that he was entitled to remain in possession till his death. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the finding recorded by the lower appellate court that the mortgagees in the year 1895 did not get possession over cultivatory rights in this plot was decisive of the claim put forward in the suit and that the High Court erred in reversing the decree passed by the trial court. HELD: (1) The finding of fact recorded by the courts below that the mortgages in the year 1890 were not in possession of the respondent was a finding of fact based on the evidence led before them. [939 E] (2) The finding that the mortgage was not in possession is a finding of law and cannot be interfered with under Article 136 of the Constitution. [940 F] (3) The finding regarding possession being in possession of a person who has become an occupancy tenant of the property in question is a finding which is not binding on the parties to the partition suit. [941 G H] (4) The finding about possession having been in possession of somebody else was not binding on him. [942 B] (5) The finding as to possession being in the possession of some other person cannot be challenged in any proceedings. [943 C]
4498: The appellant Corporation was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The objects of the Corporation are to carry on the business of insurance and general insurance in India. The Corporation is a body corporate with perpetual succession and common seal and is empowered by its bye laws to contract, acquire, hold and dispose of property, both movable and immovable, and to enter into contracts for and on behalf of the Corporation. The Corporation has been authorised to make regulations and rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. Section 48(1) empowers the Central Government to make rules to provide for all matters for which provision is expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Act and the Corporation may, after previous publication, make such rules as it thinks fit. The Corporation framed the Life Insurance Corporation (Staff) Regulations, 1981. Regulation 3 provides that every employee shall be entitled to one month 's pay in lieu of notice of three months or one month's salary in lieu thereof. The appellant Corporation made an application before the High Court challenging the validity of the said regulation. The High Court held that the Corporation had no power to alter the terms and conditions of service of its employees and that the Corporation could not alter the terms of its employees without the prior approval of the Central Government. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Corporation being a statutory corporation constituted under the Life Insurance Corporations Act, 1956, it is bound by the provisions of that Act. It cannot act arbitrarily or at will in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. [766C] 2. The Corporation can regulate its employees by making appropriate regulations in that behalf. [767D] 3. The Corporation cannot reduce the remuneration payable to its employees by way of compensation. The Corporation must pay compensation equivalent to the amount of wages which the employees would have been deprived of if they were paid their salaries. The Corporation may also pay to its employees such compensation as it deems fit. [768E F] 4. The Corporation having been given the right to alter the conditions of service, it is not open to the Corporation to reduce the same. [769A] 5. The Corporation, therefore, cannot alter the terms & conditions of service without the prior permission of the Central Govt. [770B
2966: The appellant, a company engaged in the manufacture of cloth, manufactured by it and sold its products to various dealers. In respect of the assessment years 1959 60 and 1960 61, the assessing authority levied tax on the turnover of cloth at the rate of 3 pies per rupee under section 3A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The appellant contended that the cloth manufactured by it was not "mills" within the meaning of the expression in the notification dated June 8, 1959 issued under section 3 A of the U P. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1963. The High Court held that cloth manufactured by means of power looms could not fall under the term "mills". The High Court also held that the word "mills", as used in the notification, must be understood according to the common understanding of mankind. On appeal by special leave, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that cloth manufactured and sold by the appellant was not "meetings" within the definition of "mills ". [839 E] The word "mason" is defined in section 2(a) of the Usurious Constitution of India and includes all forms of work such as making, preparing, repairing, altering, ornamenting, finishing, packing or otherwise processing, treating or adapting any goods; and so, the word "ma chin" would mean "an article which is made from a nuts or bolts or other material for the purpose of making them suitable for use as a whole. [840 F G] The word 'mason' has been used in the definition of a "mason". It is not necessary that the word 'masses ' should have been used in a particular sense. It may well be that the word may be used in one sense or another depending upon the context in which it is used in the statute. But if the word 'Mchandin ' is given a wider meaning than the word 'ma chin ', then the same meaning can be assigned to it in the context in the statute in which it occurs. [841 B C] The word used in the Notification is "masonry" and not "masonic". [842 D
3545: The appellants were members of the Civil Defence Establishments in the Defence Establishment of the Defence establishment. They filed a writ petition in the High Court to impugn the authority of the Commandants (Respondents and 3 herein) in declaring the Unions, represented by the appellants as unlawful association. The High Court dismissed their writ petition holding that the impugned action was violative of their fundamental right to form associations or unions conferred by article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned notification was ultra vires the and was struck by articles 19(1) (c) and 33 of the Constitution, and that the impugned notifications were invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 19(1), (a) and (b) of the constitution confer upon the President the power to promulgate rules for the peace, order and good government of the civil defence establishments. [560C] 2. The object of the impugned notification is to enable the Government to regulate the relations between the civil defence organizations and the civil defence organisations with respect to the matters specified therein. It is not necessary that the civil defence organisation should be an integral part of the civil service. [552B] 3. The impugned notification is not ultra vires the Constitution. [553E] 4. The impugned notifications are valid. [554F] 5. The impugned Notification is not ultra virus the Constitution. The impugned Notifications are ultra vires the provisions of article 19(i)(c). [554G]
2272: The respondent Club was granted a licence to hold racemeetings at both the courses and for which it paid a sum of Rs. 22 lacs as licence fee. The appellant Corporation sanctioned the said licence on June 1, 1954. The respondent Club thereupon filed an appeal before the Small Cause Court under section 217 of the Act against the assessment made by the Municipal Corporation. The respondent claimed that the said amount should be allowed as a deduction in computing the gross annual rent and deducting therefrom the percent deduction allowable under section 154(1) of the Act. The appellant contended that the said sum should be allowed in computing the net annual rent and deducted therefrom the percentage deduction allowable under s.154(1)(b) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1949. The Small Cause Court rejected the contention holding that the said payment was not a tax but only a fee. On appeal the High Court held that the amount of licence fee was a tax and not a fee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court erred in holding that the amount was a tax. [1301 B] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that a fee is a charge for a special service rendered to the citizens or persons who are entitled to it. [1302 D] (iii) The High Courts were wrong in holding the amount of the licence fee to be a tax. The High Court had no jurisdiction to decide whether the licence fees were a tax or a fee. [1303 C D] (iv) The High courts were wrong in thinking that the licence fees could not be treated as a tax because they did not provide for any particular method of rating out of the several well known methods generally followed in such assessments. [1304 E F]
1089: The appellants were the Managing Agents of a company which was a partnership firm. They were appointed managing agents for 20 years and were assessed to income tax on the basis that their gross total profits exceeded Rs. 1,000 per annum. The Income Tax Officer took into account the commission paid by the firm to its employees and held that the remuneration received by them was not taxable in the hands of the firm. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer but the Tribunal held that the commission paid to the appellants was not taxable as they had been employed for the purpose of earning profits and therefore could not be included in the assessable income of the firm for the purposes of the Excess Profits Tax Act. On reference the High Court held that the income from the agency business was not liable to be taxed in the hands or the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the provisions of r. 9, section 1, were properly applied in the case of the appellants and (ii) the Income Tax officer was right in taking action under section 34 and 15 of the Act against the appellants. HELD : (i) The provisions of rr. 9, 9A and 10 are not applicable to the facts of the present case. Under r. 9(1), the assessee is entitled to deduct the whole of the amount of commission paid to him by the firm during the year of account. If the amount is deducted out of the profits of the firm, the amount will be treated as the income of the assessee. [411 B C] (ii) The provisions relating to deduction of commission are contained in the Act itself. Section 2(6) of the Act defines "gross total income" to mean the total income computed under the Act. It is clear from the definition that the gross total income means the total income minus the sum payable under the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The Act does not define the expression "gross income" nor does it provide for any deductions from the gross totals. The Act only provides for deductions in respect of certain items of income. The Act also does not contain any provision for deducting the commission paid under the Act from the gross receipts.
3779: The appellant, a firm carrying on business in the Punjab, carried on business in various branches of the Punjab State. In its return for the assessment year 1957 67, the assessing authority held that the appellant was liable to pay tax under section 3 of the Punjab Professions, Trades, Callings and Employments Taxation Act, 1956, as it had been carrying on business within the State of Punjab. On appeal, the appellate authority held that though the appellant was not carrying on any profession or calling, trade or occupation within the State, it was not liable to pay any tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court, in revision, reversed this decision of the appellate authority. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: (i) The definition of "total gross income" in section 2(b) of the Punjab Act is wide enough to include all income made within the State. [866 G] (ii) The word "total" has been used in the Act with reference to the nature of the business carried on by the appellant. It does not exclude from its purview the activities which are carried on by others. The word "business" is defined in section 2 (c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as meaning "any business, profession or vocation". [867 B D] (iii) The word 'business' in section 2 of the Act includes every activity undertaken by one person in relation to any business, profession, vocation or business. [868 A] (iv) The word business means an adventure in the nature of trade, whether it be a profession or vocabulary. It does neither include any activity carried on by one person on behalf of another. [869 E] (v) The word profession must have the same connotation as the word "trade", and the expression "commercial establishment" must mean a place where persons engage themselves in trade. [870 F] (vi) The word commercial is also defined in section 3(2) of the Finance Act, 1956. The word business is defined in clause (d) of section 2 of that Act as including any business of rendering services in connection with the business of
1567: The appellant, who was the owner of a building in Delhi, let it to the respondent No. 1 for his residential purposes. The respondent No. 2, the father of the appellant, filed an application before the Rent Control Tribunal for the eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had come to know that the last owner, the father had let the building to the appellant for his residential purpose and that the case should proceed further with the eviction petition. The appellant contended that the premises had been let out by the father of respondent No. I to the appellant as a tenant and that the rent receipts were issued by the father to the appellant. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the relationship of landlord and tenant had been established on the basis of certain rent receipts granted by the respondents to the appellant and that the appellant had failed to make the payment or deposit as required by section 15(7) of the Act. The appeal filed against the order of the Rent Controller was also dismissed by the Additional Rent Controller. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant challenging the orders of the Rent Control Tribunals dismissing the appellant 's application under section 15(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of the Additional Rent Control Tribunal dismissing the appellant's appeal against the order dated March 6, 1962 of the Rent Controllers, Delhi, is not final between the parties. [639 E] (ii) The order passed by the Rent Control Tribu nal dismissing the appellant from the eviction petition cannot be said to be without jurisdiction. It is only if the order is set aside that the appellate authority can exercise its power under section 15 of the Act and pass appropriate orders. [640 F G] (iii) The order made by the Rent Controller dismissing the appellant "as not maintainable" does not operate as res judicata. [641 A B]
932: The appellant, a resident of the village in which an additional police force was stationed, was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed an appeal before the High Court challenging his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the notification issued by the State Government under section 15(1) of the Act did not specify the area in which the additional police force should be posted. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the notification issued under section 15 of the Act was ultra vires the powers of the Rajpramukh as he had no power to do so; (ii) the notification was invalid because it contravened the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution; (iii) the notification could not have been made by the Rajpuram District Magistrate without the consent of the Rajapramukh; (iv) the notification having been issued under section 5 of the Act, the Rajpraman Committee could not have acted upon it; (v) the notification being bad because it was issued under section 6 of the Act it was invalid; (vi) the notification dated March 21, 1968 was illegal since it was issued after the Rajparaj Committee had given its opinion on the question whether the Rajpraju and Muslims were liable to bear any portion of the cost of the additional police. HELD: (i) The notification was valid. [224 E] (ii) The notification is valid. [223 F] (iii) The notification does not make any provision for the posting of additional police force. It merely makes a reference to the Rajprakash Committee. It cannot therefore be said that the Rajprathar Samiti has not properly dealt with the matter. [225 G]
1090: The appellant was employed as a casual labour in the respondent 's factory at Bombay. It applied for leave to its employees on certain conditions, but it refused to do so. On the question whether the appellant could grant such leave under s.79 of the Act, HELD: (i) Section 79(1) is not intended to lay down any general rule or standardisation of leave with respect to existing laws and rules. It only provides that the employer may grant leave to an employee if he has sufficient number of days of work in a year. [306 D] (ii) In order to be entitled to earned leave the employee must have been in service for more than three years before he can claim the benefit of the Act. If he had worked for more than 240 days in a year he would have earned leave admissible to him under the provisions of the Act and would have been entitled to avail himself of the leave available to him under section 79(1). [307 B C] (iii) The provision made by the award in regard to privilege leave does not make any distinction between the existing law and the existing law. It merely lays down the principle of classification which is based on intelligible differentia having a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act. [308 E F]
3489: The respondent was a displaced person from East Pakistan. He applied to the Estate Officer for reducing the licence fee payable by him and demanded arrears of licence fee. The Estate Officer passed an order under section 7(1) of the . The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order against him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since section 7 did not put a time limit for taking steps under that section, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since section7 did not put any time limit for the recovery of arrears of rent, the High court could not have entertained the writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD: (i) Section 7 does not put a period limit for the exercise of the power of revision by the Estate Officer. It is only when the Estate officer has made an order under that section that the limitation prescribed for a suit to recover the amount shall be computed according to the provisions of section 7. [892 B] (ii) The expression "any person" in section 7 means a person who is or has at any time been in unauthorised occupation of any public premises. The expression "person" in section 2(g) includes a company or other body corporate. The expression 'person ' in section 7 includes a company as well as a firm. [893 C D] (iii) The expression 'tenant ' in section 2 (g) includes an agent or a servant acting on his behalf. The word 'occupy ' in section 3(h) means a person in possession of a building or part of a building. The word "occupy" in section 3 (h) means the right to occupy a building or a part of a buildings. [894 E F] (iv) The expression in section 7(l)(a) means a tenant in occupation of a building after the determination of his tenancy. [895 G] (v) The expression used in section 7 is not intended to cover a case where the tenant is in occupation of the building after the termination of his tenancy but is in occupation after the determination. [896 A B] (vi) The expression is not confined to a person
6954: The Peerless Company filed a writ petition in the Calcutta High Court for a declaration that the Prize Chits Banning Act did not apply to the business carried on by the Peerless. A Division Bench of the High Court dismissed both the writ petitions but appeals preferred by the Reserve Bank of India, the Union of India and the State of West Bengal were allowed by a Division Bench of that High Court. Against the judgment of the Division Bench of Calcutta High Court, the Reserve Bank filed an appeal before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD : 1. The provisions of the Prize Chit Fund Act, 1972 are not applicable to the business of the Peer Companies. [7A] 2. Section 2(e) does not contemplate a scheme without a prize and, therefore, the Endowment Certificate Scheme of the Panth Credit Company was outside the PrizeChits Banning act. [7B] 3. The Prize Chita Scheme is a scheme which provides for the payment of interest at the rate of 8% compound per annum from the date of maturity of the certificates. It is not possible to find out whether the amounts invested are in accordance with the directions given at any given point of time when there are thousands of certificates with different and varying maturity periods. If they do not, it would be impossible to find out and verify whether the amounts deposited are in accordance or not with the directions at any given time during the period. [7C D] 4. The Pritis Curiae submitted that the Priti Chits Act does not provide for any scheme other than those mentioned in the Prize chits Act. The Priti Chit Fund Act does not contain any provision for payment of interest on the amount invested by the Pent Chits. The Pritish Cyprarian Fund Act does nothing more than providing for the payment to the depositors of the Pritis Cyprous Chits Fund. The Priida Chits Act has been enacted to provide for the establishment of a fund called the Pritis Chits Fund and for the administration thereof. The Pritisation Chits Act is a special legislation dealing with the subject matter of the Priti Chit Fund. The Act is a general enactment dealing with the matters relating to the
6018: The respondent was a Sub Divisional Officer (Civil) in the State of Gujarat. He was transferred to the Gujarat Electricity Board on his own request and he joined the service of the Board on May 27, 1974. On July 28, 1974, he was served with an order of discharge from service under Regulation 113 of the Gujarat Electricity Supply Code, 1948. The respondent challenged the validity of the said order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed but it allowed the respondent 's appeal. In the meanwhile, the respondent had been promoted as Assistant Engineer in the year 1975. The respondent filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the order of his transfer. The Single Judge of the High Court quashed the order of transfer on the ground that the respondent could not be treated as a member of the Board for the purpose of promotion to the higher post. The Division Bench held that no warning as contemplated by service Regulation No. 113 was issued to the respondent nor he had been afforded any opportunity of showing cause before terminating his services. The respondent appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of Assistant Engineer in accordance with the relevant rules and regulations governing the conditions of service of the employees of the Board. [812E] 1.2 The respondent was relieved from his duties at Surat on 30th March, 1974 but he did not join at Ukai till the impugned order of discharge was passed. The respondent lost his service as he refused to comply with the order of discharge. He was relieved from the duties at Surat without giving him any notice or opportunity of showing cau se. Therefore, the order of termination was null and void being contrary to service Regulation No, 113. [813B C] 1.3 The respondent was not entitled to be treated as member of the board for the purpose for which he was appointed. [814D] 1.4 The respondent was given an opportunity of showing c ompassion and if he so desired, he should have been heard before passing the order of dismissal. [815F] 1.5 The respondent was also entitled to be heard before the order of removal was passed. [816G]
347: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal on the ground that he had no opportunity of showing cause against his conviction but nobody could show cause against his acquittal. The High Court held that the appellant had not been given an opportunity of showing any cause against his sentence, and therefore, the judgment of the lower court merges in the judgment of his High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court had no power to enhance the sentence; (ii) the High Courts ' decision was wrong because the High Court did not give a hearing to the appellant before enhancing the sentence, and (iii) the High court had no jurisdiction to enhance the sentences. HELD : (1) The High Court has no power to interfere with the order of the Sessions Judge or the High Court. It is only when the High Court comes to the conclusion that the sentence should be enhanced or enhanced that the High Court can exercise its revisional powers suo motu. [1019 D] (2) The High Courts' decisions are based on the principle that the accused person must have an opportunity of seeing the witnesses who may be produced at the trial and that right cannot be denied to him unless he is given an opportunity to do so. If the accused person does not avail himself of the opportunity given to him, the Court will not be able to take action under section 423,428 or 428A of the Code. [1018 F H]
4904: The appellant was a tenant of the respondents in respect of a shop. He had obtained a decree for possession against the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 14(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had committed default in payment of rent. The appellant contested the application contending that the respondent had not obtained any benefit under section 15(1) of the Act. The Controller dismissed the application holding that the proviso to section 14(1) did not apply to the case because the appellant had not obtained a benefit under section 14 C. The High Court held that the proviso could have no application to the instant case because, in the first ejectment proceeding which was filed by the respondent against the appellant, the latter had not obtained such benefit once in one; and, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to invoke the provisions of section 15(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proviso was applicable only if the tenant had made a default in the payment of rent and the order passed by the Controller under section 15 was not passed against him. HELD: The proviso to section14(2) is not attracted to the instant suit as the appellant had complied with the order passed under section 15. [393C] The proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 does not apply to cases where the tenant has not obtained a relief under that provision. It applies only where the tenant makes a default in paying rent. The proviso cannot be invoked to defeat the claim of the landlord for possession. [394E] The proviso must be read along with the main section. If the tenant makes default in payment or deposit as required by section 15(l), he would be liable to eviction. [395A] The proviso is not intended to cover cases where the landlord has not given a notice to quit to the tenant but has merely asked for permission to withdraw from the ejectment application. [396B] The proviso cannot apply to cases wherein the tenant has failed to pay or deposit the arrears of rent within the time stipulated by the proviso. [397D] The proviso can have no application where the tenant
3961: The respondent was appointed as a Sub Inspector of Police in 1955. He was discharged from service on July 13, 1957. On March 13, 1957, an enquiry had been made against him and the order terminating his services was passed as a simple order of termination in order to avoid a departmental enquiry under section 7 of the Police Act. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the order dated January 21, was illegal and void and that he continued as Sub Inspector of police in the Uttar Pradesh Police Service. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the order of dismissal was not vitiated by mala fides. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal is not a mere discharge simpliciter but it is one of dismissal simpliciter. It is only when the order is based upon some misconduct or gross negligence in the matter of discharge of duty, then it can be said to be punitive in nature. [1109 D] (ii)The order of termination of the respondent 's services was not founded on any misconduct or misdemeanour but was merely an order of dismissal. This being so, the order was clearly bad in law. [1107 F] (iii)The order was not one of dismissal because the respondent was found guilty of misconduct or negligence in the discharge of his duties. The order was therefore liable to be set aside. [1108 A B] (iv)It was open to the authority to terminate the respondent ' s service on the ground of misconduct or mis-conduct if it proposed to terminate the services of the respondent. But the order was not made in the background of the allegations against the respondent regarding his behaviour with Smt. Phoolmati. [1106 C] (v)In the present case, the order of termination was not made on the ground that the respondent was guilty of misconduct, nor was there any allegation that the respondent had committed any act of misconduct. [1105 E]
5665: The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellant for the supply of certain medicinal shebs. The last one was on 30th May, 1971. Between 29th May, 1972 to 19th June, 1972, the respondent accepted the four final bills and gave no claim declaration in respect of the four contracts. On 13th December, 1976, an application was filed by the respondent in the Court of Civil Judge, Allahabad, for appointment of an Arbitrator under section 20 of the (hereinafter called `the Act '). That application was dismissed as being barred by limitation. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the application was barred by limitation and directed the District Judge to refer the disputes to an arbitrator. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in dismissing the application of the appellants. [411C] 2.1 The second appellant had purchased from the Himachal Pradesh Government the right to extract and collect certain medicinal shebbs from the forests of Chamba District. On June 22, 1972, an application for filing an arbitration agreement was governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and since the period of three years prescribed thereby commenced to run from the date on which the differences arose between the parties from the month of September, 1950, the application of that period was not barred by limitation, and consequently, the application was rightly rejected. [412E F] 3.1 The question whether an application under section 20 is within time or not must be decided on its own merits. If the application is found to be barred by limitation it would be open to the court to direct the arbitrator to make an award. But if the application is held to be barred, the court cannot direct the arbitrator who has made the award to make an Award. [413F G] 4.1 The Judicial Commissioner was in error in rejecting the application of an application under Section 20 of the Act. [414B]
3897: The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the respondents on the ground of personal necessity. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants were not entitled to a decree of ejectment because the landlord required the house for his personal necessity and, therefore, the eviction was ordered. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the appellants had failed to prove reasonable requirement and the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court. 59: The petitioner, a shareholder of the respondent Bank, filed a suit for recovery of certain amounts due to it from the petitioner. The petitioner contended that the Bank was not entitled to recover any amount as the petitioner had no legal right to recover the same and that the action taken by the Bank in respect of the said amount was ultra vires. Held, that the Bank could not be regarded as a 'person ' within the meaning of article 19(1)(f) and (g), and that the petitioner 's action was not one for enforcement of his fundamental rights under article 19(i)(f). The petitioner 's right to enforce the fundamental rights conferred on him by article 19(I)(f) was not an absolute right but only a statutory right. The right to enforce a particular right cannot be equated with the right to enforce an existing legal right or liability. The right of the petitioner to enforce a legal right or to enforce a contractual right or liability is not an absolute one. The right can be enforced only by a person who has a legal right to enforce it. A person cannot be said to have a legal right merely because he has a legal duty to do so. The right must be exercised by the person or persons in whom they are interested, legally competent to take the action and at the proper time they are entitled to exercise their legal rights. The right may be exercised where some other person has a legal interest in the subject matter of the dispute. But the right given to a person to enforce a right against another person is not a right to relief unless there is a clear infringement of such right. The remedy under article 32 is discretionary and the petitioner ' s right to claim relief should not be confused with the right of a citizen to enforce private rights arising out of civil liberties. The right given to the petitioner to obtain relief against the Bank is not a personal right but a public law remedy which does not confer a special statutory right upon the petitioner. It is a right to seek relief against the bank which is not a party to the proceedings before the High Court. The right is not a mere statutory right; it is a substantive right and the petitioner has no such right. He cannot invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of a right

1201: The appellants were the owners of village Timmapet. The respondent granted a lease to the appellants for a period of 20 years on a fixed sum of Rs. 1027 10 0 per year. [623 G] (ii) The grant was not an assignment of a permanent lease. It was a bilam kharab or a bilama. It did not create any title in favour of the ancestors of the appellants. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was the heir of Naubat Singh deceased and was in occupation of the disputed shop after the death of Naubata Singh. The Rent Control and Eviction Officer rejected the application holding that the appellant had been living with the deceased Naubat singh since the date of his death and that he had been helping the deceased Naushad Singh in his business s from the date of the death of his father. The appeal preferred by the appellant against the order of the Rent Control and eviction officer was dismissed by the Appellate Authority. The High Court held that the benefit of amended section 14 as it stood prior to its amendment by the U. P. Act No. 13 of 1972 would be available to the appellant only when he was living in the premises with the consent of the landlord provided that no proceedings for his eviction were pending. In this appeal, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the right of the heirs of the deceased tenant to get the protection of section 14 as amended by the U P Act No.13 of 1972 was not available to the heirs of Naubot Singh deceased because the deceased tenant had died before the commencement of the Act and that the provisions of section 14 were applicable to the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right of the heir of the deceased landlord to get the benefit of section 14 is not available to him merely because the deceased landlord had died before commencement of the U P. Act. [704B] 1.2 The right of a person to get the benefits of section 14 cannot be denied unless the context otherwise requires. It must also be shown that the deceased landlord was in possession of the disputed property immediately before the commencement o f the Act and had become entitled to get the tenancy rights under section 14. [705C D] 1.3 The right of an heir to get the status of a tenant
3872: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. He claimed to be a occupant within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Bhopal Act of 1932. The respondent applied for mutation of his name as a Bhumiswami under section 185 of the Bhopal Land Revenue Code, 1932. The Tahsildar by his order dated 24th June 1963 directed Khushi Lal to deposit compensation equivalent to 15 times of the land revenue on the payment of which his name was to be recorded as a Bhumidar of the holdings. The first respondent filed an appeal before the Sub Divisional officer against the said order. The Sub Divisional officer held that the appellant was not an occupant and the first respondent was not a Shikmi under the Bhopal Act. The respondent filed a revision before the Commissioner who remanded the case to the Tehsildar for enquiry into the matter. The Tehsildar held that the first respondent had no right to receive the compensation. The respondent 's revision petition was dismissed by the Commissioner. The respondent then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the orders of the authorities below. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant being an occupant under the Bhopal State, was not an occupancy tenant under section 2(14) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The first part of the definition of "occupant" given in sub section (1) of section 2 includes a person in whose favour the right to receive land revenue has either been assigned or relinquished will be required to pay to the Government land revenue or rent. [585E] 2. The expression "occupant", in section 2(16), means a person in whom the right to hold land is vested. It does not include a person in possession of land direct from Government. [584F] 3. The expression 'occupant ' in section 2 (16) means a person who holds land direct from the Government. [590B] 4. The expression in section 2 is not defined in the Bhopal Act but it is well settled that the word "occupant " in section 2 includes persons in whom title vests. [592C D] 5. The expression owner in section 2 means a person to whom land revenue has been assigned.
3786: The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in the State of Manipur on 1 January 1911. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. After the Government of India took over the administration of Manipur, he was appointed as the Judge of that subordinate court with effect from 25 Januar y, 1965. On the enactment of Manipur Court Act 1955, the Court of Subordinate Judge was abolished and the appellant was appointed to that post with effect from 5 October 1949. In the meantime, the appellant was served with a notice dated 30 June 1966 by the Chief Commissioner of Manipur to show cause why he should not be compulsorily retired under Fundamental Rule 56(J) of the Fundamental Rules. The appellant replied to the same denying the allegations made against him. The Chief Commissioner after considering the explanation of the appellant passed an order retiring him from service with effect from 1 October 1966. The appellant challenged the order of compulsory retirement before the Judicial Commissioner who dismissed the writ petition of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. The main contention of the appellant was that the impugned order of compulsory retirem ent was null and void because the Fundamental Rule 56 at the material time contained no reservation of any powers in the appointing authority to retire a Government servant after he had attained the age of 55 years on three months notice without assigning any reason. The appellant also contended that the impugned orders were illegal because they were passed in violation of the Fundamental Rule 57. Held: (i) The power conferred on the appropriate authority to retire an employee after he has completed 50 years' qualifying service is absolute and unfettered. It is open to the appropriate authority or the appropriate government to consider the entire record of service and overall performance of the public service and determine if it feels satisfied that it is in the public interest to retain the officer in its custody. There can therefore be no doubt that the power conferred on it is in public interest to do so. [47 F] (ii)The power to retire an officer compulsorily from service is a power which is exercised for public good and generally for maintaining efficiency in the service. The exercise of the power must be based on some rational principle applicable alike to all cases and it cannot be allowed to be tinkered lightly
6138: The Bombay Municipal Corporation, the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 416 of 1972 and the appellant in C.A. No. 417 of 1972, were candidates for admission to M.D. By the impugned judgment, the High Court allowed the writ petitions filed by the respondents and struck down the impugned rule 4(A) in whole and rule 5 (wrongly stated as rule 6 in the High Court judgment), in whole and Rule 5 (would be read with Rule 6 in the impugned notification dated June 18, 1973. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned rule is discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it provides for collegewise institutional preference for admission to the Government Medical College both the rules providing for college wise institutional preference and the impugned rule has been made arbitrarily without any reasonable basis and that the impugned provision is discriminatory and therefore unconstitutional. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1. The impugned rule is not discriminatory or unreasonable. It is a valid piece of legislation. [766C] 1.2. The impugned Rule 4(A)(i) in whole is discriminatory and violates Article 14 of t he Constitution. [767E] 1.3. The impugned provision is not discriminatory but is only a measure of protection provided by the impugned rule. It is not discriminatory. [768F] 1.4. The impugned clause in the impugned rule does not offend Article 14 of th e Constitution. [776G] 1.5. The impugned section is not discriminatory because it seeks to provide for collegewise admissions in all medical colleges. The impugned provisions are not discriminatory because they do not affect the students who pass their final MBBS examination from the colleges situated within the jurisdiction of the same university. [777H; 778A B] 1.6. The impugned Section is not discriminatory since it merely provides for college wise admissions in all the medical colleges. [778B] 1.7. The impugned proviso to sub-section (1) of section 33A of the Act is not discriminatory and is not violative of Article 19(1)(g). [779C] 1.(a) The impugned proviso is not discriminatory nor is
1045: The appellant, a recognised association of oilseeds, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale and purchase of groundnuts. The agreement provided that the appellant should sell oil to the respondent at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per acre per annum. The respondent made an application to the Bombay City Civil Court under section 8 of the , for setting aside the award on the ground that forward contracts in groundnuts were illegal as the making of such contracts was prohibited by the Oilseeds (Forward Contract Prohibition) Order, 1943, issued under the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, and hence the arbitration clause contained in it was null and void. The appellant contended that the contract in groundnut was not in terms of the Act but was in fact in terms of bye laws of the Bombay State and that the arbitration clause therein did not apply to the forward contracts in question. Held, that the contract was not in law invalid because it was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The contract in ground nuts was not in contravention of the provisions of section 8 of Act X of 1946, and therefore, the arbitration clause in the forward contract in ground 'nuts was not valid.
6183: The appellants filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 15,40,000/ with interest and costs against the respondents. The respondents pleaded that the depositions were not signed by the witnesses as required by Rule 4 of Chapter XXII of the Calcutta High Court Rules, 1914. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the depos itions were not proved in accordance with law. The first appellate court reversed the judgment of the trial court and decreed the suit. In second appeal, the High Court held that the deposition of each witness was not taken on record and therefore, it could not be relied upon. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The requirement of Rule 4 of Order XVIII of the Code of Civil Procedure is mandatory and not directory. [412E] 1.2. The object of Rule 4 is to enable the Courts to decide cases in which they have been recorded without taking into account any evidence or documents produced before them. It is only when the Court comes to the conclusion that the evidence or document s are not admissible that the Court can take such view. [413F G] 1.3. The object behind Rule 4 is that the Courts should not allow their own statements to fall back upon for the purpose of contradicting the parties. [414A] 1.4. The object is to ensure that the party who has made a statement under Rule 4 of the Rules of procedure is not permitted to make a false statement. [415B] 1.5. The rule does not require that the Court must examine the deponent of the affidavit in his defence to find out whether he had actually seen the deponent. If the deponent is not examined, the question of examining him does not arise. [416C] 1.6. The object underlying Rule 4 is not to fill up the lacuna but to remove the defect. [417D] 1.7. The object and purpose of Rule 4 being to prevent the parties from making false statements at the time of recording of their evidence, the Court may permit the same. [418G] 1.8. The object appears to be to avoid unnecessary delays in disposal of cases. [419H; 420A] 1
231: The plaintiff and the defendants were members of a joint Hindu family. They acquired properties in the hands of their father, who was a member of a Kulkarni family. The plaintiff 's case that these properties were ancestral, or were acquired with the aid of joint family funds was not established. The trial Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to a half share in section Nos. 639 and 640 on the ground that they belonged exclusively to the family as ancestral properties; but the High Court held that had not been established. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the plaintiff had failed to discharge the burden which lay on him of establishing that the acquisitions were made without the aid of the joint family funds. HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence from which it could be held that the joint family property was acquired by members of the family. [641 B] (2) The plaintiff was entitled under the decision of the Privy Council in Anant Bhikappa Patil (Minor) vs Shankar Ramchandra Patil(1), to claim a half share on the ground of his being an adopted son. [642 C] (3) The plaintiff had failed in proving that the properties were acquired by members living in the family. The fact that the properties are acquired by members residing in the family is not conclusive proof of the fact that they were acquired by the members of the joint families. [643 D] (4) The High court was right in holding that in the absence of a title deed showing that the sites were acquired by persons living in the joint family, the plaintiff could lay no claim to them. [644 E]
5358: The petitioners in these petitions challenge the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court of Calcutta dismissing their writ petition. The petitioners were appointed as Chairman, Vice Chair man and Administrative Member of the Administrative Tribunal by the Central Government under section 3(1) of the . The petitioners challenged the appointment of the Chairman, Vice Chairman and Administrative Members of the Administrative Tribu nal on the ground that they did not possess the requisite experience of 5 years as a Judge of the High court to be appointed as Chairman of the Administrative Tribunals. The petitioners also contended that the appointments made to the post of Vice Chair pearers should be set aside because of the fact that they had been appointed as Chairman and Vice Chair men and administrative members of the AdministrativeTribunals. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The observations made by the Supreme Court in the case of the petitioners are not binding upon the High Courts. [766A] 2. The observations of the Supreme Court have no bearing on the question whether the High Court has power to appoint a person who is qualified to be a Judge of a High Court or to appoint a retired Judge of the Supreme court. [767B] 3. The observations cannot be read as an obiter dicta. They must be read in the context of the facts of each particular case. In the present cases, the petitioners have not been able to show any such rule which would enable them to claim the benefit of the observation of the Supreme Cour t. [768C D] 4. The observations in the case are not binding on the High Courts but only on the Supreme Court. [769D] 5. The observations are not intended to lay down any general proposition of law. It is for the appropriate authority to decide what is best for it. [770E] 6. The observations do not touch upon the question of equivalence of judicial opinion. [771F] 7. The observations have no bearing whatsoever on the question of the equation of the Judges of the High Courts in the matter of appointment of Judges to the Administrative Tribunals and the High Courts, and the same are not binding. [772G]
6070: The appellant, an Indian company entered into a memorandum of understanding with a Norwegian company at Paris. Under that agreement the Norwegians were to provide technical know how and technical services including facilities for the training of personnel, to the appellant in connection with the manufacture of computers. Eighty five per cent of the consideration was to be paid from credit provided by the Norwagian authorities and the balance fifteen per cent was to be made available by the State Bank of India, London Branch. The appellant applied to the Commissioner of Income Tax for a direction to the Income tax Officer, but the Commissioner refused to do so on the ground that the appellant had not been able to furnish any evidence to show that it had been engaged in the business of providing technical know how or technical services. The appellant filed a Writ Petition challenging the constitutional validity of section 9(1)(vii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that having regard to the provisions of section 9 (1)(vii), the payment constituted income which was deemed to accrue or arise in India and was liable to deduction of tax at source. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 9(i)(vii) is ultra vires inasmuch as it enables the levy of income tax on the Norwesegian company in the one case and the American company in the other in circumstances which appear to show that the statute operates extra territorially without the need for any nexus between anything done in India and the person sought to be taxed. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "profits" has not been defined under the Income Tax law. It means profits arising out of sale, exchange or transfer of capital assets. [999C] 2. Section 9(1) (vii) of Income Tax Act is intra vires the Constitution. It is a provision enabling the levy of tax on the income of the assessee. It is not a provision for imposing a charge on the income. It is only a machinery for collecting the tax payable by the assessee. [996D] 3. The word 'profit ' has not been used in the Income Tax Law. It is used in the sense of profit
3853: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed his appeal on the ground that he had been acquitted by the trial court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witness Hari Singh, P.W. 1 who saw the accused running away after the incident was not reliable as he did not know the name of the assailant. It was further submitted that the other injured witnesses were not examined by the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The conviction is based solely on the testimony of the eye-witness Hari Singh, PW 1 who saw him in the murder case. The evidence of the witness Hari Singh was not corroborated by any independent source. The evidence was not reliable. [801 G] (2) The evidence of PW 1 was not reliable because he was a close relative of the deceased. His presence at the time of occurrence cannot be doubted. The fact that he was one of the assailants does not affect the credibility of the evidence of PW 2. [802 B C] (3) The evidence given by PW 2 was not reliable and the conviction was based only on the testimony given by him. [803 A B]
4749: The petitioner was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and retired from service on 31st January, 1981. He had been drawing salary in the pay scale of Rs. 1200-2040. In the year 1983, he was granted leave without allowance for a period of one month. On February 2, 1983, the Union of India in the Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs addressed to the Registrar General of India requesting him to sanction cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at his credit subject to the ceiling of five months. The Accountant General of Madhya Pradesh informed the petitioner that he was entitled to payment of cash equivalent of the leave salary in case of leave on full allowances as defined in section 3 and 9 (1) of the Act. The AccountantGeneral of Madhya Pradesh by letter dated March 25, 1983 intimated the petitioner that the maximum limit of five months mentioned in section 5(3) of the , would be applicable. The petitioner 's representation against this was rejected by the Government. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid letter of the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Central Government had no power under section 5A of the Act to grant cash equivalent of unutilised leave due on the date of retirement. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Central Government has no power under Section 5A of The Act to grant leave on full allowance. [856 F] 2.1 The Central Government is not bound to sanction the cash equivalent of any leave salary in the case of leave with allowances of any kind. It is open to the Central Government to refuse to sanction the leave salary if it is satisfied that the leave was taken voluntarily or otherwise. If the Central Government decides to sanction the encashment of the leave on the ground of voluntary retirement, the Central Government will have to take into account all relevant facts including the reasons for such decision. [857 G H; 858 A B] 2.2 The Central Government cannot refuse to sanction leave on the grounds specified in section 5A(1)(a). The Central Government can refuse to sanction a leave on the basis of the reasons stated in section 5B(1).
1550: The appellant was convicted under section 463 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the court. She filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed her appeal on the ground that she did not know of the existence of a case against her husband, and that she had no knowledge about it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the word "fraudulently" in section 464 of the Indian penal Code must be construed as meaning that the person who has done the act with intent to defraud is guilty of cheating; (ii) the appellant could not be found guilty of forgery unless she had the intention to cause injury to the insurance company and as in the present case the appellant had never had the intention of causing injury to the company, and (iii) the appellant 's conviction under sections 463 and 464 of I.P.C. was not sustainable because the appellant had not signed the proposal form as required by law. [589 F] (2) The word 'fraudulously' in section 465 of the Indian, Penal Code does not mean that the person should have some dishonest intention at the time when he signed the proposal. It only means that the deceitful design is to be proved either by direct evidence or by conduct. [590 B C] (3) The word is used in criminal jurisprudence to give every person, who is guilty of any crime, a right to sue until he is absolved from liability. But it does not mean merely that he will be liable for the acts done by others. He may be made liable even if he has acted fraudulently or with impunity. It is an agreement between two or more persons to do one thing with which they areCC jointly concerned, or to do a particular act which may or may not be final or invalid at the time of doing of act. It may be partly lawful and authority over other persons does not become unlawful. But it

3182: The appellant was the owner of a shop in suit. She let out the premises to the respondent on a rent of Rs. 125/ per month. On September 10, 1962 the respondent applied under section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for evicting the appellant on the ground that she had sub letting the entire premises to one Sohan Singh who was running a business under the name of Royal Dispensing Chemists and Druggists in the shop. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was the legally wedded wife of Sohan Singh and that she was entitled to possession of the shop premises as a tenant. The appeal filed by the respondent against the order of eviction was dismissed by the Rent Controller. In second appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of section 14 of Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent 's status as wife was not established. It was further contended that the appellant had sub let the entire premises and the sub tenancy had been terminated by the landlord 's notice dated November 30, 1962. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant was a wife or a husband is a mixed question of fact and law which can be decided only by the trial court. [641 B] (2) The High Court has rightly held that the question whether the respondent was the wife of Sohail Singh could not have been decided by the Rent Controllers. The finding of the courts below that the appellant 's wife was the wife is based on evidence and cannot be said to be perverse. [642 C D] (3) The High court was right in holding that the appellant could not be said to have sub let the whole premises to Sohan Singh. [643 E] (4) The High 'Court was right in its conclusion that the appellant being the wife of the respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 14. [644 A] (5) The High Courts decision was correct. [646 F]
1255: The appellant was the owner of a private forest in Bihar. He had obtained a permit from the forest authorities for felling of trees and for removing timber from the forest. In the meantime, the forest authorities issued notices to the appellant under section 15(1) of the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1946, requiring him to remove the timber within a specified period failing which he would be liable to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000/. The appellant challenged the validity of these notices by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the notice required by section 14 or other provisions of the Act were invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 2 of the Act. It also held that the notification dated March 30, 1949, was invalid as it contravened the provisions of section 2. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. HELD: (i) The notification dated March 31, 1949, is valid. [306 D] (ii)The notification dated March 29, 1949, does not contravene any of the provisions of the Bihar Forest Act, 1947. The notification merely declares that the forest authorities have decided to issue a permit to fell timber on certain specified dates. The notification does not purport to declare that the forest officers are authorised to issue such permits. The notification only directs that the forest officer should issue a permit in respect of timber which has been felled. The notification cannot therefore be said to be invalid because it contravenes the provisions of sections 2 and 3 of the Bihar Act. [307 B C] (iii)Section 2 of the Bihar forest Act, 1947, provides that no person shall fell any timber except under and subject to the conditions prescribed therein. Section 3 of the Act lays down that no person who is not a citizen of India shall fell any such timber except under, and subject to, the conditions mentioned in section 4. Section 5 of the Act provides that no forest officer shall cut any timber without the previous permission of the State Government. Section 6 of the Act gives power to the State Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. Rule 8 of the Rules framed under the Act requires that every forest officer shall maintain a register showing the number of timber which he has reserved for himself and
2373: The appellant was a tenant of certain properties belonging to the respondent. He had fixed the valuation of the properties at Rs. 3,25,000/ . On his revision, the Sessions Judge fixed the valuation at Rs. 1,25, 000/ . The Sessions Judge fixed it at Rs. 2,00,000/. On appeal by the respondent, the Sessions judge reduced the value to Rs. 90,000/ and on further appeal by the appellant, the High Court reduced the valuation to Rs. 1.50,000/ , In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (1) the word "rate" in section 73(1) of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, means the annual letting value as defined in section 3(1) Of the Act; (2) the word 'rent ' has been used in the sense of rent which is ordinarily payable by the tenant to the landlord and not in the sense in which the word is used in the Act; and (3) the word `annual rent' has been used only in respect of buildings constructed after the date of the Act and not in respect of any other building. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The word "annual rent" in section 76(1)(a) of the Act means the annual rent which is usually payable by the person who is liable to pay the property tax. [675 C] (2) The word 'annual rent ' in section 73 (1) of Bombay Municipal Borne Tax Act, 1949, means the monthly rent which is generally payable by the owner of the building or land or both. [676 D] (3) The word `annually ' in section 76 (1)(a), means the annual rental value as defined under section 3(i) of the said Act. [677 E] (4) The word, 'annual ' in section 77(1)(b) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963, means the gross annual rent which would be payable by the occupier of the building, if it were let out. [678 F]

The proviso to section 83(1)(b) of the Act is applicable to the case of the respondent. 4878: The assessee company was incorporated in the year 1948 and it was a public limited company. In its assessment for the assessment year 1949 50, the Income tax officer determined the taxable income of the assessee at Rs. 5,76,678. The assessee contended that there could be no liability to super profits tax in respect of a company in liquidation since the formula laid down in the Second Schedule to the Act for calculation of the 'standard deduction ' was inapplicable on account of the fact that a company in winding up could not be said to have paid up share capital as on the first day of the year of account relevant to assessment year and whether any portion of the fund can be distinctly designated as representing paid up sharecapital of the company or as 'reserve'. The Income tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee and held that the assessee had not submitted any return under the Act, a notice under section 9(a) of the Act calling upon the liquidator to pay the amount of the share capital within 30 days from the date of receipt of the notice failing which the liquidator would be liable to pay interest at 12% per annum till payment. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal held that in the hands of the liquidator there is only one integral fund which could not be split up into share capital, reserve and profits. 508: The petitioners who were displaced persons from Pakistan, were allotted agricultural lands in the State of Punjab. They were allotted in 1949 a total area of 38 standard acres and 13 units of agricultural land. In 1950, they were allotted in the year 1949 a total number of 13 units of evacuee property. The allotment was cancelled by an order dated July 31, 1951. The petitioners moved the Custodian General for revision of this order under section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950. The Custodian General directed that out of the 1,263 standard acres and 1 3/4 units of evacuee properties, the petitioners should be allotted to them in accordance with certain rules and instructions. The petitioners challenged these orders on the ground that they had acquired rights in the lands which constituted property within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to the protection of article 31 (2) of the Constitution. The right to compensation is a very valuable right and it cannot be taken away except in accordance with law. The right of compensation is a just equivalent of the loss or damage suffered by the person affected by reason of the deprivation of his property. It can never be a mere arbitrary or fanciful consideration. The right is not always a just one but has to be exercised in a reasonable manner. The object of the impugned order is to give relief to the persons affected by the action of the Government in taking over the possession of the property. The order does not take into account any other considerations. The order merely directs the restoration of the property to the petitioners. The order did not take into consideration any other relevant considerations.

1825: The appellant firm was incorporated in the year 1948 as a partnership firm. In its application for registration under section 26A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, it was stated that the firm had been formed by the partners of the said firm and that the firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act. The Income tax Officer refused to register the firm on the ground that different firms could not constitute a valid partnership. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm constituted a genuine one and that the registration of the firm was not invalid. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the partnership was not a genuine one but was a genuine one. The High Court dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The firm was not a legal entity distinct from the partners of its individual partners. [306 D] (ii) The partnership deed did not contain any provision for registration of the firms. It merely provided that the partners should carry on business in partnership with the firm. The firm was formed only for the purpose of carrying on the business of banking and commission agents. The firm had no right to collect the commission of the entire match production of the larger partnerships. [307 E F] (iii) The firm is not a legal person within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Indian Partnership act. The firm has no right to be assessed as an unregis tered firm. [308 A B] (iv) The firm has not been formed for the purpose or for the benefit of the partners. The firm is a body corporate. The firm can sue and be sued in its own name. The firm cannot sue and be assessed in its own capacity. [309 C] (v) The firm had not been formed by itself for the purpose and for the benefit or benefit of the members of the family. [310 G H; 311 A B]

2861: The respondents in both the appeals were the mortgagors of the suit properties. They sold the same to the appellants on April 26, 1912 and the sale deeds executed by them were registered on April 26. 1952. The appellants claimed that they had purchased the rights of the mortgagor under exhibit P 5 dated April 26, 1904. The trial court decreed the suits except for the mortgage dated January 20, 1878. In second appeal the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court but dismissed the appellants ' claim for redemption. In second appeals the appellants contended that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit was within time. The High Court held that the suit is barred by limitation. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit filed on November 27, 1961 was beyond time because the acknowledgment made by the mortgagers under the original of exhibit P 5 was not a mere acknowledgement of the right of the mortga ted to redeem the mortgage. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The suit is barred under section 90 of the Evidence Act. It cannot be made after the period of two years from the date when the right to redeem accrues. [109 A B] (3) The acknowledgment is complete when it is signed by the person making it either expressly or impliedly. The person executing the document may do so either sign the document himself or refer to him in writing. If he does so, his signature alone becomes an acknowledgment of liability. [111 F] (5) The fact of execution of the document is not material. [112 C] (6) The fact whether the document is executed by the person executing the deed or by someone else is immaterial. 1707: The petitioner filed an election petition in the High Court for a declaration that the election of respondent No. 1 was void on the ground that he had been improperly reception, refusal and rejection of votes at the time of counting. The High Court rejected the application for inspection holding that the ballot papers were rightly called for from the Returning Officer and were not liable to be rejected under section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in rejecting the application for production of the sealed boxes of ballot papers; (ii) the Tribunal was bound to grant an order for inspection; (iii) the Tribunal had failed to exercise its jurisdiction in allowing inspection of ballot papers which was necessary for the purpose of deciding the dispute between the parties; and (iv) the Tribunal having refused inspection of ballot paper, the Tribunal could not have granted inspection of ballots. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in refusing to grant inspection of ballot papers. [847 C] (ii) The High Courts power to grant inspection is conferred by section 100(2) of the Act. Section 100(1) provides that the High Court may make rules for the inspection of records relating to the proceedings in the High Courts. Rule 2 of the Rules provides that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply mutatis mutandis to all matters arising out of the execution of the orders or decrees of the High Court.
