In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to enquire into any ground of disqualification which was not taken before the returning officer; (ii) that the nomination paper was improperly rejected; (iii) that the returning officer had wrongly rejected the nomination paper; (iv) that the rejection of nomination paper was illegal because the appellant had failed to prove that he was disqualified under sections 7(1) (c) and 7(2); (v) that the decision of the Tribunal was based on conjectures and surmises; (vi) that the appellant had not proved that he was interested in the nomination paper and that he was therefore disqualified under section7(1)( c) of the Act. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that the nomination papers were rightly rejected. [627 F] (ii) The appellant could not have been allowed to challenge the validity of the rejection of its nomination paper. [628 A B] (iii) The appellant had not established that he was not interested in the acceptance of the nomination papers. He had only produced some documents showing that he was a member of the Legislative Assembly. It is difficult to believe that he would not have been able to produce those documents if he had been a member of that Assembly. [629 C D] (iv) The appellant was not entitled to raise the question whether he was interested or not in the acceptance or rejection of the nominations. [630 E]

1385: The appellants were accused of having committed offences under sections 120B, 420 and 471 I.P.C. The first respondent was the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta. He dismissed a complaint under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against four persons who were the appellants in revision. The High Court set aside the order of dismissal on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the complaint as the offence alleged therein was one punishable with death or imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants: (1) that the High Court had no jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code to quash the proceedings; (2) that the complaint was barred by limitation; and (3) that the cognizance taken by the Magistrate was bad because the sanction required under section 197(4) of the Code was not obtained. HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the complaint could be quashed on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 1257: The appellant was convicted under section 307, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for five years. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The offence of attempting to commit murder is not an act capable of causing death but must be an act during the course of committing that offence. [766 D] (2) The offence committed by the appellant in the present case was a single act which could be said to have been committed with the intention of committing an offence. It was not an act which would constitute the offence of murder. [767 B C] (3) There was no evidence to show that the appellant had intended to cause any injury to the deceased. The fact that he did not intend to cause any such injury as was likely to cause death, was sufficient to establish that he intended to cause that injury. [768 A B] (4) The appellant 's conviction under section 307 was therefore justified. [769 E]
1982: The appellant, a sugar factory, manufactures sugar and sells it in its own factory. Respondent No. 1, the State of Madhya Pradesh, enacted the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply & Purchase) Act, 1958, which was made applicable to the State of Bhopal by section 3 thereof. Section 23 of the Act provided for the method of collection of cess. Section 21 of the Act prescribed the mode of collection of tax payable under the Act. The appellant 's contention before the High Court was that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act did not provide for payment of any tax or cess levied by the State Government but only provided for the recovery of the amount of tax due from the appellant. The High Court struck down section 21 of the Madhya Pradesh Act prescribing the mode of recovery of tax payable by the appellant. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Act does not contain any provision for the levy of any tax. The Act is a piece of delegated legislation. The Act does no more than prescribe the mode of assessment of tax payable. The Act has been passed with a view to provide for the collection of tax leviable from dealers who are liable to pay the tax. [532 C] (ii) The Act provides for the recovery from the dealer of the amount due from him as if it were an arrear of land revenue. The Act also prescribes the mode of payment of tax. The scheme of the Act shows that the tax is imposed primarily on the dealer and is not on the person who pays the tax. The tax is levied primarily on the person liable to pay it. The Act therefore lays down the mode of realisation of tax and the manner of recovery. The Act thus makes clear that the tax can be recovered only by the person who makes the payment. The Act further provides for the mode of realization of tax. [553 D E] (iii) The Act is not a law providing for the recovery by the State of any tax payable by a dealer. 1643: The appellant filed a petition under section 10(1)(a) of the , in the City Civil Court, Bombay, for judicial separation on the ground that she had "deserted" him for "a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of her petition". The respondent contended that the appellant 's husband had no intention to desert his wife and that he was not entitled to maintain her. The trial judge held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent had an irrevocable determination to break up the matrimonial home when she left the matrimonial home on February 26, 1954, and did not return to her husband thereafter. He also found that the appellant was guilty of desertion under section 10 (1) (a) of Act. On appeal the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the appellant ' s suit. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the trial judge that the appellant has established that the respondent 's husband 's husband was living with the intention of deserting the appellant was erroneous and that the burden of proving this to the reasonable satisfaction of the Court was on the appellant. Held, that the appellant could not succeed in establishing that the respondent was living with her husband without any reasonable excuse for not returning to the matrimonial home at the time of her marriage. The fact that the appellant did not inform the respondent about her arrival from Bombay or her refusal to accept the offer made by her father to go to Bombay would not make the case of the respondent as true. 1886: The appellant company was a company which had been allotted land in pursuance of an order made by the Government under the Defence of India Rules. The land was requisitioned by virtue of an order passed by the Government on February 18, 1944. The Government acquired the land and delivered it to the company. The company entered into contracts with the Government for purchase of plots in pursuance of which the land was requisitioned. The company claimed that the acquisition was not unlawful as it was not possible for the company to carry out the work of construction of roads and drains during the continuance of the war and because the land had been requisitioned under the Defence Act. Held, that the acquisition of land was not unlawful but the acquisition was illegal as it was impossible for the company, when the land was taken possession, to carry out its obligations under the contract. The mere fact that the performance of an essential condition of the contract has become impossible due to supervening circumstances would not render the acquisition invalid. The mere circumstance that the performance could be completed within one month from the date of the requisition or within such further time as the Government might allow would not make the acquisition invalid unless there is some other reason why it should not be held to be unlawful.

3259: The appellants were licensees under section 10 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961 and were also pucca arhtiyas. 1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. He was sentenced to six months ' rigorous imprisonment by the High Court on appeal against acquittal under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but he was not taken into custody till January 6, 1958. On April 29, 1958, Bipat Gope moved a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the District Magistrate and the High Court directed on May 1, 1958, that Bipat be taken into custody and sent him to jail. On May 1, 1959, Bipta Gope moved an application stating that he had filed the above mentioned petition in the High Court and that he had to appear there on Monday following which he prayed that he be allowed an opportunity to present his case to the High Court. The High Court ordered on May 1st, 1959, that Bpata Gope should appear before it on Mondays and he would be released from custody. The respondent moved this Court under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the order of Bipta. Held: (i) The order of the High Court is without jurisdiction as it has no power to pass any order for release of a prisoner who does not have a right to move the High Court under article 226. The order of Bpata was passed on the basis of the report of the Superintendent of Police, Patna, and the High court was wrong in directing Bipta to surrender to the State. The order was made after considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant rules. The order did not amount to a direction for the release of Bipat. It was not a direction to the State Government to release Bipat on bail. The order merely required Bipta being detained for a period exceeding six months. The order could not be said to be a direction to Bipta for the purpose of enabling him to move the Court.

The said Article provides that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the Union or a State. Article 338 of the Constitution empowers the Parliament to frame rules for regulating recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State. The proviso to Article 338(2) lays down that nothing in article

2140: The respondent, a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1953, purchased cotton from unregistered dealers and paid purchase tax on it. During the assessment period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1956, it purchased unginned cotton worth Rs. 5,93,266/from unregistered dealers and sold by it. During this period, the respondent applied for refund of the purchase tax paid by it. The Assistant Collector of Sales Tax confirmed the order of the Sales Tax Officer on the ground that the purpose underlying the respondent 's purchases was primarily the production of ginned cotton for sale. The respondent filed a revision before the Gujarat Sales Tax Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected the revision on the ground: (i) that the purpose of the respondent ' s purchases was primarily for production of ginning cotton for sale; and (ii) that the main product was used in the manufacture of other goods. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The primary object of the respondent is the production of cotton seeds for sale. Therefore, the purpose for which unginned Cotton was purchased was the sale of cotton seeds. [866 B] (2) The primary purpose of the purchase was primarily the use of cotton seeds in the manufacture or processing of cotton. The primary purpose is the production and processing of cotton seeds and not the manufacturing process. [865 C] (3) The primary activity of the respondent was to sell cotton seeds and ginned and pressed by it. It was therefore not reasonable to suppose that the primary purpose of its purchases was primarily to produce cotton seeds. The primary object was the production of seed and ginning of cotton seeds, and not the processing of cotton seed. [864 D E] (4) The primary and incidental product was the raw material for the manufacture of cotton seeds but not the primary one. [863 F]
3930: The plaintiff was the owner of a land in which he was carrying on business. He executed a Power of Attorney in favour of defendant No. 34 who was a Minister in the Nizam 's Government and who had been appointed as an attorney by the Nizam for the purpose of managing the affairs of the State. The power of attorney was duly registered with the Registrar of Firms, Madras. The plaintiff alleged that in October 1949 he came to know that defendants nos. 1 and 34 were perpetrating fraud when on 25th October, 1949 he came out with a false Power of Attorney and got the lands transferred from the plaintiff. The plaintiff also alleged that the said Power of Attorney was obtained fraudulently by the said defendants. The plaintiff further alleged that the defendants were not giving any notice of the sale of the land and the sale deed was illegal and void. The plaintiff claimed that the defendants had no right to sell the land and that the sale deed should be cancelled. The defendants denied that they ever entered into any transaction with the plaintiff or that they were induced to enter into a fraudulent agreement. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not the owner of the suit lands but was a benamidar and that the Power of Attorney did not confer any title upon the plaintiff. On appeal the High Court held that the Powerof Attorney could not be cancelled without notice to the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the plaintiff was never the owner of any property; (ii) the Power of Attorneys were not executed by the plaintiff; (iii) the Powerof Attorneys could not be revoked without notice to all the parties; (iv) the Power Of Attorney was not executed by any person other than the plaintiff; and (v) the Power-of Attorney was not created by the plaintiff. The Power Of Attornment has nothing to do with the rights of the parties. [111 C D]

3805: The appellant purchased the properties situated in village Devanoor and Gudipadu in the State of Andhra Pradesh. 1187: The petitioners were migrants from Pakistan. They had become evacuees and their shares in the properties could be properly declared evacuee property. A notice under section 7 of the was issued for the purpose of declaring these persons evacueess and their shares, as evacuee properties and evacuee property respectively. This petition under article 32 challenged the validity of the orders made by the Custodian on August 14, 1952, and March 23, 1954, as violating the petitioners ' fundamental right to hold property, to wit, their shares in them, as evacuee property and evacuee property. The petitioners contended that they had become evacuees and their shares were evacuee property and their shares could not be declared evacuee property, and that the order was a nullity as the notice under section 6 was bad for the reason that it was issued to Abdul Aziz who was admittedly not an evacuee. Held, that the order did not affect the rights of the petitioners to hold property which they had acquired under the order. The order merely stated that the petitioners were entitled to hold the property in question subject to certain conditions. The order did not purport to affect the rights or interests of the petitioners. The order was not a mere formality but was intended to provide for the enforcement of the rights of all persons who may have been evacuee. The order does not purport to effect any change in the rights of any person. The order is not a mere direction to the Custodian to take possession of the property. It is only a direction to the custodian to take possession. The order cannot be said to affect the interest of the petitioners in the property. The order has nothing to do with the rights of persons who may be evacueee. The order must be construed as a direction to those persons who are evacueees.

5544: The appellant was a tea estate owner of 100 acres with some buildings, machinery and equipments. The Corporation had to purchase the property for about Rs.1,65,000. The Corporation itself had to purchase it for about Rs, 1,65,500. There was long standing dispute between the workmen of the estate and the previous management relating to payment of their wages. The Corporation also received certain amounts from the appellant. The Corporation therefore invited tenders for the sale of the property. In response to the notification dated January 18, 1983, the appellant submitted his tender along with the appellant in response to the said notification. The Corporation accepted the tender and thereafter the property was sold in public auction. On January 7, 1982, the Corporation got possession of the entire estate. It therefore, invited tenders for sale of the said property. The Corporation filed an application before the District Court for setting aside the sale on the ground that the Corporation had not taken steps to get the property for its own benefit and that the sale was vitiated by fraud. The District Judge dismissed the application holding that the Corporation was not entitled to sell the property as it was not in a position to pay the amount due to the Corporation. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the District Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Corporation is not justified in selling the property for Rs. six lakhs or more. The Corporation has no right to sell the same. [875C] 2. The Corporation cannot take advantage of its own wrong. The Corporation must dispose of the property by public auction. The Corporation can very well realise the sale proceeds from the property sold. The Corporation may be able to recover the arrears due to it but it would not be in a position either to pay the balance of the sale proceeds to the Corporation or to pay the sale proceeds in favour of the Corporation. [877D E] 3. The Corporation should have sold the property for the purpose of recovering the arrears due from the appellant and the sale proceeds should have been deposited in the court. The Corporation could not say that the sale proceeds were not sufficient to cover the dues of the Corporation and that the Corporation did not want to pay the remaining amount of the sale

[505 F] (6) The right in question is an incident, not a mere prerequisite for the right to be exercised. [506 G] (7) The right can be enforced only by the person claiming the right. 2166: The respondent was prosecuted for contravening section 7 of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for six months. On appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's imprisonment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 13(2) of the Act confers a right on the accused vendor to have the sample sent for examination by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory. It is not necessary that the Director should himself be examined in the case. He must also be examined as a witness before he makes out a report of the result of the analysis. [119 D E] (2) The report of the Public Analyst is conclusive evidence of the fact that the sample was adulterated. The report of an expert cannot be used as evidence of the facts stated therein unless it is shown that he had applied his mind to the facts as well as the question whether or not the sample contained adulteration. [119 F H; 120 A B] (3) The report given by the Public Analyst does not contain any reference to the report of the Director of Central Food Laboratory, nor does it indicate that the Director had applied his independent mind to the report. The report may contain some other material which may be relevant to the matter under consideration. But such material can be taken into account only for limited purposes mentioned in sub section (2). [121 C D] (4) There is no provision in the Act which requires the Director of a Central Food Laboratory to send the sample to the Director of his own choice. The Director of the State Government has been made a party to the complaint. The Director has been impleaded as a party to it. [121 G H] (5) The report submitted by the Public analyst is conclusive evidence against the person who gave the report. [122 D]
2148: The appellant, a teacher in the State of Assam, was appointed as an Assistant Teacher in the school run by the respondent No. 1. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted for offences under sections 161, 165 and 165A of the Indian Penal Code. The respondent challenged his dismissal before the High Court which held that the order terminating his services was illegal because the Deputy Inspector of Schools did not act as an "Assistant Secretary" within the meaning of section 14(3)(iii) of the Act and therefore the orders were bad. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Deputy Inspector could terminate the services of the respondents only if he was found guilty of misconduct; (ii) the Deputy inspector could not terminate the services without holding a departmental enquiry; (iii) the Deputy Inspectors could not be said to have been appointed under section 14(1) of the , and (iv) the Deputy Inspectress could not terminate their services without holding any departmental enquiry. HELD: (i) Section 16(2) of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899, provides that all appointments made or purporting to be made under the Act shall be deemed to be valid until they are superseded by rules made under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. [950 D] (ii)The Deputy Inspector of schools is not a "Assistant Secretary", but he can only be an Assistant Secretary. It is only when he is appointed as such that he can be said to be "an Assistant Secretary". [951 E] (iii)Section 16(2), read with section 18 of the 1915 Act, makes it clear that the Deputy Inspector can terminate the services by giving one month 's notice. If the Deputy Inspector has been appointed under the 1954 Act, he cannot be said to hold the post of Assistant Secretary. [952 C]

2529: The plaintiff, a public body, brought a suit for the recovery of Rs. 12,044/ 19 and future interest from the defendant on the basis that he had paid the bid amount to the Board. 5255: The appellant was a public servant. He filed a complaint against the respondent bank under section 120(b) read with sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code alleging that he had been appointed as a Manager in the Bank and that he was holding the post of a Deputy General Manager. The Magistrate held that section 197 is attracted only when a public servant is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government and therefore it was contended that the Regulation framed by the Bank was ultra vires the powers of the Central Government and therefore the view taken by the Courts below was not correct. The High Court rejected the Revision Petition and dismissed the same. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the nationalisation of the bank, the appellant will fall within the definition of public servant and therefore the word 'public servant ' would include the appellant who was holding the office of a Deputy Manager. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Regulations framed by the bank are made for the purpose of taking disciplinary action against public servants. They are framed with the previous approval of the Central Govern ment. Therefore the view taken in the Courts below is not correct. The Regulations do not provide for any other procedure except those which are prescribed by the Regulations. The Regulations are framed with a view to regulate the conduct of the officers and employees of the bank. The Regulations have to be read along with the Regulations. It is not necessary that the Regulations should be framed with a particular object. The Regulations can also be framed with such modifications as may be considered necessary. [876D E] 1.3 The Regulations are not intended to be mandatory but they are merely directory. The Regulations cannot be treated as mandatory unless they are expressly stated to be so. [877E F] 1.4 The Regulations are meant to be operative till they are modified or amended by the appropriate authority in accordance with law. 3522: The appellant was convicted under section 16(1)(a) read with section 16(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a term of three months and to pay fine of Rs. 500/ in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one month more. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to six months RI. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to section 16(l) is not applicable to cases where the accused pleads guilty on the basis of evidence adduced before the court. [712B] 2. The proviso cannot be applied in exten sion and the conviction of the High Court has to be up held. [713C D] 3. The proviso does not apply if the offence is under sub clause (i) of clause (a) and is with respect to an article of food which is adulterated under sub clause(ii) of clause(ix) of section 2 or misbranded under sub clause.(v) of section 3. The possibility of long argument in a case where the accused has pleaded guilty arises because the provision does not provide for any separate trial for the offence under section 16 (1)(a). [713D E] 4. The proviso can be invoked only when the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a period not less than six months or with fine of less than one thousand rupees or both. [714E F] 5. The proviso must be read as a whole and not in isolation. It is not possible to accept the contention that the proviso should be applied in all cases where the offence is not punishable with imprisonment upto six months. [715F G] 6. The proviso would have been attracted if the offence was punishable with imprisonment of more than six months. But the proviso could not be applied in cases where the offender had pleaded guilty. [716G H] 7. The High court has taken the view that the proviso applies only to cases where there is no specific provision in the statute for the application of the proviso. In such cases the court may either convict the offender or remit the sentence. [717A B]
1100: The appellant was the Mahant of a certain estate. He was appointed Receiver in 1939 and under the order of the Subordinate Judge he handed over charge of the estate to the appellant on January 15, 1950. On January 15, 1951, the appellant submitted a return of income of the estate for the Fasli year 1355 corresponding to September 16, 1948, to September 15, 1949. The Agricultural Income tax Officer assessed on August 7, 1950, the agricultural income of the appellant to tax at Rs. 90,507 2 6 and ordered him to pay Rs. 20,290 13 0 as agricultural income tax. Appeals against the order of assessment preferred by the appellant were unsuccessful. In the appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (i) the appellant could not be legally assessed for the agricultural income derived from the estate; (ii) the Agricultural Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the appellant under section 3(3)(a) of the Bihar Agricultural Income tax Act, and (iii) the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 13 of the Act. HELD: (i) The appellant was not liable to pay agricultural income tax because he held the property from which income was derived in the year of account. [1357 D] (ii) The appellant could not claim exemption from payment of agricultural income tax under section 3 of the Bihar Act because he did not hold any interest in the estate. [1358 B C] (iii) The appellant cannot be said to have acquired any interest in his estate. [134 E] (iv) The appellant is not entitled to the protection of section 13 because he has not been able to establish that he was not liable for the agricultural incomes derived from the properties in question. [134 G]

245: The Indian States entered into a covenant on the Constitution of India with the Government of India. Under the terms of the covenant each Ruler was entitled to the full and exclusive authority, jurisdiction and powers for and in relation to the governance of the State of Uttar Pradesh. In pursuance of this covenant each Ruler agreed to surrender his sovereignty to the whole but there was no further surrender of sovereign powers to the Dominion of India beyond those already surrendered in 1947, namely Defence, External Affairs and Communications. The Revenue Officers of the newly formed Vindhya Pradesh Union tried to interfere with the grants made by certain Rulers before the integration; among them were the grants in question here. The Revenue Minister 's order of that date runs "After considering over the whole matter it has ,been decided that such grants made by the Rulers before signing the covenant should be respected, because constitutionally the V.P. By the same instrument, each Ruler cedes to the Government of the Indian Dominion as from the same date. The Revenue Officer of the newly constituted Vindhya Madhya Bharat Union tried to intervene and say that the grants in favour of the Rulers were not validated by the fact that they had been ratified by the Government of U.P. The Revenue officer rejected the contention and held that the grants could not be validly terminated under the provisions of the V. P. Act. On appeal, the High Court upheld the decision of the Revenue authorities. The State cannot be forced to accept the grant in its entirety without its consent. The State can only act according to its own whims and fancies. It cannot act according to any whim or logic. [550 D] (ii)The Vindhya Bihar Missan was a State within section 3(1)(a) of the Vindhya Pashu Kendra Act, 1956. The Vindhy Pradesh Missan being a State within article 12 of Constitution, the Vindhy Miss
2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 4 months ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court set aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial court but convicted them under section 186, Indian Penal code. The appellants contended that the conviction was bad as it contravened the provisions of section 195, Criminal Procedure Code, and that the prosecution was barred under section 195, Cr. P.C., and that the appellants were entitled to be acquitted. Held, that the conviction under section 352, Indian Penal Cod e, was not justified. Section 195, Cr, P.C. provides that no Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 351, Indian Penal Coo, or under section 354, or under any bailable or nonbailable one, except on a complaint in writing made by the public servant concerned or otherwise than in accordance with the procedure prescribed for trial of warrant cases instituted upon a police report. The section does not say that the prosecution is barred under the provisions of the section. It only says that the prosecution must be held to have been barred if the prosecution has been instituted without the sanction of the Government. The section applies only where the prosecution is instituted by a public servant acting or purporting to act in discharge of his official duty. The section cannot apply where the prosecution has already been instituted by a private person. The section merely lays down the rule that the prosecution should be held to be barred if the accused person had acted in good faith in prosecuting the prosecution.
2027: The workmen of the company filed a reference under section 10(1) of the , claiming that they were entitled to gratuity at the rate of 60 years. The company contended that the age of retirement should be fixed at 55 years for clerical and subordinate staff and 55 years for factory workmen and that their age of retirement was fixed at 55 yews. The tribunal held that the age fixed by the company was not correct, but it allowed the claim of the workmen to the extent of 65 years. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The tribunal has rightly fixed the age of superannuation at 55 years in the case of factory workmen also in the present company. [529 B] (ii) The company had to retire on attaining the age of 58 years. It is not possible to accept the contention that the age at which the company would retire must be the same as in the case before the tribunal. The company could have been well advised to fix the age of retiral benefits at the same level as in the other cases. [530 C D] (iii) The company was entitled to raise an industrial dispute regarding the age of the retirement of its employees. The company did not raise any such dispute. The company therefore could not raise the dispute about the age of its employees because the company was bound to pay the employees the difference between the age of their retirement and the age of 55 years. [531 E F]
317: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 300/ for the offence under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He preferred an appeal to the Sessions Court which was also dismissed. The High Court on revision directed that the sentence be suspended pending disposal of the appeal. On the question whether the appellant had committed any professional misconduct or not. HELD : (i) It is well settled that in order to establish a charge of professional misconduct it must be shown that the accused has been guilty of conduct which constitutes an offence under the Act. The expression "conduct" in section 5(3) of the Act means "acting in any manner prejudicial to good order and public health". [821 G] (ii) In order to constitute a criminal offence there should be some material to show that the accused was habitually absent from duty without any intimation or permission. If he does so, his conviction by the trial court would be illegal. But if he does so it may be presumed that he did not intend to continue his service and that he will be deemed to have resigned from service. [822 B C] (iii) A person who commits an offence cannot be placed under suspension until the charges against him are proved. An act of moral turpitude can be said to be an offence under section 161 I.P.C., if it amounts to an offence under sections 5(2), 5(1) (c) and 5(1). [823 D E] (iv) The word 'professional misconduct' in section 5 (2) of the , includes acts done in any other way. [824 F] (v) The word "misconduct" as used in section 5 of the Act must be given its ordinary meaning. It is not necessary that the offender should have acted honestly or reasonably. It is sufficient if he acted in a fiduciary capacity. [825 H; 826 A] (vi) The word `misconduct ' in section 5 is not confined only to mere breach of orders or defaults but it extends to all such acts as are synonymous with misconduct as defined in section 4
2613: The appellant Bank, a Co operative Society, filed a dispute under section 10(1) (d) of the Andhra Pradesh Co operative Societies Act, 1964 before the Industrial Tribunal, Andhra Pradesh. The Tribunal held that the reference was invalid and directed the Registrar to refer the dispute to the Registrar for decision. Cooperative Societies Act, 1965 does not exclude the jurisdiction of a civil court to decide the matter relating to the constitution, management or the business of a society. [211C] 2. The expression "any dispute" occurring in section 61(1) of the , includes all disputes arising out of contracts and whether or not they relate to the matters specified therein. It is therefore clear that the jurisdiction conferred on the Registrar or his nominee under section 61(I) of the . is not confined only to the disputes mentioned in section 61 but extends also to disputes as regards disciplinary action taken against the employees of the society. The word `dispute' in section 61 cannot be restricted to disputes between members or between a member or between a rival group of persons claiming through members or between two different groups of persons claiming to be opponents of one group. 6920: The appellant purchased a large extent of land in the State of Andhra Pradesh for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 and sold it to the respondents on January 24, 1967. The respondents claimed that they were entitled to compensation @ Rs. 10 per sq. yard. The Trial Court and the High Court accepted the contention of the appellant and awarded compensation at Rs. 10per sq. yard with solatium at 15% and interest at 4 per cent. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was not justified in excluding the sale deeds, exhibit B. 6, B. 7, B. 8 and B. 10 from consideration. [7A] (2) The High court had rightly held that the sale deed dated January 24, 1966 could not be relied upon as the same was executed after the notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act 1894 was published in the State Gazette on November 21, to acquire an area of about 5 acres and odd under acquisition. [7B C] (3) The High Courts have taken the view that the sale deeds are genuine transactions and should not be ignored while determining the market value of the land. [7C] (4) The High courts have also taken the view, though not expressively expressed their opinion that the sale transactions are genuine transactions but have not considered the question whether the sale deeds were genuine or not. [7D] (5) The Highs Court has rightly taken note of the fact that the sale transaction is not genuine one. It is true that the sale price fixed by the Government is much higher than the market value prevailing in the locality. But the fact remains that the sale is not genuine. [7E F] (6) The High 'Court was right in taking the view that there was no evidence to show that the sale was genuine. [8F] (7) The High Cour t erred in ignoring the sale deed which was executed after a period of nine months from the date of the notification under s.4(1). The High Court ought to have seen that the sale did not take place within a reasonable time. [8G]

The respondent landlord applied for fixation of standard rent in respect of the flat occupied by the appellant. The Rent Controller fixed the standard rent at Rs. 1,000 per month and the Appellate Authority allowed the landlord 's appeal in part by setting the standard rent as aforesaid. The Appellate Authority held that the premises were governed by the provisions of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, and the Calcutta Municipal Rules, 1930 framed thereunder. The Appellate authority however, allowed the landlord to increase the standard rent by a certain percentage on the ground that the premises had been let out to a tenant who had not paid the rent for three years before the date of the application. The landlord appealed to the High Court which set aside the order of the Appellate Authority and restored the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that (i) the Rent Controller was not authorised to deal with the tenancies in question because the premises were outside the scope of the Act; (ii) the Rent Control Order did not apply to the tenancies covered by the Act; and (iii) the Rent Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the premises were within the scope of section 9 read with Schedule A of the Act. HELD: (i) The Rent Controller had no power to fix the standard rent under the Act. [880 E] (ii) The Rent Control Order does not confer upon the landlord any special right or privilege but merely provides for the regulation of letting and the control of rent. It is only when the landlord has been given an opportunity to do so that he can claim the protection of the Rent Control Act. If the landlord has not done so, the Rent Controller cannot exercise his powers under the Act and pass orders fixing the standard rent. [881 F G] (iii) The Rent Tribunal had jurisdiction to go behind the Rent Control Orders and determine the standard rent even though the Rent Controller had not given its decision on the question of standard rent. The Rent Control Orders are binding on the parties and they have to be followed strictly. [882 B C] (iv) The Rent Controllers had no jurisdiction under the
844: The appellant was appointed a Health Inspector in the Municipality of Howrah. He had been given the power to sell sweetmeats, betel leaves and cigarettes etc., but not specifically included in the list of articles which he could dispose of under section 407 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923. The appellant 's case was that the Health Officer had no jurisdiction to order prosecution in any case regarding the Health Department and that power delegated to him by one of those orders had not been revoked and therefore the Health Officer was competent to sanction the prosecution. Held, that the powers delegated to the Health Officer were not valid because the Health Officer did not have the authority to sanction the prosecutions. The power conferred on the Health Officer by section 407 was not an independent power but only a power to withdraw from legal proceedings under the Calcutta Municipal act, 1923, as in force in the Municipality. The power was not exercisable at all when the Health Officer passed the order sanctioning the prosecution. The power delegated to the health officer was not an essential part of his functions under the Act.
125: The appellants were the owners of a flat in a building known as "Sunama House" situated at Bombay. The first respondent, a limited company, was carrying on business in the said flat and it had let out the same to the second respondent for a period of three years from November 1, 1947, at Rs. 370 per month. The first appellant was the owner of the said flat. The second respondent was the tenant of the said premises. The first defendant was a limited company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and the second respondent was its managing director. The first plaintiff was the owner and the second defendant was the tenant in respect of the said property. The second defendant was a tenant in respect thereof. The first defendants filed a suit against the second defendant for ejectment from the suit premises on the ground that the second defendant had sublet the premises to the first defendant without the consent of the first defendant. 2519: The appellants were detained under section 3(1) of the . The appellants challenged the validity of the speech on the ground that it did not interfere with the course of justice. Held, that the speech was calculated to interfere with the due course of justice and was therefore liable to be declared as contempt of the Court. The speech was intended to be an expression of the view of persons who had no intention to interfere with or obstruct the administration of justice. The speech must be such as would satisfy the requirements of the Constitution. The speech may be so interpreted as to make it necessary for the purpose of maintaining law and order or for maintaining peace and harmony in the area. It cannot be said that the speech has been calculated to interfere or interfere with the proper administration of justice because the object of the speech is to discover the truth and to prevent any further evil. The speech can only be justified if it interferes with the due administration of justice and does not interfere with its administration. The speech is not merely a statement of what I have said but it is intended to be evidence of what the speaker understood. The speech need not necessarily be direct evidence of what he has done but may also be evidence which the maker of the speech has reasonably believed. The speech should be such as will satisfy the requirements in the case of contempt of court.

Rule 5 provided that the Assistant Engineers who have been recruited on probation shall not be eligible for confirmation unless they are considered fit for such confirmation. Therefore, he cannot claim the benefit of his service from 1972 to 1984. [878F G] 4. The petitioner 's appointment to the post could not be treated as ad hoc or stop gap arrangement. The petitioner was not entitled to any benefit of the said service. [877A B] 5. The petitioner had accepted the position as stated in the seniority lists of Excise Inspectors but he accepted the position in the seniority orders. He accepted that he can be considered to have been promoted to the next post of Excise Superintendent. [876B C] 6. The petitioner is not entitled to the benefit of service rendered by him as Excise Inspector. [871D]
333: The plaintiffs carried on business in the name of cotton cloth dealers at Lyallpur. They used to make lump sum payments to the defendant against their purchases. In the course of their business they used to make a lump sum payment to the defendant, and on 27 7 1950 the defendant delivered cloth worth Rs. 43,583 0 0 to the plaintiffs against this amount at or about that time. On 27 7 1950, the defendant company delivered cloth worth about Rs. 43.583 0 to the plaintiff. The plaintiffs paid the defendant interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of the suit till the date of payment. The defendant 's representative sent a notice to the plaintiffs demanding payment of the money but the defendant did not pay any heed to it. The plaintiffs therefore filed a suit for recovery of the money due under the decree. The defence of the defendant was that the plaintiffs had been carrying on business in India and the demand for payment made by the defendant was unjustified. Held, that the defendant was carrying on business as a manufacturer of cloth and was liable to be sued for the amount due to him. The defendant was not carrying on business either as a manufacturer or a dealer. The defendant had no concern with the goods in question. The defendant could not have been held to be carrying on business only as a manufacturer. The defendant is not carrying on any business as a dealer. It was not necessary that the defendant should have been carrying on the business of a manufacturer. It was also not necessary that there should have been a contract between the defendant and the plaintiffs. The defendant has not proved that the plaintiffs were carrying on business exclusively as manufacturers of cloth. The defendant did not carry on any business in India. The defendant cannot be said to be carrying out any business in the country. The defendant, therefore, was not entitled to recover the money due to him under the decree passed against him.
7102: The appellant was a Mazdoor in the Punjab State Electricity Board. He belonged to the general category and was appointed as a Mazdoor on September 20, 1973. Respondent No. 3 was a Mazhbi Sikh and was appointed in the post of a Mazdoor. On November 19, 1974, the appellant was given appointment as a Mazidar in the Punjab Electricity Board. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in dismissing the petition because the appellant did not fall within the zone of consideration for promotion to the post of Assistant Engineer. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The appellant was entitled to be placed at Point Nos. 7 and 8 in the Rhata Gate of the Punjab Electricity Supply Corporation. [511C] (2) The appellant has not been shown to have been selected by any Selection Committee. His name is not shown in the Rota of the Rota. [512E] (3) The appellant could not be said to be senior to the respondent No.3. [513F] (4) The appellant had no right to be considered for promotion to a post in the Round 1 of the Rotary Rota. 904: The appellant company was a textile mill engaged in the production of carding and other items. In addition to this, the workmen employed in its Carding Department were paid wages on piece rate basis. The workmen raised an additional claim for payment of bonus for the period from January 1, 1948 to March 31, 1955. The Government amended the issue by substituting therefor the following: " Whether the employers have wrongfully and/or unjustifiably reduced the wages of these workmen 's workmen, if so, to what relief are the workmen entitled and from what date ? 493 " The Tribunal held that the Government order did not require or justify the employer including these bonuses in the calculation of the rates of basic wages for the purpose of the order, but allowed the claim for payment for the period between January 1, 1949 to March 31. 1955. The appellant company appealed to the High Court which set aside the Tribunal 's decision and directed the Tribunal to decide the question whether the additional emoluments payable by way of production bonus and incentive bonus had been taken into consideration by the company while arriving at the revised piece rates. The High Court held that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the Government Order did not require the employer including the additional emoluments being paid by way of Production Bonus and incentive bonus. It also held that the appellant company had failed to prove that the additional emoluments paid by way Of production bonus and the incentive bonus had not been taken into account by the company before the amendment of the issue by the order dated April 25, 1955. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that there was no justification for the Government order dated April 21, 1955, that the additional wages paid by wayof production bonus and incentives bonus should be taken into consideration while determining the wages for the purposes of the order. The words " basic wages" in cl. 8 of the order refer only to the basic wages as defined in the order and not to the basic wage as defined in cl. 2(b) of the order and the Tribunal was justified in holding that it was not necessary to consider the question whether production bonus and Incentive bonus had been properly taken into consideration.
2946: The appellant was appointed as a Head Mistress of a school run by the Government of Madras. She filed an appeal against her order of reduction passed by the Manager, but she did not succeed in that appeal. On the question whether the order of the Manager removing her from the post of Head Mistri was within its power and whether the rules were valid under section 56(1) of the Madras Elementary Education Act, 1920, Held, that the order of reduction was within its powers and could be enforced at the instance of the appellant. The rules framed under the Act for the first time by the Government were made applicable to the school in question and the appellant had no right to enforce them in a court of law. The rules were merely administrative instructions and not statutory rules. The rules which were framed under the Madras Elementary School Code were not statutory rules and they could not be continued even after the repeal of those rules. The rule making authority was entitled to make rules which would give rise to a remedy enforceable at the instance or by an employee of a school aggrieved against its management.
39: The appellant was arrested on the 27th of October, 1947, and was granted bail. On the 1st December, 1947, the Government appointed a Special Magis trate to try offences under the Act and on the 1st of December, 1947 the appellant was arrested by an order issued by the Magistrate on the 22nd of October, 1948. The appellant was produced before the Special Mag ist and was granted his bail. On his arrest he was released on bail. On a petition made by him for a writ of habeas corpus, the High Court dismissed the petition but directed that the appellant be taken into custody. The appellant contended that when the warrant of arrest was issued by the magistrate on the 22 nd of October 1947, the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and, as no sanction of the Government had been obtained before that day, the initiation of the proceedings against him was illegal. Held, that the order which may be applied for and made during the police investigation by virtue of section 3 of the Act is before the Magistrate has taken cognizance of the offences and, as the appellant was not arrested without an order of the Magistrate, the proceeding initiated against him was without jurisdiction. The order which may have been passed by the Magistrate in October, 1947 could not be said to be without jurisdiction.

5395: The assessee was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of certain goods. It had a fixed capital investment of Rs.1,00,000 in its undertaking. 38: The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal breach of trust under section 409, Indian Penal Code. He pleaded that he had been guilty of the offences for which he was tried and convicted by the trial court. The trial court found him guilty of the offence but on appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that though ordinarily a person should not be held liable for the acts of another, he must be held to have committed the offence of a criminal breach of fictitious liability and that in any event the appellant could not be held to be liable for the act of another. HELD : (i) It is well settled that where a person has been charged with an offence for which he can be punished for the same offence, there is no reason why the accused cannot be held liable if the facts proved against him are established beyond reasonable doubt. [821 G] (ii) The appellant was not charged with the commission of an offence of criminal conspiracy. His case was that he had supplied petrol to two other persons who were not named as accused in the first information report. The charge against him was that he did so without taking delivery of the petrol from the car at Guntur. The evidence showed that the appellant had taken delivery of the vehicle at Guntuwall and that he had also delivered the goods at Guntupur. There was thus no evidence to show that the appellant knew or had reason to believe that the goods were being transported in the car at the time when the offence was alleged to have been committed. [822 A B] (iii) The appellant could not therefore be said to have committed an offence of a civil nature unless he was charged with an off ence of criminal conspiracy and the prosecution must prove that the other person actually committed the offence. [823 C D] (iv) The appellant had not been charged with the theft of petrol nor had he been charged with any criminal conspiracy. The charge was that he was responsible for the theft of the petrol. [824 E]
1758: The appellants were displaced persons who had been allotted land in Hyderabad State. They applied for allotment of land under the Displaced Persons (Claims) Act, 1950. The Deputy Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Rehabilitation issued a notification on September 7, 1954, under section 33 of the Act, declaring that the terms of the lease would be revised only after five years. The appellants filed an application before the Regional Settlement Commissioner under section 33(1)(b) of the Act for revision of the order of the Deputy Secretary. The Deputy Director of Estates rejected their application and the appeal against it was dismissed by the Central Government. Thereafter, the respondents made representations to the Regional Settlement Commis sioner, Hyderabad, claiming that they should cultivate the lands personally. The Deputy Commissioner rejected them but the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Central Government had no power under section 33 to revise the order of a Deputy Secretary. [839 E] The word "transfer" is not defined in the Act. It has been used in the definition clause in the Act, and the word "transfer", as well as the word "mutation" have been used in section 2(h) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The word "allotment" is defined in section 2 (g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as meaning "a transfer of title to or part of a property for consideration paid or promised or other consideration; a transfer of a right to enjoy or use a property for a price paid or promised. "The word "transfer of title to" means the transfer of the title to or from a property to the gift or tenure. [840 F H] The word 'transfer' is defined in the General Clauses Acts, 1897, and the General Clauses (Act No. 1 of 1897), as meaning "the transfer of a thing, the transfer of any interest therein, or the creation of any rights therein, or (if there are no such interests in the property) the transfer of a share therein, or any other form of transfer of the right to enjoy the property." [841 B C] The word transfer is defined in s.2(f)

The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the decree for eviction passed by the trial Court was nullity and the same could not be executed against respondent No., 1. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had committed an error in dismissing the writ petition filed by respondent No. I. But the High Court has rightly held that the order of dismissal of the writ petition was without jurisdiction. [385C] 1.2. The High courts are bound by the principles of law laid down by this Court in the case of S.R. [387E F] 1.4. The High court was right in its conclusion that the decree of the first appellate Court was a nullity and could not be enforced against respondent No, 1. [388B C] 1.5. In connection with this business, the company had given a notice to the Union of the appellant workmen that out of 21 depots mentioned in the notice, the management would be closing down with effect from 30th September, 1963. 124: The appellant company was incorporated in 1939 and it had a managing agency of the Mills. In 1941, the Company resigned from the managing agency and thereafter became a new managing agent. On the resignation of the managing agency, the two members of the Company resiled from the agreement with the Mills and filed a suit for rectification of the register of the Jawahar Mills Ltd., At all material times, the Company continued to act as the managing agent of the Mills till the 30th June, 1939, on which date it resigned the managing agency. The Company did not pay either of the calls but only sent notices to the two members who were the managing agents of the Mills, calling upon them to pay the amount due to them. The Company 's case was that the two members had entered into an agreement with one Mulchand and Govindaraju Chettiar, and that the latter had agreed to pay the shares held by him to the two other members. The Company claimed that the two persons who had signed the agreements were the managing agent and the three other members of the company and that they were entitled to be treated as the members of the managing agents. Held, that the two managing agents were not entitled to any relief under section 38 of the Indian Companies Act. The fact that the two other persons had signed the agreement with Mulchand could not affect the rights of the two managing agencies. The two managing agents had no right to bind the other or to claim any benefit out of the agreement. The two members of Mulchand were not entitled, as a matter of law, to take advantage of the agreement between them. The two persons had no right at all to bind the others. The two directors had acted in good faith and had acted bona fide. The two shareholders had acquiesced in the action of the two members. The two Directors had acted bona fidently and had acted in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The two companies had been formed by the members of MULCO and the two managing Agents had acted bona fides. The two other directors had acted bona facile in taking proceedings under section 38 and the two directors had taken steps to enforce their rights.
3112: The respondent was a citizen of India and entered India on April 4, 1955. He applied for and obtained an Indian visa which was valid upto January 26, 1955. On January 27, 1955, he again applied for and obtain a permit under cl. 7 of the Foreigners Order, 1948 as amended in 1959. The Additional District Magistrate, Silchar convicted him under cl.7 of the Foreigner Order, 1948 read with section 14 of the and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for six months and directed that he should deported from India after he had served out the sentence. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent was not a foreigner when he entered India in April 1955; (ii) the respondent having left India for Pakistan in August 1947 after he had been served out the said sentence, he could not be deemed to be a foreigner within the meaning of article 5 of the Constitution; (iii) the respondent being a natural born British subject, he was governed by the definition of a foreigner in the before the Act was amended in 1957; (iv) the respondent had migrated to Pakistan in August, 1947 after he has opted for service in Pakistan and therefore, he would be deemed to have migrated to India from March 1, 1953; (v) the respondent 's plea that he was not a foreign national was not accepted by the High Court; and (vi) the respondent could not be said to have migted to Pakistan after he had come into India from Pakistan. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was a foreigner even though he had not migrated to any country outside India. [644 C] (ii) The respondent was not entitled to the benefit of article 5. [645 D] (iii) The respondent had not miged to Pakistan during the period of his stay in India. His application for and obtaining a permit under the Foreigners Act, 1946 was rejected by the Additional District Magistrate. The order of the Additional District magistrate was confirmed

3116: The appellant was tried for offenses under sections 120B, 218 and 5(1)(a) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He was acquitted by the special judge. The State appealed to the High Court against his acquittal. The High Court dismissed the appeal against the acquittal of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the case against the appellant had not been proved and the State appeal in that respect also was liable to be dismissed. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence on record clearly showed that the appellant was a member of an unlawful assembly and was a member within the meaning of section 141 I.P.C. The evidence did not show that he was a member or a member of any unlawful assembly. [306 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not be convicted for offense under section 161 I.P C. The charge against him was that he had demanded bribe from P W I Niranjan Dass and had given him a letter written by him to P W I Naranjan Dass. The evidence showed that the letter was written by P W I and was signed by P W 1 Naranjan Das. There is no reason why the evidence should not have been accepted as correct. [307 B] (iii) The evidence showed how the appellant was involved in the trap case. The evidence disclosed that the appellant had demanded and accepted Rs. 2,000 as bribe from P.W. I Naranjana Dass. The appellant had no motive to commit the offence. The evidence also indicated that the appellant wanted to get out of the trouble and that he would be again entangled in the case. [308 A B]
5172: The appellant, a tenant in the premises in question, filed an eviction petition against the respondent, her husband, and two sons, alleging that they were in occupation of the ground floor premises as tenants. The respondent claimed that she could not continue living there permanently or indefinitely and that the accommodation with her niece was limited being only two bed rooms with a common bath room and that her niece was also limited to one bed room and that the other bed room was used for residence by her. The respondent pleaded that she needed the premises for her residence and that she had no means to live in Delhi. The trial court dismissed the eviction petition holding that the respondent was not a tenant but the appellant alone was the tenant and that the respondent had failed to prove that she required the premises for his personal use and that the requirement of the landlady was bona fide. The High Court confirmed the order of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent did not require the premises for residence and that the premises were required for her residence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent is entitled to protection under section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. [811C] 2. The respondent has proved that she requires the premises for herself and her children. The respondent cannot be said to have any means to reside in the premises. [812D] 3. The respondent had taken the plea that she wanted to keep the ground floor accommodation which was vacated and relet in 1974 and 1977 at a higher rate than the one prevailing in the year 1974 and 1977. She had no means. It was her case that she wanted her own house and that she would like to stay with her husband if he wanted to reside with him. The respondent was not able to show any other source of income. [813E F] 4. The respondent did not produce any evidence to show that she had any other source to live in the premises and that she was not in possession of any other accommodation. [814F] 5. The respondent failed to establish that she required it for her residence for her residence, and that she should be allowed to live with her husband.
3668: The appellant was the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family. In the assessment year 1955 56, the appellant claimed partition and separate possession of his share in the joint family property. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant had not produced any document to show that he was a partner in the family. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant 's case was covered by section 25A of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and accordingly dismissed the appeal. On further revision, the High Court held that the income tax authorities were entitled to assess the appellant as an individual for the years in question. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was ill advised to file the writ petition and to pursue the matter upto this Court; (ii) the proceedings for assessment of the income tax for the assessment year 1956 56 were invalid because the appellant was not a partner in a firm which was not a Hindu Undis tinal Firm; (iii) the order passed by the Income tax Officer refusing to record partition and directing the respondent and his subordinates to cancel the assessments made against the appellant was illegal and void; and (iv) the proceedings initiated by the Income Tax Officer for recovery of the taxes so assessed were invalid because no notice under section 25A was served upon the appellant. HELD: (1) The appellant was not entitled to maintain the writ petition. [103 B] (2) The appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced because he did not produce any document to prove that he was the kartar or partner of the family. [104 C] (3) Section 25A of Income Tax Act is a provision providing for the computation of the total income of a Hindu undivided family. It provides for the determination of the tax payable by a Hindu undivided Family by making an application to the Income tax officer for the purpose of making an assessment. The Income Tax Officer has to make an enquiry into the facts and determine the amount of tax due from the person concerned. If the Income tax authority finds that the applicant is not liable to pay the tax, then he can proceed to make an assessment. [105 D E]
364: The petitioners, who were the owners of certain properties in Touzi No. 28 of the Collectorate of Hazaribagh, filed a suit against the State Government and the Company for a declaration that the properties were not vested in the State on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, and for possession of the same. The Company contended that the lands were not included in the estate of the petitioners as they did not vest in the State under the provisions of the 990 Act. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 declaring that the estate of petitioner No. 1 was not vested in it. On the question whether the lands were 'land ' within the meaning of the 991 Act, HELD: (1) The Act does not contemplate vesting of any interest in the property by the State Government. It only contemplates vesting of the property in the State. [992 B] (2) The Act is intended to provide for the acquisition of estates and to make provision for the distribution of compensation among the proprietors of the estates. Section 7 of the Act provides for the vesting of the estate in the State and the vesting of all rights therein in the State, including the right to recover rent or other dues payable to the proprietor. The vesting of the land in the State is complete when the State Government issues a notification under s.3(1) of the Act. The vesting takes place when the State has acquired the interest in the land. The vesting does take place when the interest vests in the State but does not take place until the State Government issue a notification under sub section (4). [993 C F] (3) The vesting of an interest in the estate does not take effect unless the State Government gives notice to the persons interested that the interest will be acquired. The vesting is complete when both the parties have given their consent in writing to the State Government to acquire the interest. [994 D] (4) The vesting does not take away the title of the State Government in respect of the land which vests in it. The vesting can take place only after the State Government has given its consent in writing. [995 E]
2670: The assessee was a registered shareholder of the Kedarnath Jute Manufacturing Co. Ltd., which was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. In its assessment for the year 1956 57 for which the previous year ended September 30, 1955, the assessee purchased 11,900 shares of Kedarnth Jute Manufacturing Company, and credited it to the profit and loss appropriation account. The assessee received dividend on the said shares from the company in the accounting period. The assessee claimed that as the arrear dividends pertained to the years 1945 to 1954, the assessee was not liable to tax as income. Held, that the question whether the sum of Rs. 43,925/ received by the assessee represented business income arising under section 10(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, did not correctly and accurately describe the stand and contention taken by the assessee throughout which was that no part of the arrear dividends paid by the assessee was income at all liable to tax. The assessee had a right to claim the dividend declared by the company in respect of the years 1945, 1946 and 1946. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 12 of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee was entitled to deduct the amount of dividend received by it from the company 's profits and gains of the previous year.
49: The respondent firm was a private limited company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of cloth. In 1941, the appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent firm for supply of goods to the respondent firm. The respondent firm delivered to the appellant bales of cloth which were not supplied by the appellant. The appellant sent a telegraphic notice to the respondent 's firm on 20th November, 1941, to the effect that the respondent firm had failed to deliver to them the goods mentioned in the letter dated 20th November 1941, and that the goods should be delivered by the 17th November,41, and that they should be delivered at the appellant 's factory at Kanpur. The respondent 's main plea was that the performance of the contract had been frustrated by circumstances beyond their control and hence the appellant ' s claim must fail. Held, that the appellant ' could not succeed in its defence on the ground that the performance was not complete when it received the goods from the respondent firm and that the contract was not completed. The contract was not complete till the goods were delivered to the respondent. The contract did not create any obligation or liability. The contract merely required the delivery of the goods to the appellant. It was not a mere formality but a term of the contract between the parties. The contract provided that the goods were to be delivered to the buyer at the time and place specified therein. The contract further stipulated that the goods would be delivered to him at the time of the delivery and not thereafter. The contract also contained an express condition that the goods shall be delivered to them at the time agreed upon. The contract therefore did not create an obligation or liability on the part of the respondent firm to deliver the goods at the time specified. The contract, therefore, did not create a right or liability on behalf of the respondent.

1432: The appellants and the deceased were charged under section 302 read with section 149, I.P.C. for having committed murder of one Raja Ram Singh. The prosecution case was that the appellants had collected in front of the house of Kali Charan appellant, two of them armed with lathis, one of them spears and another with a gun. The first information report was lodged at about 3 30 p.m. on July 28, 1957, by the informant who was an eye witness to the occurrence. The second information report was recorded at 3 30 p.,m. on the same day. The first Information Report was registered at 4 30 p. m. on July 29, 1957, and the investigation commenced on July 29. The Investigating Officer prepared the inquest reports and sent the dead body for post mortem examination. The doctor who conducted the autopsy found that the death was due to asphyxia as a result of ante mortem injuries which were sufficient in ordinary course of nature to cause death. The appellants were convicted under section 302/149, I. P. C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the appeal against the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the first information report did not mention the names of the assailants but only mentioned the names of some of the accused; (2) the first statement made by the deceased before the police was inadmissible because he was not examined by the prosecution; (3) the first report was not proved in accordance with law; and (4) the second statement was not admissible in evidence. [827 F] (2) The first information Report was not admissible under section 162, Cr. P.C. 3072: The appellant, a religious and charitable institution, was appointed as an Archaka of the temple of the respondent. The respondent, who was the manager of the temple, was appointed by the State Government to perform the functions of the office of Archakas in the temple. The appellant challenged the appointment of the respondent under section 55(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Institutions (Officers and Servants) Act, 1960, on the ground that the appointment was contrary to the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appointment of a person as an Ar chakadar was not valid under section 55 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment could be made only by the State government and not by the trustee of the temple. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of a trustee is not invalid merely because he has been authorised to appoint a fit person to perform the duties of the office or to discharge the functions of a trustee. [819B] 2. The appointment can be made by the State or by any authority subordinate to it. But the State cannot make such appointments without the consent of the authority competent to remove the person in accordance with law. [820C] 3. The appointment may be made by a duly constituted body or authority which, after due enquiry, finds it necessary to remove its name from the list of voters. [821D E] 4. The appointment is not invalid if it is made by the authority empowered to remove the public servant. [822F] 5. The appointment does not confer on the public servant a title to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation. 5205: The petitioners in the petitions were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They challenged the validity of clause (3) of Article 371 D read with Clause (5) of Article 372 of the Constitution on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the proviso to Clause (5), which is a substantive provision, cannot be said to have been incorporated by reference to the proviso. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to Clause(5) is not merely procedural but is also substantive. It is only procedural and not substantive. [885 H] 2. The proviso is not merely a procedural provision. It is essentially a substantive provision. It has been introduced for the first time after the Constitution came into force. It is an additional safeguard against any possible conflict between the provisions of the Constitution and the proviso. It is a substantive right. It is not merely the procedural right. It must be given its full play. [886 G H; 887 A B] 3. The proviso does not create any new rights of appeal or revision. It merely provides that the State Government may by special order made in writing and for reasons to be specified therein, modify or annul any order of the Administrative Tribunal before it becomes effective and in such a case, the order of the Adminis trative Tribunal before it became effective and insuch a case, it shall have effect only in such modified form or be no effect, as the case may be. [887 C D] 4. The proviso cannot be construed as creating any new right of appeal or enhancement of pension payable to the officers who are already in service. [888 E] 5. The proviso applies only to cases where the Administrative Tribunal is constituted under the Act. It does not apply to cases where there is no existing right of appeal. [889 F] 6. The proviso clearly indicates that the power conferred by it on the Administrative Tribunal can be exercised only if it is satisfied that the conditions mentioned in Clauses (a) to (e) of Article 217(D) are fulfilled. [894 G]
