2587: The respondent purchased cotton seeds from the appellant company. The appellant company sold them to registered dealers and claimed deduction under section 5 (2) (a) (vi) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The assessing authority did not allow the deduction holding that the goods were not the goods in respect of which purchase tax had been levied. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the assessment order. The High Court allowed the writ petition on the ground that the goods sold by the respondent were not the same as those purchased by the registered dealers. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was entitled to the exemption under section 5(2)(a)(vi) of Act No. 46 of 1948. 4741: The petitioners who were members of the Maharashtra State Civil Service (Executive Branch) and Members of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission (M.P.S.C.) had applied for admission to the State lotteries in the State of Maharashtra, but they were denied admission on the ground that the State lottery tickets were not sold within the State. They challenged the validity of the ban imposed by the Government of Maharashtra on the sale of outside State lottery tickets. The petitioners contended that the Union Government had no authority to impose such a ban as it was not competent to do so under article 258(1) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The ban imposed by article 258 is valid and does not contravene the provisions of article 298 of the Constitution; (ii) The ban is not unreasonable because it is not inconsistent with the provisions of Article 19(6). (iii) The ban cannot be held to be invalid merely because it is imposed after the commencement of the Constitution or after its enforcement. (iv) The ban can only operate if it is consistent with the provisions contained in article 298. (v) The ban could not be said to be inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution and therefore, the ban cannot be struck down.

The appellant challenged the grant of the permit by filing a writ petition before the High Court. 4235: The appellant tenant gave a lease of two plots to the respondent tenant for a period of 15 years commencing from 1st December, 1948. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent tenant on the ground that he was a statutory tenant of the land and that he had become a statutory tenant under section 2(g) of the Bombay Rent Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. HELD: (i) The appellant tenant is not entitled to the protection of the Act because the respondent tenant has failed and neglected to pay the arrears of rent and taxes due in relation to the lands and buildings which he erected. [912B] (ii) The appellant is not entitled either to the protection or to the benefit of the Bombay Act. The respondent is not entitled, therefore, to the protection. [913C D] (iii) The appellant cannot enforce the terms of the contract between the parties. The respondent has no right to claim the protection of section 28 of the Bombay Tenancy Act. 4259: The petitioner was convicted for an offence of rape under section 376 I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In this special leave petition, it is contended that there was no corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix and her evidence was not worthy of credence. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, HELD: 1. The conviction of the petitioner for an offence under section 376 IPC cannot be sustained on the mere absence of corroborative evidence. [405D] 2.1 The law requires a careful scrutiny of the testimony by the court and the judge before whom the case reaches for conviction. If the court finds that the testimony of a witness has been tutored or is otherwise unacceptable, it must record its satisfaction that such evidence is reliable and trustworthy. It is only in exceptional cases where the court finds it absolutely unsafe to act upon the testimony of such witness as a result of the Munsif 's observation, or the statement made by him while deposing as a witness in the case, that the court can look into the surrounding circumstances and find out whether corroboration is necessary. [404E F] 3.1 The court should carefully examine the testimony of each witness and if satisfied that the testimony is reliable, reasonable and trustworthy, it may accept the same. But if it does not believe the testimony of any witness, then it would be open to the court to consider the reasons given by the witnesses for discarding their testimony. [403A B] 4.1 The courts have to take judicial notice of the fact that the victim of sexual assault is a child of tender age. The court should also bear in mind that the victim is a person who has lost his sight and is unable to speak. [402B C]

2093: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling groundnut oil. The company had imposed a ban on forward trading in groundnuts and refined groundnut seed. The company did not follow the rule "first come, last go" as laid down by the Supreme Court in its decision in the case of State of Mysore vs M/s. C. Papayya and Ors., [1960] 1 S.C.R. 787. The company 's case was that the management had acted mala fide in retrenching the workmen. The Labour Court accepted the contention of the workmen and held that departure from a principle which was part of the law relating to industrial employment rendered the retrenchment of all workmen could not exceed the number retained by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the management had not followed the rule "First come, last going" and (ii) the rule "second come, last gone" was not applicable to the facts of the case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The management has recorded a resolution which sets out the reasons for retention of the employees who were affected by the departure from the rule. The management cannot be allowed to take advantage of the said resolution if it is found that the said reason was not properly recorded. [772B] (a) The management had not adopted any other method or procedure which would have been open to it. It had not taken into account the fact that the appellant had been working for more than 240 days in a year. The management had failed to prove that the said period was not calculated according to the practice prevalent in the industry. [773E F] (b) The management was justified in taking the view that the appellant was not justified in taking a contrary view. [774A B] (c) The management could not be permitted to take advantage under the rule. [775F] (d) The management cannot take advantage of its own wrong. [776G] (e) The management can take advantage of a mistake committed by the management. [777D]

1076: The assessees were assessed to Income tax for the chargeable accounting periods ending April 13, 1943, April 12, 1944, April 12. 1945, and April 12, 1948. The assessees contended that they had paid to their employees in the years of account 1942 43 to 1947 48 under agreements executed from time to time a share in the special emergency commission received by them from the I. In appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order which allowed the amount of commission paid to the employees of the tax payer may be permitted as a deduction in the light of section 10(2)(x) of the Income tax Act and r. 12 of Sch. 1 to the Excess Profits Tax Act. Held, that the test of reasonableness is not whether prescribed by any commercial or commercial law but whether reasonable standard has been followed in making the payment; and where the payment is made by the assessee it must be shown that the payment was made in accordance with the practice prevailing in the country in which the payments are made. Held, further, that the object of the provision contained in s.10(2)(X) of the Indian Income tax Act is to enable the assessee to claim deduction in respect of expenses incurred in excess of the amount which he receives as remuneration under an agreement entered into by him with his employer. The object of the provisions of the Act is to provide for the levy of income tax on the assessee at a certain percentage of his net profits and to prevent evasion of tax. The object is to ensure that the assessee does not get double benefits in respect of the same year. The object being to give relief to the assessee in case of loss, the expenditure should be allowed as a deduction.

4798: The respondent was the owner of a house in Bombay. He served a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the Dominion of India through the Defence Secretary under section 80, Indian Evidence Act, to the effect that he had been appointed as a trustee for the State of Bombay and that he should be discharged from his duties as such. The appellant contended that the notice was not sufficient because it did not specify the names and addresses of all the trustees and therefore the suit was not maintainable. Held, that the notice must be deemed to have been given by two out of three plaintiffs and the suit was competent. The notice must be held to be valid if it substantially complied with the requirements of s.80 of the Code. The notice is required to state the cause of action and the reliefs claimed. It does not require any particular form or procedure but merely requires the particulars of the claim to be stated. The notice need not contain the name of the person or persons against whom the suit is sought to be instituted; it may also contain the name or names of the persons against whom they are sought to be sued. In the present case, the notice was issued by the Government of Bombay and not by the Union of India. The notice was not necessary because it was addressed to the Secretary of State for India. The High Court was wrong in holding that the notice could not be said to be proper unless it was signed by the Secretary of the State. The notice should be read as a whole and the words "in the case of a public officer" should be construed as referring to the authority which has to issue the notice.
532: The respondent was dismissed from service under the State Government on December 21, 1948. He filed a revision application before the Inspector General of Police which was rejected by the Inspector General on April 22, 1950. The respondent then moved the High Court for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of dismissal passed against him and for his reinstatement in service with all back wages. The High Court held that the order of the Inspector General dismissing the respondent was not final as it had not become final until the Inspector General gave his decision on the revision petition and that as the last mentioned order had been passed after the Constitution had come into force, the respondent could not be permitted to do so for the first time on a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition and the High Court should have entertained it and set aside the order of its own. The High Courts power to issue writs is discretionary and the discretion must be exercised judicially having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not correct to say that the High Courts are invested with wide powers under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and they can only exercise such powers in cases where the interest of justice requires interference or there is an error of law apparent on the face of the record. The High courts cannot interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the authorities below when they have acted within their limits. If there is some legal evidence on which the findings can be based, the adequacy or sufficiency of that evidence is a matter which the High Court can examine in exercising its extraordinary jurisdiction. The High court has no jurisdiction to reappraise the evidence and substitute its own conclusion for that of the authority conducting the enquiry or revising it if the finding is perverse. The High 'Court could not, however, interfere with the orders of the authorities holding the enquiry were illegal or without jurisdiction. The jurisdiction of the High Court to issue a writ of Certiorari is limited to seeing that the tribunal functions illegally or improperly and is not acting as an appellate authority. The jurisdiction to issue a prerogative writ is discretionary and has to be exercised on sound judicial principles. 2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1957, were made by the Governor of Mysore under article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 4 of the said Rules provided that recruitment to a service or post is to be made by selection and consultation with the Commission was required. The Mysore Public Works Department Officers ' Recruitment Rules, 1957 were framed in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of Constitution. The Mysore State Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 1959, were amended from time to time. The Mysore Government issued a Notification dated October 1, 1958, appointing Assistant Engineers and Assistant Engineers in the Executive Cadre of the Mysore Public Works Departments as Assistant Engineers for a period of one year. The appellants who were working as Assistant Engineers in various departments of the State Government challenged the validity of the said Notification on the ground that it violated their fundamental right guaranteed under articles 14 and 16(1)(c) of the Constitution and that they had been discriminated against arbitrarily and that the rules were violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they contravened the provisions of article 335 of the Constitution which enjoined upon the State Government to consult the Commission before making appointments to the posts of Assistant Engineers and determining the conditions of service of the Assistant Engineers. Held: (i) Article 309 of the constitution does not contemplate any legislative power to enact laws. It only provides for the framing of rules for regulating the conditions of services of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State. The power to make rules under article 309 is subject to the provisions of entry 56 of List I and entry 7 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power of the State Legislature to legislate in respect of matters enumerated in List II of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution cannot be restricted by any other entry in the Constitution. In the present case, there can be no doubt that the power to prescribe qualifications for appointment to the posts in question is vested in the Governor. The power under entry 7 of the Concurrent List is exercisable by the Governor and not by the President. The power is subject to entries 6 and 7 of List I of the Seventh Scheduled to the Constitution and entries 6 and 8 of List III. The power being subject to entries 62 and 66
2736: The plaintiffs, who were the sons of a Hindu, adopted plaintiff No. 2 as a son and partitioned the property in dispute between them and the defendants. After the death of their father, the widow of the deceased, the first defendant, adopted plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2, and the second defendant, adopted the third defendant, the first respondent. The first defendant was not given any consent to the adoption of plaintiff No.2 by plaintiff No. 1. The first plaintiff, however, filed an application for being impleaded as a party to the suit. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the adoption was not valid. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the evidence showed that the adoption of the first plaintiff was made with the object of proper performance of ceremonies for the benefit of her deceased husband and other ancestors, though she had no authority to do so. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) the evidence showed the motive of the widow, plaintiff No. I, for making the adoption; (2) the evidence shows that the adoption took place after the death of the first defendant 's husband; (3) the evidence also indicated that the adoption had been made with the intention of proper performance; and (4) the evidence clearly established that the adoption did not amount to a fraud or coercion. HELD : (i) The evidence showed that there was nothing to show that the adoption made by plaintiff No, 2 was in accordance with law. [501 B] (ii) The evidence clearly established the fact that the adoption deed was executed by plaintiff No., 2 with the object, of proper performance, of the ceremonies for her deceased husband. [502 C] (iii) There is no reason why the evidence should be rejected because the evidence does not establish that the adoption has taken place in accordance with the custom. [503 D] (iv) The evidence establishes that the adoption is not illegal. [504 F] (v) The evidence shows that there was no occasion for the widow, the natural mother, or the natural sister of the first appellant, to make the adoption. [505 E]

6148: The petitioners, who were working as Directors of the Nationalised Banks, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the circular dated March 5, 1970 issued by the Central Government. They contended that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and the Natio nalisation Scheme, 1980. The petitioners also contended that the Circular is contrary to Section 3(1)(c) of the Act and the Scheme insofar as it cuts at the root of representative form of selection for appointment to the Board of Directors as contemplated by the statute. The petitioners further contended that the impugned circular is contrary t o the letter and spirit of the Act, and the Scheme so far as it cut s at the root or the representative form of selecti on is concerned. Dismissing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The circular in question does not lay down any procedure for selection of the non workman Director. The only requirement postulated is consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. [766C] 2. The object of the Act is to provide for the better management of the affairs of the banking companies. It is intended to give effect to the provisions of the Act. The Act has been enacted to regulate the business of banking companies. The object is to ensure that the banking industry is efficiently run and the banking industry goes into production. The object can be achieved if the banking sector is allowed to go out of the country. The object may be to make provision for the proper management of the banking industry. The object should be to secure the interests of the banking sector. [767D E]
3110: The appellant 's land was acquired by the Government for the purpose of construction of a Club. The Land Acquisition Officer, Ranchi, assessed the market value of the land at Rs. 90,000/ per acre and awarded compensation for the same. On appeal, the High Court reduced the compensation to Rs. 90/ per acre. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in not taking into consideration the fact that the land was situated on the main Ranchi Chaibasa Road, a strong objection was taken against adopting the price as a basis because it was not only 1/2 mile away from the land under acquisition but what was sold was only the leasehold right in the land. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the land in question is situated on the road side and not on the main road. [229C] (a) The land in question was situated on a very short distance from the land acquired. It was not just and proper to adopt the price as the basis for determining the market value. [230B] (b) The High court has also rightly pointed out that the land which was acquired was situated on an interior part of the road and was not on the roadside. The land in the present case was situated on its eastern side. There was no evidence to show that in fact there had been any depreciation in the land in dispute. [231E F] (c) The High Commission report shows that the land had been acquired for the purpose mentioned in the sale deed. The land was situated in a narrow lane and was not suitable for the purpose. The land being situated on the east side of the road, it could not be said that it was not suitable or that it would have been more suitable for the purposes of the land. [233A B] (d) The High Commissioner report shows that there was no evidence whatsoever to show that the land comprised in the sale deeds was suitable for the development of the land and the land was not suitable. [234F] (e) The High Commissiion did not take into account the fact that there was a small strip of land
273: The appellant, a resident of Pakistan, was tried for an offence under section 3(1) (a) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He filed a complaint against him before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon who took cognizance of it on the ground that he had acquired the citizenship of Pakistan by reason of his migration from Pakistan to India. The trial court held that the appellant could not be said to have acquired the citizenship because he did not come within the definition of " citizen " in section 2(2)(b) of the Act. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's imprisonment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a citizen of India at all as he never intended to remain in India for any length of time and he could not therefore be said to be a citizen of Pakistan. [701 B] (ii) The word "resident" has been defined in section 2 (4) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which defines the expression "person" to mean "any person who is or was a citizen of a foreign country". The word "person" has also been defined in the General Clauses Acts of the United Kingdom. [702 C D] (iii) The word 'citizen' in section 2 of the General clauses Act means a person who has the right to enter into contract with the Government of India. The word 'person ' in section 2 has been used in the sense of a citizen of the country. [703 E F] (iv) The word person 'in section 2(4) of Act 1 of 1947, is defined in section 3(3) to include a foreigner. [704 A] (v) The word `foreigner ' in section 3 (3) means a person whose name is entered in the electoral roll of a constituency for the time being in force. [705 G] (vi) The word Native Indian 'or Foreign ' shall have the same meaning as in the Indian Penal code. [706 B] (vii) The word native Indian 'and Foreign ' shall mean a person who is a national of Pakistan and who has entered India after the partition of India
387: The appellants were charged with having committed offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. The jury returned a majority verdict that both the appellants were guilty of the offence under section 435 and were sentenced to six months ' rigorous imprisonment each. The Assistant Sessions Judge disagreed with the said verdict and made a reference to the High Court stating in the letter of reference that on the evidence recorded before him the appellants had been in possession of the Palani and Punjaul but were dispossessed of the same some time prior to the passing of the decree in the title suit, and that the reference was in the circumstances not competent. The appellants obtained from this Court special leave to appeal under article 136 of the Constitution and hence this appeal. Held, that the appellants were entitled to have their convictions set aside. The appellants were not guilty of the offences under sections 403 and 435 of the Indian penal Code and were therefore liable to be acquitted. The appellants could not be convicted for the offences under section 434 or section 435 of Indian Penal Code because they were not guilty.
2470: The respondent firm was awarded a contract for the supply of timber to the appellant. The contract contained an arbitration clause which provided that the respondent firm would offer inspection of the store at its own premises at Halisahaar and Lillooah. The appellant refused to do so on the ground that the respondent had not been able to produce any evidence in support of its claim. The Subordinate Judge held that the dispute regarding the excess quantity of timber alleged to have been delivered by the respondent firm was not a dispute arising under the contract but was a matter between the parties. On appeal, the High Court held that the disputes were not covered by the arbitration agreement and hence the arbitrators had no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the dispute about the excess quantity was not a claim arising out of the contract; that the dispute was not a question of law or fact but merely a question of fact and therefore the arbitrators had jurisdiction to decide the matter. HELD: (i) The dispute regarding the amount of compensation for deterioration of the stock was not a matter between two parties. It was not a case of a breach of contract. [287 F] (ii) The dispute relating to the excess quantity could be decided only by the arbitrators appointed by the parties. The arbitrators had no power to decide the dispute as they did not possess the power to decide it. [288 B C] (iii) The arbitrator had no jurisdiction in the present case to decide the question whether the respondent firm had suffered loss due to the deterioration of stock. [289 D]

6683: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the same and set aside the conviction and sentence passed against him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court has gravely erred in allowing the second revision petition filed by the respondent without examining the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the defence witnesses and recording the statements of the accused under Section 342 of the old Code, the High Court had failed to exercise its jurisdiction under section 540 of the Code and thereby committed a gross error in allowing the two applications both of the appellant and the respondent for recalling them for further examination under section 537 of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the Court under section 538 of the Code is not confined only to cases where the accused is charged with the offence of murder but also to cases where he is charged with murder. [716B] 2. It is well settled that the powers under section 539 are discretionary and they should be exercised sparingly and cautiously. [717C D] 3. The High Court while exercising its revisional jurisdiction under section 397 of the Code cannot interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial court as if sitting in appeal over the decision of the trial court. [718E F] 4. The High court can examine the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order and re-appreciate the evidence on record. [719F G]
1878: The Dual Auto Mill was a large industry and it had several branches. It was granted on January 21, 1962 special leave to appeal against the award of the Third Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal dated September 29, 1962. The workmen belonged to what is described as the Baby Mill. These workmen belonged to the Dual Automobiles and the twelfth was working on what is described in the Dual auto mill. These workmen were dismissed after a domestic enquiry commenced on February 4, 1965. The workmen did not choose to be present before the Tribunal because they refused to do so. The workmen raised an industrial dispute which was referred for adjudication by the State Government under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that the enquiry was not proper and some of the witnesses were re examined before the Tribunal whose verdict was against the Company and hence this appeal. The workmen contended that the enquiry should have been set aside on the ground that the enquiry itself was defective. The management contended that the evidence adduced before the Tribunal consisted only of the statements made by the workmen and no other persons who could have given any statement in answer to the charge. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the workmen and held that the inquiry was not proper. The workmen appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the enquiry being fair and proper, the Tribunal was justified in interfering with the findings of the Enquiry Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in its conclusion that the enquiry conducted by the Management was not proper or legal. [851C] (ii)The Tribunal was wrong in its view that the enquiry must have been held properly. The Tribunal was entitled to look into the evidence and come to its own conclusion. [852A] (iii)The Tribunal has erred in law in holding that the punishment imposed on the workmen was disproportionate to the charges proved. [853D] (iv)The Tribunal had gone wrong in its finding that the enquiry is not proper. [854F] (v)The Tribunal committed serious error in holding that there was violation of principles of natural justice. [855B]
6474: The appellant, a resident of India and a resident of the Eastern India, entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the formation of a National Capital Territory of Delhi known as the North East Frontier Agency. Under the agreement, the appellant was to be allotted a territory known as the South East Frontiers Agency. The agreement provided that the appellant "shall not be entitled to any compensation or damages in respect of the land allotted to him except for the use of the land by the Government of Delhi and the Union Territory of Delhi". The agreement further provided that the allotment shall be made only from the date of the agreement and not earlier. The appellant 's case is that the agreement was not binding on him and he was entitled to retain the land allotted. The appellant contended that the agreement did not come into effect when it was signed by the Government and that the agreement had no legal force. The High Court held that the agreement could not be said to have been executed by the Government. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The agreement does not amount to cession of any part of the territory of India. [911B] 1.2 The agreement does neither create nor extinguish any existing right in the territory of the country. It merely provides that the agreement shall remain in force for a period of one year from the date on which the agreement comes into force. The agreement has nothing to do with the area of the territory. It is not intended to operate upon the territory of any other country. [912C D] 1.3 The agreement does no more than provide for the allocation of the land to the appellant. The agreement does nothing more than providing for the allotment of the land. [913D] 1.4 The agreement does n ot refer to the agreement of 1974. The agreement also does not refer to the fact that the agreement would continue to exist after the agreement came into force. [914E] 1.5 The agreement does none of the two things. It is intended to operate in respect of all the territories of India. It is meant to operate in relation to all the territories. 3303: The appellant, a tenant in respect of the land in question, was allotted a land in the State of Karnataka. He filed an application for allotment of the land to him under section 19B of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961. The Land Tribunal rejected his application on the ground that he had not been able to prove that he was a small farmer and that he was not entitled to be allotted any land. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the land was not acquired by voluntary transfer but by inheritance or other operation of law; (ii) the land could not have been allotted to a person who was a small landowner and (iii) the land should have been allotted only to a person whose land was acquired by voluntary transfers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The land was not a small land owner but was a small holder. [631C] 2. The land could not be allotted to a tenant who was a big landowner. The land would go to the landless poor person. It is not possible to say that the land was acquired for the purpose of a small landowner. [632F] 3. The land cannot be allotted to the small landowner. The small landowner can be given the land which is available for allotment to him. [633A] 4. The land has to be used for the purpose for which it is allotted. [634E] 5. The land must be used for a small landowner as a whole. [635G] 636 A] 636 1. The Act does not provide for the acquisition of land by voluntary transfer. The Act provides for the acquisition by voluntary transfer of land. Section 10(1)(b) provides that the surplus area shall be determined after making such deductions from the total holding of the land owner as may be prescribed. [637D]

The scheme also provided that the State Transport Undertaking may, after giving due notice to all the persons likely to be affected by it make an application to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal for exemption from the scheme. The appellant State Government issued a notification dated June 4. 1975 exempting the routes specified therein from the operation of the scheme. It is not necessary that there should be a complete ban on the operation of any particular scheme. The scheme has to be published in the Official Gazette and also in such other manner as the State Government may direct. [68E F] 1.3 The scheme does not suffer from any infirmity. The scheme provides that the routes mentioned therein shall be operated in the notified areas or routes. The schemes are intended to provide for an efficient, viable, economical, properly coordinating road transport service and for the purpose of providing an efficient, economical or properly
3971: The appellants were importers of yarn. They paid duty under protest and applied for refund of the excess duty paid on the ground that the goods were assessed to duty at a certain figure. The Customs Authorities rejected their applications, but they filed appeals before the Central Government. The Central Government dismissed the appeals. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amended section 14 of the Act was applicable to the consignments in question as the goods had been received, stored and assessed to duty before the promulgation of the Ordinance, and that the appellants were entitled to refund of the amount paid under protest. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The amended section 14 is not applicable to the cases in which the goods have been received, kept or assessed to duty prior to the promulgation. [311C] (2) Section 15(1)(a) of the Act provides that if any person makes an application for refund of any duty paid by him, he may make an application for such refund to the proper officer. The appellants paid the duty under protest. The Central Govt. rightly refused to grant refund. [312E F] (3) The appellants did not pay the duty under the amended section. [313B] (4) The amended provision applies only to cases where the goods have already been cleared for home consumption. It does not apply to cases where there has been no assessment of duty. [314F] (5) The appellants were not entitled to refund because the amended provisions are not applicable to them. [315G]
3896: The assessee was a private contractor. He carried out certain works on behalf of the Government and in view of a conflict of decisions on the point among different High Courts, the matter was referred to a Full Bench. The Full Bench held that the cost of stores or material supplied by the Government to the assessee could not be added to the figure of cash payments received by the assessee on the ground that the stores (material) supplied by the Department to the assessee were 'timations ' received by the Department while ascertaining the profits of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of Revenue that the cost incurred by the assessee for the purpose of carrying on the work should be taken into consideration while estimating the profit of the assessee and that the amount paid by the assessee towards the price of the stores should be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. HELD: 1. The cost of stores/material supplied by the assessee to the assessee cannot be added to his income from the contract. [22G] 2. The cost incurred by an assessee for the purposes of carrying on a business is not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, because it is a matter of common knowledge that the assessee has no concern with the transactions which are entered into by him in the course of his business. [23F] 3. The cost to the contractor is not necessarily the real value of the goods purchased by him but the real value is the real value. [24H; 25A] 4. The cost must be the real value or the real value as ascertained by the assessee himself and not merely by the actual payment made by the assessee. [25B] 5. The cost is the real price of the goods sold by the assessee and not the real price. [26C] 6. The cost should be the real price at which the goods are sold by the contractor. [27D] 7. The cost may include the cost of the materials used in the construction of the building, the cost of labour employed, the cost incurred in the execution of the building and the cost of interest on loans and advances. [28E]
3794: The respondent was an employee of the Electricity Board. He was served with a charge sheet on 1st October, 1957 alleging that he had committed certain irregularities in the preparation of the departmental exam sation and that he had failed to pass the examination within the prescribed time. The charges were enquired into by the Enquiry Officer who found him guilty of all the charges. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of his dismissal from service as also the order of the appellate authority rejecting his appeal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to promotion as he had not passed the examination. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions of the Board dated 19th May, 1969 and 5th January, 1970 as having been made under section 79(c) of the Act and that the High court should have held that the respondent could not be said to have passed the S.A.S. examination before the date of passing the examination. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the Board is competent to issue the impugned orders. [866F] (2) The High court was right in its conclusion that the respondent cannot claim promotion as of right since he had not cleared the S. A.S. Examination. [867C] (3) The High Cour t was wrong in holding that the Board was competent to issue such orders. [886D] (4) The High 'Court was right in holding that there was no substance in the contention of the respondent that the Board could not issue the impugned order. [887E]
5965: The respondent assessee was a company belonging to the same group. In its agreement for the Assessment Year 1959 60, the respondent claimed deduction in respect of the loss of the sale of certain shares of Bharat Starch & Chemicals Ltd. and Greaves Cotton & Co. Ltd. The Income tax Officer took the view that the sale had been affected only to enable the assessee to claim the loss and could not be allowed as genuine. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner accepted this finding and held that these shares were sold to a company which was an allied concern of the assessee. The Tribunal also took the view on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties that the shares had been sold to a subsidiary company of the assessee and that the shares were purchased by the subsidiary company. The Tribunal further held that the shares did not have any value or market value and hence, they were not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. On reference, the High Court held that the transactions entered into by the assessee in the purchase and sale of shares of Bharat Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. amounted to a capital loss and not a business loss. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the transactions in question were not genuine. [766A] (ii) The Tribunal had rightly relied upon the fact that the shares in question were purchased by a subsidiary company and the shares were acquired by the subsidiary companies. The Tribunal has given cogent reasons for coming to the conclusion that the transactions were genuine. [776B] (iii) The Tribunal has taken the correct view of the matter. [773C] (iv) The Tribunal is justified in taking the view that there was no sale of the shares in the instant case. The shares were purchased in the name of the subsidiary company and were transferred to the subsidiary company in the name and style of the subsidiary. The subsidiary company was a subsidiary of the assessee company. The subsidiary companies were incorporated in the year of account. The subsidiary was a subsidiary company. It was a subsidiary and a subsidiary company formed with the object of acquiring the shares of the subsidiary companies and selling them to its subsidiaries. The subsidiary Companies were incorporated in January,
748: The appellant, a contractor, was employed by the respondents in the factory of the respondent. He claimed that he had been employed in the factory as a workman under section 2(1) (m) of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948, and as such he was entitled to overtime wages under section 59 of the said Act. The claim made by him was rejected by the Railway authorities on the ground that the appellant 's establishment was not a factory within the meaning of section 2(i)(m). The appellant filed an application before the Payment of Wages Authority for making a claim for overtime wages under the proviso to section 59 of that Act. The application was dismissed by the authority on the ground of delay. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution against the order of the authority. The High Court held that the appellant was not a worker within the meaning Of section 2(k) of the Act and that the claim made by the appellant was barred by limitation. It also held that the claim was barred by the proviso to sub section (2) of section 59 of Act II of 1948. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a worker within section 2(kk) of the said act because the definition of " factory" in section 2(j) of the , does not apply to the facts of the present case. The definition of " Factory" in section2(j) is not exhaustive but only illustrative. The definition is inclusive and includes all factories or establishments in which persons are employed. In view of the definition of a factory in section 2 (j), it cannot be said that the appellant is a worker within that definition. The definition does not include factories or establishments mentioned in section 2. The definition therefore does not exclude factories or establishments from the purview of the definition. The appellant was not an employee within the meaning given to it in section 2 of the Act. The appellant 's case was that he was a worker within its meaning and that he was entitled under section 59 to overtime wages.

4035: The appellant was detained under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971. The High Court rejected the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the order of detention must always be made before or during prosecution; (ii) that the detaining authority must invariably consider the possibility of a prosecution being launched; (iii) that the question whether the facts disclosed the tendency of the petitioner to act prejudicially in the manner mentioned in the detention order would vitiate the order of preventive detention is not considered by the High Court; (iv) that the detenu 's right to make an effective representation against the order of his detention has been infringed because the detaining authority did not apply its mind to the question whether a person should be prosecuted before making an order of detention. HELD : (i) The question as to whether the facts disclose the tendency of a person to act prejudicially and prejudicially in the matter of dealing with persons involved in the smuggling activities cannot be decided merely by reference to the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority but by reference to all the relevant circumstances including the nature of the offences committed by the detenu. It is not possible to lay down any rigid rules as to what principles shall have to be applied in each individual case and it will depend upon the facts of each case. [587 B C] (iii) The question about the sufficiency of the grounds for the making of the order of the detention is primarily for the detaining authority to decide and not for the court to decide. The provisional liquidator took charge of the textile undertaking on November 30, 1966 and the management of the textile undertakings was taken over by the Government on December 31, 1966. The respondent filed an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying that the provisional liquidator be directed to handover the management of its textile undertakings to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisional Liquidator had no jurisdiction to take over the management of a textile undertaking. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The Provisional Liquidator is not a person authorised or competent to act as such in any matter relating to the textile industry. He has only the power to take over management of the Textile Undertaking. [942C] (ii) The expression "any other person" in sub section (2) of section 4 of the Act means a person who is authorised or competent under the law to take over and which has been authorised by the Central Government by a notified order made under section 18A of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 to be a sick textile undertaking. The expression "a textile undertaking" in sub clause (i) of section 2(d) includes a textile undertaking which is deemed to be a textile undertaking under sub section (3) of section 3 of the Act and the expression "an industrial undertaking" in the second proviso to sub section (5) of section 5 of the Act would include a textile undertaking also. [943D E]
6753: The decree holders filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 5001/13/6 against the judgment debtor, Gopal Rao Mutatkar and G.R. Wakhle in the execution proceedings on the ground that they were not made parties to the execution case as they had ceased to have any connection with the Mahila Vidyalaya. The executing court granted instalments to the decree holders. The judgment debtors filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decree holders were necessary parties to the suit; (ii) the order passed by the executing court granting instalments did not affect the rights of the decree holders as they had become owners of the property under section 16(2)(b) of the Act; (iii) the order of the executing court dated 31st March, 1942 was void as it was passed without jurisdiction; (iv) the decree holder could not be said to be a party to the execution proceeding; and (v) the decree was not executable as it was obtained by fraud. HELD: (i) The decree holders were not necessary parties to a suit for declaration or injunction. [811 E] (ii) The decree holder was not entitled to execute the decree in view of the provisions of section 16(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [812 F] (iii) The decree was not executed because the decree holder was a stranger to the proceedings before the Debt Relief Court. [813 D] (iv) The decree in question was not a nullity as it was not executed by the judgment debtor. [814 B] (v) The decree passed in favour of the appellant was not a mere formality but a substantive one. It was not a final decree. [815 C]

4364: The appellant company was a public limited company carrying on business of manufacture and sale of aluminium products. It had its registered office at Bombay. 7131: The respondent assessee was a dealer in cement. He purchased cement from the appellant and paid tax under section 5(1) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957. The tax was not disputed by the State Government but it was contended that the liability to pay tax was governed by section 20 (3) of the Act. The High Court held that the additional tax levied under section 6B of the Act was a levy distinct from the impost under section 5 (1) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 20(3) of Karnataka Sales Tax is as under: "No appeal against an order of assessment shall be entertained by the appellate authority unless it is accompanied by satisfactory proof of the payment of the tax and penalty not disputed in the appeal." [766 F] 2. The provisions of section 20(3), which are similar to section 20(2) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act are also identical. The provisions relating to refund or exemption from tax are similar to those contained in section 20(1). The provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder including those relating to refund and exemption from tax apply to the sales or purchases of goods. [767 C D] 3. The provisions regarding refund or exemption of tax are not identical with the provisions relating to the levy, assessment and collection of the additional tax under section 613 of the Act, and therefore, the provisions of section 5(3) and section 20(4) of the State Act would have no application to the case. [768 E G]
159: The appellants were charged with an offence under section 182, Indian Penal Code, and the case was transferred to the Sessions Judge for trial. The appellants contended that they had been falsely implicated in the case by the police and that the complaint made by them did not disclose any offence against them. The Magistrate held that the allegations made in the complaint did not constitute an offence under sections 182 or 211, Indian Penal code, but he took cognizance of the offence only on the basis of the statements of the complainant and his witnesses recorded under section 164 Cr. P. C., and that the Magistrate could take cognizance only on a complaint by a proper authority under the provisions of section 195, Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offences mentioned in section 190, Criminal Procedure, and (ii) the Magistrate was not competent to take cognizance as there was no allegation in the complaint that the appellants had committed an offence under s.182 or s.203, Indian Penal, Code, and that the magistrate had no jurisdiction under section 195, Cr. P., Code, to take cognizance. HELD : (i) Section 195, Criminal P.C., is not applicable to the facts of the present case because the complaint does not disclose any commission of an offence under the Indian Penal Code. It merely provides that the offence specified therein shall be triable exclusively by a court of session. [174 D] (ii)The Magistrate has no power to take cognizance if the facts alleged in the complaint are not such as would constitute an offence either under section 181 or section 211, Indian penal Code. [175 E] (iii)Section 195, Cr, P.C. applies only where the facts constituting an offence under that section are alleged to have taken place in course of the performance of a public duty. [176 F] (iv)In the instant case, the Magistrate had jurisdiction to take the complaint. [177 G]
5889: The appellant and other institutions challenged the cancellation of their recognition by the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the conditions laid down for grant of permission were not complied with. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the conditions have been substantially complied with. [897C] 2. The High Cour t erred in holding that the conditions are substantially complied with since the grant of permission is made on the basis of the recommendations of the Selection Committee. The High.Court could not have gone into the question whether the conditions laid out for grant of approval were substantially complied with or not. [898D] 3. The High 'Court did not accept the contention that the conditions had been substantially complied. The High,Court should have directed the appellant to comply with the conditions. [899E] 4. The High Courts' power under Article 226 is very wide and can be exercised only when there is an error of law apparent on the face of the record. It cannot go into the question as to whether the selection committee had properly applied its mind to the relevant aspects of the matter before granting the approval. [900F] 5. The High courts' power under Articles 226 and 227 is very limited. The Highs. Court can interfere only if the decision making authority exceeded its jurisdiction or acted in excess of it. [901G] 6. The High has no power to sit in appeal over the decision of the authorities. [902A] 7. The High is not a court of appeal against the order of the authority. The High would be entitled to examine the correctness of the decision itself and may call upon the authority concerned to reconsider it. [892B]
4605: The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College by an order dated April 27, 1981. He was required to present himself before the Manager of the College on May 1, 1981 and take over charge within 15 days of the receipt of the order of appointment failing which he would be deemed to have been appointed as Principal. On his selection, the Manager of a recognised institution submitted an application for being relieved from service with effect from May 1, 1982. The appellant was informed that as permitted by him he had assumed charge of the post of Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated May 7, 1981 passed by the Director of Education. The High Court held that the radiogram dated April 7, contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee of Management of the College had no power to set up a Selection Committee nor the selection committee had any power to make any appointment and therefore the appointment of the appellant alleged to have been made on May 1 was not valid. The High court also held that the Tikewalla Committee had no power under section 16F(1) of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 to appoint teaching staff including principal and directed the Director of Higher Education to cause inspection of the Institution and submit a report to the State Government. The High 'Court further held that the scheme of Administration was to inter alia provide for constitution of a Committee of Management vested with authority to manage and conduct the affairs of the Institution. The High. Court held that since the radiogram was not received by the Committee of management, it could not be said that the Committee of the Management had failed to appoint teaching employees possessing such qualifications as are necessary for the purpose of maintaining the educational standards in the Institution. It was further held that since there were no guidelines for appointing teachers, the Committee of Managements had no power or authority to make appointments and therefore the order of the Director of Secondary Education was illegal. The High: Court accordingly allowed the appeal and set aside the order of termination of services of the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave.

The appellants were the owners of certain goods. They were intercepted by the Directorate of Enforcement on April 9, 1974 and seized some documents. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the search warrant issued under section 132A of the Income Tax Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was nothing illegal in issuing a search warrant under section 132(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence had no power to issue a search warrant for the purpose of seizure of the documents; (ii) the Directorate had no authority to issue a warrant of authorisation under section 132 A of the Act; (iii) the Directorate could not have issued a search warrant without recording the grounds of belief that any documents which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to the proceedings under Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 are secreted in any place; (iv) the Directorate did not have the power to issue an order of authorisation under Section 132A of Income Tax Act, 1961; (v) the Directorate has no power to authorise any officer of Enforcement to search for and seize documents; and (vi) the Directorate was not empowered to issue a notice of demand of the value of the goods seized. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Directorate of Enforcement is a statutory body created under the Foreign Exchange Regulation (Amendment) Act, 1973. It is entrusted with the duty to carry out the provisions of the Act and to perform the functions assigned to it under the Act. [766C] 2. The Directorate has no authority to make any search warrant without making any enquiry as contemplated by the Act. The Directorate can only make a search if it thinks fit. If it does so, it may issue a search warrants without making any inquiry as contemplated by sub sec. (2) of section 132A. [767D E] 3. The Directorate cannot exercise its powers under sub sec.

(2) of Sec. 132A of income tax Act, 1961. [768F] 4. The Directorate exercises its powers under the Act and makes the search and seizure. The Directorate is not authorised to issue a show cause notice of demand

5478: The appellant was the Principal of the Institution. She was suspended by the Vice Chancellor of the University on January 27, 1986 and an enquiry was held against her. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report to the Vice Chancellor. The Vice Chancellor after hearing the appellant dismissed the appellant from service in exercise of the powers under section 58 of the U.P. State Universities Act, the Authorised Controller. The appeal filed by the appellant before the Vice Chancellor was dismissed by the ViceChancellor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition of the appellant holding that the two reports dated August 1, and July 18, of the Joint Director of Higher Education, U.P., were not before the ViceChancellor and that the said reports were not relevant for the purpose of the enquiry. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the two Reports dated August 1 and July 18 are not before the Chancellor, the Vice Chancellor had no power to review the order of dismissal passed by him. [362B] 1.2 The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition on the ground that it was not maintainable. [363C] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that the two Report dated August 1. and July 18 is not relevant for deciding the question whether the punishment imposed upon the appellant was justified or not. [364D] 1.4 The High Court ought to have considered the report of the Joint Registrar of the University which was a material piece of evidence and which was not before the High Court. [365E]
3656: The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Teacher in the Primary School, Northern Railway Colony II run by the Education Department of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi with effect from October 1, 1958. By order dated July 30, 1968 he was placed under suspension pending enquiry into certain charges against him. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that it was not a quasi judicial order and was therefore invalid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice served upon the appellant was not a mere formality but was intended to be a step in aid of the departmental inquiry which had been initiated against him. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order of dismissal passed against the appellant is not a quasi Judicial order. It does not contain any reasons for the passing of the order. [839E] (2) The order is not a mere administrative or quasi judicial order. It must reflect the application of mind both the delinquent officer and the affected party. If no reasons are given in the order, that would render the final order illegal. [840F] (3) The order has to be tested on the touchstone of the test of reasonableness. If its validity can be tested only by applying the test of self assessment of the authority, such an exercise of power will become bad. But if it is found that the authority has made some material departure from the procedure followed by him in the conduct of the disciplinary proceedings, it will not be just and proper for the court to substitute its opinion as to the quantum of punishment and record a finding whether the same is based on some evidence and the court cannot substitute its own opinion merely because the findings recorded by the disciplinary authority may be wrong. [841G H; 842A B] (4) The requirement of law is that there should be complete application of mind to the contentions raised before the Tribunal and the materials produced before them. The Tribunal has to apply its mind to the materials and decide the matter objectively and dispassionately. [842C D] (5) The Tribunal has not applied its mind to these aspects of the case. The Tribunal ought to have considered the nature of the misconduct alleged against the appellant and the penalty imposed on him. [8
4018: The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the acquisition of the lands in possession of the appellants. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and granted a decree declaring that the notification dated 10th October 1952 issued under section 4 was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government had no power to issue the notification under sections 4 and 6 of the Act after the expiry of two years from the date of the notification; that the Government could not have issued the notification under the provisions of section 4 after the expiry thereof and that the Government should be deemed to have acted in exercise of its powers under section 6(1)(a) of the Act. HELD: The Government could not be said to have acted merely because the Government had made a declaration under section 6 of the Land Acquisi tion Act. [539 B] The Government could have exercised its powers under the provisions contained in section 6(2) only if it was satisfied that the declaration under section 4 had been made within the time prescribed by the statute. But the Government did not do so. It is true that the Government might have thought fit to make a declaration under s.6 of the Act but that does not mean that the Government cannot act arbitrarily or without mala fide exercise its powers. [540 C D] The Government can exercise its powers under sections 4 & 6 only when it is satisfied that the declarations under section 6 are necessary and that there has been undue delay in making the declaration under s 6. [541 E] The Government may also consider whether the declaration under secti on 6 is necessary or not. If the Government finds that the declaration is necessary, it would be open to the Government to take action under section 6. [553 F]

The appellant challenged the dismissal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the respondents had not been able to prove that they had committed any misconduct within cl. 17 (b)(viii). On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that the respondents were guilty of any act or omission which would constitute a breach of cl. 7(a) of the standing orders. It does not mean termination of service for any fault on the part of the employee. It means termination of service without any stigma at all. A termination of service may be effected either by way of punishment or by way of penalty. If it is a case of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank, the same cannot be said to be a punishment. It must have the meaning given to it in common parlance. It must not be confined to the words employed therein. It must refer to some kind of employment. It must also be given in the context of the statute. In the present case, the appellant had not been employed in any capacity whatsoever with the respondent company. The appellant had no control over its employees. The appellant was not in a position to give any particular type of employment to its workmen. 4620: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Revenue Service, was a member of a family consisting of his wife and two children. He married the respondent in 1972. In 1972, he filed a petition for divorce on the ground of cruelty against the respondent. The respondent alleged that the marriage had been consummated and that the petitioner 's daughter, Gurinder Kaur, was not happy with her husband. The petitioner also alleged that the respondent had illicit relations with his wife and that the respondent used to harass him and his family members. The police after investigation found that the allegations were true and the petitioner was guilty of the offence under section 498A I.P.C. The Magistrate took cognizance of the case and committed the case to the Sessions Court. The Sessions Judge framed charges against the petitioner and the respondent for offences under sections 498A and 304B read with section 34 I.P,. Code. The petitioner challenged the framing of charges before the High Court which quashed the proceedings holding that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was responsible for the conduct of the petitioner. The petitioner appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The trial court has rightly held that the charge is not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [114E] 2.1 There is no reason why the evidence should be discarded as unreliable. The evidence of the witnesses examined by the prosecution cannot be rejected merely because they are interested witnesses. The evidence given by the witnesses must be scrutinised carefully and independently possible so as to find out whether any offence has been made out. It is not necessary that all the witnesses have to be examined. All that is required is that the accused must be questioned about the circumstances in which the crime was committed. If the accused denies the guilt, the onus lies on the accused to prove that the act complained of was not done. [115F G] 3.1 The evidence of PW 1, the father of the girl, who was present at the time when the occurrence took place, is not reliable. 4079: The appellant filed a suit for possession of the land in dispute on the ground that he was in possession of the same. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court dismissed the appeal. HELD: (1) A Magistrate is not bound by the provisions of Section 146 to make an order under Section 145(1), but he must act judicially and fairly according to the well established rules of procedure. [631G] (2) It is not necessary that there should be actual physical possession of the property in question from the party against whom it is due and that the party who is entitled to possession must be in actual possession of the premises. [632A] (3) If the Magistrate has reason to believe that the party against whose possession is sought to be put in possession was in actual possession, he can direct the parties to appear before him and take such steps as may be necessary to protect their rights. [633B] (4) The object of Section 146 is to enable the Magistrate to decide whether the party claiming to be in possession is in actual possession or not. It is only when he comes to know that the party claiming possession is in possession, he will have to proceed further under Section 145. 795: The appellant was a devotee of " Shri Venkatesh Balaji Deity" and "Shri Vyankatesh Balji Deity". The appellant denied that there was a trust in the matter of Shri Venkateshsa Balaji Deities and claimed the idol and the properties as private. He claimed that the deity was not a family or private one and that the deity had been given the right to use the property for religious purposes only. The District Judge held that the suit properties were not the personal or private properties of the appellant and that the temple was not a public temple and that the documents conferring the properties on the appellant were inadmissible in evidence. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the documents were not admissible in evidence because they did not show that the temple itself was a family or a private one and therefore the documents were inadmissible in view of section 4(1) of the Act. Held: (i) that the documents showed that the temple had been established and that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the properties. The fact that the temple is a private one would not make any difference. The fact of a private temple being a public one would not necessarily mean that the temple has been established. A temple is a place where worship is permitted but not a place where the worship is performed. It is not necessary that there should be a temple at all. There must be a temple which is a place of worship and the mere fact that there are no other temples at all does not establish that the temple belongs to a particular person.

2337: The appellant was suspended from service by an order dated March 14, 1952. HELD : (i) Rule 151 does not confer any inherent power on the Government to suspend a Government servant pending inquiry into his conduct even though there is no such term in the contract of appointment or in the rules. It merely confers a power upon the Government to pass orders of suspension pending enquiry into the conduct of the Government servant. [584 D] (ii) The order of suspension is not a punishment and it is only a dismissal or removal from service which can be imposed under the rules. The order of dismissal or removal is not a penalty. It is only when the Government has decided to remove the employee from service and the Government has taken action to suspend him pending further orders from the Government. If the Government decides to remove the Government servant from service, then the Government would have no right to continue him in service until the order of removal is approved by the Government. [585 B C] (iii) The order is not one of punishment. It is one of dismissal or reduction in rank. It is a punitive measure. It is not a punitive order. It is based on misconduct, misbehaviour, or other like charges levelled against a Government servant. These are all grounds for disciplinary action. But if these grounds are not sufficient for the Government to take action, it may be necessary to challenge the authority and the Government could place the same before the Tribunal. [586 E F] (iv) The order was made without giving the Government servant concerned a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him.

The respondents claimed exemption from assessment in respect of the sales effected by them on the ground that such sales took place "in the course of the export of the goods out of the territory of India" within the meaning of article 1115 286(1) (b) of the Constitution. Held, that the sales were completed before the goods were shipped and could not be considered to have taken place in the course of export and hence they did not fall within the exemption under article 286(1)(b). The sale was complete before the goods had crossed the customs frontiers of India and therefore the sales were exempt under article 286 (1) (a) of the constitution. The sales were completed within the State before the goods commenced their journey as found by the Sales Tax Authorities. The sales being completed before the export of goods, the sales were exempted under article 286

(1) of the Con stitution. The sales having been completed before the import of goods into the territory of the State, the sales being completed after the export of those goods, the sale must be deemed to have taken places in the course or the import of the goods within the State.
5869: The Rajasthan University, the respondent No. 1 in these appeals, had conducted Post Graduate Medical Courses in the five Medical Colleges affiliated to the Rajasthan University and had passed the qualifying examination from the College of Postgraduate Medicine, Rajasthan. The candidates who were successful at the entrance test for Post Graduate courses in the five medical colleges in Rajasthan, viz., Jaipur, Bikaner, Udaipur, Jodhpur and Ajmer, applied for admission to post graduate courses in the said five medical colleges. The appellants who were the writ petitioners before the High Court challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification dated June 30, 1990 issued by the Rajasthan University, Jaipur, which provided that the candidates who have passed their final MBBS Examination from the College to which admission in post graduate course is sought shall be allowed to appear at a competitive examination called PMG Entrance Examination to be held by the Rajasthan State Board of Technical Education and Training, Rajasthan. They contended that the said notification was ultra vires the provisions of the Ordinance No. 278 E (d)(ii) of the University of Rajasthan which provided for additional 5% marks in the percentage of aggregate marks by way of institutional preference if the concerned candidates had passed his final MBBS Examination; that the said provision was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it conferred arbitrary powers upon the University to prescribe minimum qualifying marks in any one of the five Medical colleges in Rajasthan and that the said prescription was violative of Articles 19(1)(g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The writ petitions were contested by the respondents contending that the Ordinance No 278 E(d)(ii)) of the University was perfectly valid and constitutional. The Ordinance No.278 E (D)(ii) is ultra vires the provision contained in Ordinance No. 47 of the University Act, namely, Ordinance No. 288 E (b) of the Ordinance. [51F] 2. The Ordinance does not provide for any separate entrance examination for Post Graduate Medical Course. The Ordinance provides for separate entrance examination to be held for Post Graduate Courses.

2405: The respondent brought a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute, which was sold under a sale deed dated February 6, 1942. 2436: The plaintiff Bank advanced a sum of Rs. 11,723.56 nP to defendant No. 1 on the guarantee of defendant No. 2 Paras Nath Sinha. On the date of the suit, defendant No. I had borrowed money from the plaintiff bank and executed a promissory note in favour of the plaintiff bank. The amount was not paid by the plaintiff bank to the defendant No.1. The plaintiff filed a suit against the defendants for recovery of the amount due. The defendants resisted the suit contending that the debt was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the suit was barred by time because the creditor had obtained a decree against the principal debtor; (ii) the surety had no right to restrain execution against the principal; (iii) the suit being one for enforcement of the security bond, the question of limitation did not arise; and (iv) the suit having been instituted within three years from the date of contract, the suit was not barred by limitation as the principal debtor had discharged his liability under the bond. HELD: (i) The suit was not governed by section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1235 G] (ii) The suit is barred by limitation, because the creditor has not exhausted his remedies against the principal. [1236 A B] (iii) The suit being one which could be brought by the surety, the Court passing the decree cannot pass any decree against the surety. [1237 D] (iv) The suit having been brought within three years of the date of agreement to pay the principal amount, the suit is clearly barred by limitation and the suit is liable to be dismissed. [1238 E] (v) The suit has been rightly decreed by the trial court. [1239 F] (vi) The suit does not suffer from any infirmity. [1240 H] (vii) The suit must fail. [1241 C]
1585: The appellant, a contractor, entered into two contracts with the respondent, a Deputy Commissioner of Bhandara, for construction of a hospital and for the maintenance of a hospital. The contract was to be completed within six months from the date of its execution. The appellant entered into the contract on June 22, 1953, and the contract was to remain in force till the end of the term of three years. The contract contained an arbitration clause which provided that all disputes arising out of or relating to the contract shall be referred to the arbitration of the Deputy Commissioner, Bhandara, who alone could decide the dispute.
