[983 C] (ii) The Deputy Commissioner, who had signed the contract at his own discretion, was not competent to execute the contract. He was only entitled to receive the money paid under the contract and to recover it from the person who executed it. [984 D E] (iii) The Deputy commissioner was not competent under section 175(1) of the Act to enter upon the contract. [985 F] (iv) The Deputy Collector was not competent even to sign the contract. It was not necessary for him to do so. [986 B] (v) The Deputy Director was not competent either to sign the agreement or to institute any proceedings in respect thereof. [987 G]
894: The appellant filed an election petition for a declaration that the respondent was duly elected. The Election Commission dismissed the petition under section 90(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 on the ground that section 117 of the Act had not been complied with. The respondent appealed to the High Court which set aside the order and remanded the case to the Tribunal for disposal in accordance with law. The High Court held that the order dismissing the petition under sections 98 and 99 of the Act was appealable. It also held that the appellant 's contention that the receipt enclosed with the petition was not for reasons which will be mentioned later in terms of section 96(3) was not correct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the Tribunal dismissing the petition was made at the conclusion of the trial by the Tribunal for as is known to the respondent 's counsel, that it was not an order under section 98 or section 99 of the Representation Act but only an order under s.98 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) Section 98 does not provide for any appeal from an order dismissing a petition under the powers contained in section 90(1). The provision is intended to give effect to the provisions of the Act and to enable the Election Commission or the Speaker or Chairman of the House concerned to make orders under the said sections. [957 D E] (ii) An order dismissing a Petition under the powers enumerated in section 90 is not an order passed under section 98 and it is therefore not appealable. [958 F G] (iii) The order of the Election Commission dismissing the petition has no relation to the merits of the case. It is merely an order under the powers conferred by section 90(2) of the Act which is applicable to all proceedings before the Election Commission. [959 H; 960 A B] (iv) The order passed by the Election Commission is not appealable under section 90 of the Act because it is an order under sections 98, 99 and 100 of the Act, and it is one of the matters covered by section 100(4)(a) of the 1951 Act. [961 C D]
3404: The respondent assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1955 56 under section 22(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. He filed returns on March 31, 1956 and April 1, 1957 respectively in respect of the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59. In the return he disclosed a total income of Rs. 2,00,000 as agricultural income. The Income tax officer issued notice under section 34(1) of the Act on March 30, 1959 requiring the assessee to furnish certain information but the assessee did not furnish any such information. On May 5, 1960 the Income tax Officer served on the assessee a notice under section 35A(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon him to show cause why an order should not be made against him under section 34 (1). The assessee submitted his explanation which was rejected by the Income tax officer. Thereafter the assessee filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notices. The High Court held that the notices were invalid because they were issued after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year and could not be sustained. It also held that the Income tax authorities had no jurisdiction to issue the notices under section 34. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) Section 34(1), contemplates two categories of cases for re opening the previous assessment (1) where there has been omission or failure on the part of the assessee to make a return of his income under section 22 or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment; and (ii) where there is omission or failure to disclose fully or truly all material fact necessary for his own assessment. [971 B C] (iii) The expression "any person" in section 34(I)(a) includes a company or other body corporate. [972 D] (iv) The word "person" in section 33(1)(b) means a person who is a citizen of India and is ordinarily resident in India. [973 E] (v) The word 'person ' in section 34 does not include a company or body corporate. The word 'company ' in section 33 (1)(a), therefore, refers to a company or a body corporate only.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1944 and it had its registered office at Calcutta. In 1944 the appellant entered into an agreement with the managed company for a period of seventeen years for which the relevant previous year ended on June 30, 1954. The managing agency agreement was terminated by the appellant on July 1, 1955. The appellant filed a return of income for the assessment year 1956 56 for which the Income Tax Officer held that the managing agency was not liable to tax under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not liable because the managing agency had been terminated by the company. The Tribunal however held that the termination of the managing agency could not be regarded as a voluntary transfer of the managing agent and that the compensation received by the assessee was taxable under section 10 (5A). The High Court answered the question against the revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The payment made by the assessee to the managing agents of the managing agencies is not a payment made by a person who has no authority to receive the amount from the managing agency. [775 C] The payment made to the managing agent is not a voluntary payment but is made only to the managing agency which is appointed by the assessee. It is a payment made to a person who is appointed by him to act as such. [776 D] The payment is not a mere payment made to another person. It is made to the person who is so appointed. It is not paid to the person whose appointment is terminated. It is paid to the managing director or other person who acts as such. It is therefore not a payment to the managing directors or other persons who are appointed to act as managing agents. [777 E F] The payment to the Managing Director is not a remuneration in respect of any business carried on by the assessee but is a payment to a person acting as managing director. [778 B] The payment of compensation to a managing director is not a sum payable to him by way of compensation under section 10

(1) Of the Income Tax. Act, 1922, but is a compensation paid to the Managing director. [776 G H; 779 A]
208: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1950 under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a paid up share capital of Rs. 1,000 and its shares were held by one of its preference shareholders. The company was incorporated on September 30, 1948, as a private limited company with a paid up capital of Rs, 1,000. The company had a paid-up share capital of only Rs. 1 lakh. The company claimed that it was not liable to pay any dividend or other dues to the shareholders of the company. The company contended that the provisions of section 12(1) of the Act had no application to the company because the company had been incorporated for the purpose of carrying on business in India and that the company had not taken any part in the management of its affairs. Held, that the company was not liable for the payment of dividend or other debts due from it to the shareholders. The definition of "company" in section 2(15) of the Companies Act, 1956, includes an association of persons who are members of the company but does not include a private company which is not a body corporate. The definition is not confined to companies which are incorporated solely for the purpose and object of carrying on the business of the company; it covers companies which have been incorporated for some time before the incorporation of the company and which have not been incorporated for a long period. The definition does not extend to corporations incorporated solely for profit. The definition has reference to companies which have not yet been incorporated for profit. In the present case, the company was incorporated for the purposes of carrying on a business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn and cloth and other articles. The company did not carry on any business in India. The company could not be said to be a corporation incorporated outside India. The definition also does not cover corporations incorporated solely to carry on business of manufacture and sale of goods. The definition therefore does not apply to corporations incorporated exclusively for trade and commerce. The definition being merely to save private property from being taken purely by executive action and the only clause which limits its operation to private property, the company cannot claim protection against the State 's liability to pay dividend or other sums due to it.
6304: The petitioners in these petitions are manufacturers of motor vehicles. They manufacture and sell motor vehicles. The petitioners challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification before the High Court. The High Court held that the impugned rule was not a law made by the State Legislature but was a measure of taxation which was compensatory in nature and hence it was not a taxing statute within the meaning of article 301 of the Constitution. It also held that the imposition of tax was not a restriction on trade, commerce and intercourse guaranteed by article 301 of Constitution of India. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioners that the impugned rules were not regulatory measures and were therefore not hit by article 304(a). The impugned rules do not offend article 301 of any of the Constitution of India and are not restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between States. [746D] 3. The impugned Rule is not a tax on the import of goods at the point of entry, that the impugned Rule is made with an eye on the place of origin of the goods. [747E] 4. The impugned Rules are not a law passed by the State legislative power. [748F] 5. The impugned notification does not impose any tax on the sale of motor vehicles as such. [749G] 6. The impugned Notification is not a taxing provision. It is a measure imposing a tax on a particular class of motor vehicles and is not a measure of a general revenue. [750B C] 743

3147: The appellant was charged with an offence under section 9 of the Punjab Security of State Act (Punjab Act 12), 1953, for having made a speech or published any statement of fact which is false in material particulars. He was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for three years. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the charge framed against him was not sustainable as he had been punished for an offence under the Act without giving him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against his conviction. 5786: The respondent imported wool materials from the appellant. The Customs authorities, after examining the goods in question, found that the wool materials were not woollen products other than wool tops/raw wool and were classifiable under heading 5301. The Additional Collector of Customs held that the goods were not wool waste but processed wooller products other than Wool tops /raw wool. The Revenue preferred an appeal to this Court against the order of Appellate Tribunal. 5231: The appellant, a Government of India undertaking, entered into an agreement with the respondent, Western Company for carrying out certain works in the USA. Clause 2 of the said agreement provided that the work would be carried out by the appellant on its own risk and responsibility and the appellant was to pay to the respondent, the cost of the work as per schedule. Clause 3 provided that the appellant "shall not carry out any other work or do anything which may prejudice the rights and liabilities of the parties hereunder". Clause 4 provided that the contractor shall have no claim against the appellant for any loss or damage caused to the work done by the appellant. Clause 5 provided that the contract shall be subject to the provisions of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940. Clause 6 provided that the award shall be final and binding upon the parties. Clause 7 provided that the parties were free to determine their own terms and conditions. Clause 8 provided that the decision of the arbitrator shall be final, conclusive and binding on both the parties. The appellant, the Western Company, filed a petition under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1996 before the High Court of Bombay challenging the arbitral award passed by the Umpire on the ground that it was contrary to the Indian law and the Indian Courts had jurisdiction to affirm or set aside the same. The High Court held that the award was not enforceable in India as a domestic award inasmuch as a foreign award could be enforced only in India and not in India. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The arbitration clause contained in the contract between the parties is not applicable to the present case because the arbitration clause contained therein is not applicable. [198F] (2) The arbitration clauses contained in the said contract are not applicable to cases where the parties have agreed to refer disputes to arbitration. The arbitration clause in the said contracts is not applicable in the instant case because the parties have expressly agreed to refer all disputes arising out of the said contracts to arbitration. [199G H; 201A B] (3) The arbitration agreement contained in the two contracts cannot be construed as one agreement providing for arbitration. It is not necessary that there should be an express reference to arbitration. There can be no doubt that the arbitration clause in each of the contracts is not inconsistent with the main contract.
5500: The appellant, a medical college established and administered by the Christian Medical College, Vellore, was converted into a medical college with degree courses in 1942. In the year 1947, when the common judgment of the High Court of Madras in the three writ petitions filed by the appellant, out of which this appeal arises, was delivered, there were about 500 students including post graduate students in the medical college in the State of Tamil Nadu. The appellant, who was a student of the medical college at Vellore for the academic year 1947 47, was admitted to the medical college as students. The medical college was converted into one medical college with a degree course in 1942. The appellant was also admitted to the college as students on the basis of the marks obtained in the first semester examination. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that it violated Articles 30(1) and 30(2). The High Court held that the provisions of section 9A of the Act were not applicable to educational institutions established and administered under the Act and that the appellant had no locus standi to challenge the vires of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 10(3)(a) of the Act are not attracted to the facts of the case. [554C] 2. The Act is a self contained code relating to all educational institutions. It is a complete code in itself. The Act does not provide for any other matter like the right to establish an educational institution. The Act has been enacted to regulate the conditions of service of teachers and employees in recognised private schools. The Act provides for the recognition of private schools. Section 3(f) of the said Act provides that the provisions contained therein shall apply mutatis mutandis to all educational Institutions established or maintained by any person or body corporate incorporated by law in India and affiliated to the University of Madras. The Act further provides that the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on January 1, 1973. [575H; 556B C]
4873: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that the premises were bona fide required by him. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in appeal, reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was not justified in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the courts below. [835C] (2) The High Courts are not bound by the concurrent finding of fact recorded in the suits. They have only to see whether the findings are based upon some evidence or otherwise. [836A] (3) The High courts are not bound to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact unless they are shown to be perverse. [837B] (4) The High court has no jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to reappraise the evidence and come to its own conclusion. [838D] (5) The High 'Court is entitled to interfere with findings of facts even if it is erroneous. [839E]
3529: The respondent was a candidate for election to the Orissa Legislative Assembly from Bhadrak constituency. He filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant on the ground that he had incurred a disqualification under section 9A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) from seeking election. The Election Tribunal held that the appellant was disqualified under section 9 A of the Act from contesting the election and declared the election void. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court set aside the order of the Election Tribunal holding that the appellant had incurred a disquali ty in terms of section 9A. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant has not been able to make out any case for interference with the judgment of the High Court. [56C] 2. The appellant 's nomination papers were rejected on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of section 33(1)(b) of the Act. The rejection is based on the fact that the appellant did not file his affidavit in support of the nomination paper. The appellant could have easily produced the affidavit if he wanted to do so. But the appellant failed to do so and the election petition was rightly dismissed. [57D E]

[240B] (2) The word 'textual ' in the Explanation includes all other material having its place in the fabric itself. [241C] (3) The word is used in the context of goods which are made of cotton, silk, woollen, rayon, nylon or any other thing which is made of cotton. It is not necessary that the fabric must be made of cotton or silk or other things. [244E] (4) The word in the Explanation is
922: The assessee was carrying on business in the United Kingdom. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the assessee had not produced any evidence to show that the business was carried on by the Baroda business. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to set off the losses incurred by it in its Indian State and allowed the deduction. The Tribunal however held that the business being carried on by a Baroda business, the assessee was not liable to tax under section 4(1)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because the business was not carried on by it but by a Bar Association or a Society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proviso to sub section (1) of section 24 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 is not applicable to the facts of the case. It applies only to cases where the business is carried on by an individual who is resident in India and not ordinarily resident in India. [801 B C] (ii) The third proviso to sub s. (1) does not apply to the facts found in the present case. The business was carried out by a Bara Bazar Baroda Baroda Baranas and the Baroda Barasis were operated by the Bara Bazar. The Baroda Bara Bazar was a Baroda Barley Bara Bazar and the Bara Barley Barasis are operated by Baroda Barges. The Bara Bazar is a Baroda barley Bara Barzo Barley Bargon Bara Bargole Bargon. 5970: The appellants were the owners of a truck owned by the deceased. The deceased left behind him his wife, the appellant No. 1 and a daughter, then only a child. The appellants filed a petition before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal claiming a sum of Rs. 1 lac as compensation. The Tribunal held that the accident which resulted in the death of Hari Singh was due to the rash and negligent driving of the car. The Tribunal awarded a sum of 5,000 as compensation against the Insurance Company. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the Insurance Company on the ground that it had not been proved that the deceased was a student at the time of his death. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended for the appellants that the High Court was not justified in affirming the award of the Tribunal for Rs. 10,000 only as compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal was inadequate. [764A] (2) The High court was not justified, in affirm ing the award of compensation in favour of the appellants against the Insurance company. [765B] (3) The High Courts order was correct. [766C]
2018: The appellants were the occupancy tenants of certain lands in the Punjab. They had been in possession of the land for more than 12 years and had been paying rent to the Government. In the year 1915, the Raja of Faridkot transferred his rights under the decree obtained against him by the respondent. On February 19, 1915, the respondent filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the lands on the ground that the adoption of the appellant was invalid. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as the suit was governed by article 144 and not by article 144, the limitation prescribed by article 144 would be attracted. HELD : (i) Article 144 is applicable only when the right claimed by the parties is determined or extinguished by a judgment, decree or order of a court or any other authority. It does not apply where the question of title arises from a private act of a person which has been adjudicated upon by a competent court or authority. [901 G] (ii)The expression "lawful owner" in article 144 means a person who holds the property for the benefit of the owner and not a mere trespasser. [902 B C] (iii)Article 144 applies only when the question of law is finally decided between the parties. [903 D]
4881: The Respondent, who was a tenant in respect of a Government accommodation, filed an eviction petition against the Appellant under section 14A (1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his own occupation. The Rent Controller held that the Respondent was not entitled to recover possession of the premises from him and dismissed the eviction petition. On appeal by the Respondent, the Appellate Authority affirmed the order of the Rent Controller. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the respondent was not in occupation of reasonably suitable alternative accommodation as contemplated by section 14A(1) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 14A(2)(e) of the Act does not contain any condition that the Government servant who made an application under section 14 A(1) should not be in possession of reasonably suitable accommodation as was the case under clause (e) of proviso to sub section (1) or clause (e), but only if such a factor were to be taken into consideration, it could not be said that the respondent had no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. [766C D] 2. The expression "any person" in clause (e)(i) of section 14A has been used in a wider sense so as to include all persons who are not merely agricultural labourers but also dependents on them. The expression 'any person' in clause (c) of the proviso to sub sections (1) and (2) of section 2 means a person who is actually occupying the premises or occupies the same. [764F G] 3. The expression used in clause (a) of the second proviso to sub sec.(1) of section 13B is wide enough to cover every person who is not a mere member of the family. It cannot be said that a person who has no other reasonably available accommodation can be said to be in occupation of the premises let for residential purposes. [765G H; 767A B] 4. The expression, "any person", in clause (b) of the first proviso to sub s.(1) and sub s.(2) of s.13B must mean a person who
4192: The appellant was declared evacuee property by the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Delhi. He filed a revision application before the High Court challenging the order of the Custodian of evacuee property. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that the notice under section 7 of the Act was not valid and that the appellant had no locus standi to file the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the notice issued by the Custodian was invalid as the appellant had failed to show cause why he should be declared an evacuees and his property should be treated as evacuee property; (2) the notice did not disclose any reason for declaring the property to be evacuee property; and (3) the notice was bad because the appellant had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed declaration. HELD: (1) The notice was not in accordance with law. It was not necessary for the appellant to show cause before the notice could be said to have been issued. [875 C] (2) The notice did not state that the property was being transferred to Pakistan or that it was being used for purposes other than those mentioned in the notification. The notice merely stated that the property is being transferred to the Pakistan. The notice did mention that the property has been acquired by the appellant and his brother. The notice also does not refer to the transfer of the property to Pakistan. [876 D E] (3) The notice must be read as a whole and not in isolation. If the notice refers to the transfer, then the notice must be construed as a notice to show cause. [877 F] (4) The notice referred to the transfer and the transfer of property to Pakistan and the notice must contain the grounds on which the property was sought to be attached. The notice must specify the grounds on the basis of which the property is sought to be proceeded against. [878 G H] (5) The notice does not say that the property will be deemed to be evacuee properties. It only states that the property may be transferred to Pakistan. The words "in respect of" indicate that the notice must relate to the transfer. [879 B] (6) The notice refers to a transfer of property from one person
5483: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. On his death, his wife and children were brought on record as legal representatives of the deceased landlord. The respondent No. 1 filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1)(e) of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The appellant contended that the rent was deposited on account of the appellant 's husband, and after the death of the appellant, his wife had become the tenant in his own right. The Rent Controller rejected the contention holding that there was no evidence to show that the rent had been paid by the appellant or on behalf of the deceased. The Appellate Authority also held that the rent in respect of the premises had been deposited in the name of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the rent which was deposited on behalf of his deceased wife and children was not the rent received by them from the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appellant was not a party to the proceedings before the Rent Controller. [311C] (ii) The appellant did not dispute the fact that the rent deposited on behalf was received by him. It is therefore clear that the appellant was not entitled to be heard in the matter. [312E] (iii) The appellant could not be said to have surrendered the tenancy. [313F] (iv) The appellant has not been able to establish that he had any other source of income except the rent which he had deposited in the court. [314G] (v) The appellant had not produced any document showing that the rent of the premises was paid by him to the landlady. The appellant had failed to prove that he had paid the rent to the land lord. [315B] (vi) The finding of the High Court that the rent received was not the amount of rent received by the appellant is not correct. [316D]
2270: The respondent, a tenant of the Union of India in respect of certain lands filed an application under section II of the . The Compensation Officer held that the said lands formed part of the protected forest and the appellant 's claim was not tenable. He also held that the respondent was not entitled to proprietary rights in the said lands. On appeal, the Compensation Officer held, that the lands were not forest areas but were part of the forest area and that the respondent had no right of occupancy in them. The appellant 's revision petition to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Act did not exclude the applicability of the Act to the State; (ii) since the respondent was mentioned as an occupancy tenant in the Jamabandhi, he was entitled to proprietary right in the said land; (iii) since the appellant was not a tenant of any other person, the respondent could not be regarded as a tenant of a protected forest. HELD: (1) The Act does not exclude the operation of the Act merely because the respondent is mentioned as an occupant in the Jamabandi. [650 F] (2) The Act has been enacted for the protection of the interests of the cultivators and the cultivator who are in possession of the lands. It is a piece of legislation with regard to the matters enumerated therein. The Act is intended to protect the interest of the cultivator and the cultivators. [605 D] (3) The Act is not intended to apply to the Union or to lands owned by the Union. The Act does nothing more than to regulate the cultivation of the lands belonging to the Union. [604 B] (4) Section 11 of the Act provides that the compensation payable to the owner of the lands shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Section 12 provides that the amount of compensation shall be determined by the Collector in the manner provided in the Act. [607 C] (5) The Act makes a provision for the payment of compensation to the owners of the lands whose lands are situated in the Union Territory of Delhi. The Act gives power to the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act and the Rules made thereunder
6716: The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. M.S.M. Industries Ltd., a partnership firm. In the year 1957, the respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground of arrears of rent, etc. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that as a result of the declaration by this Court of the constitutional invalidity of clause (ii) of section 30 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, which barred the jurisdiction of the civil court, the decree passed by the civil court became null and void and inoperative. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court rightly held that the decree passed under section 9(1) of the Act is not a nullity for the Act has not barred the jurisdiction, but only prohibits execution of a decree for eviction otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [839C] 2. The High Courts decision is correct and does not call for any interference. [840E] 3. The High courts judgment is set aside. [841F] 4. The High court was wrong in holding that the decree of the civil Court was not a nullity. [842A] 5. The High 'Court committed an error in holding that there was no valid decree for eviction. [843B] 6. The High Cour t erred in holding that it was a nullity because the decree was passed by the Civil Court without a certificate from the Controller. [844D] 7. The High CM.P. No. 623 of 1980, decided on April 8, 1981, referred to.
653: The appellant leased out certain sugar factories to the respondent for a period of three years. The lease was for a period not exceeding one year and the lease was for the remainder of the term of the lease. The lease expired on December 6, 1954. The respondent applied under section 33A of the , before the Industrial Tribunal for permission to terminate the lease by giving notice of one month in writing. The Tribunal granted the permission but the High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application; (ii) the appellant was not a party to the proceedings before the Tribunal and therefore the application was incompetent; (iii) the Tribunal having been constituted under the Act, the Tribunal had become functus officio and could not have proceeded with the adjudication; (iv) the Tribunal was not competent to deal with the matter as the Government of Bihar issued a notification referring certain disputes between the Managements of the Sugar factories specified in Appendix I thereto and their workmen represented by the Unions specified in Appendix II thereto and their workers represented by the Union and the said notification did not contain any reference to the appellant. HELD : (i) The Tribunal had no power to decide the question whether the appellant was a workman or not. [550 C] (ii) The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to go into the question whether there was an industrial dispute or not. It is only if the Government of India has made a reference to the Tribunal that the Tribunal can proceed with the adjudication of the dispute. [560 D] (iii) The Tribunal was not entitled to go into all the questions which were referred to it. [557 E]
6375: The respondent company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a lubricant shop at Bombay and its business was to supply lubricants to the appellant firm. In the year 1983, the respondent company entered into an agreement with the appellant firm for supply of all kinds of lubricates to the appellant company. The respondent company had been supplying lubricating oil to the appellant 's firm since February, 1965. The respondent Company was also supplying lubri c oil to the appellants firm from February, 1965 to 27th May, 1983. The respondent No. 1 company was also supplying the lubrication oil to the appel lant firm from February 1965 to 27.5.1983. The respondent 's case is that the lubris were released by the respondent company to the said appellant firm on 25th January, 1965 by Invoice No. 146668 and there after the firm had promoted the sales of the products of the company successfully inasmuch as from February,1965 to 27th 5th March, 1966 and the firm had received and uplifted the supply of lubris. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the action of the appellant company in terminating the supply of all types of lubries to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent company had not made any promise or assurance to the appellant that it would be able to supply all kinds of Lubricants at the price fixed by the respondent Company. The respondent appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent company has been making supplies of lubrica s to the appellant Company since February,1965. The respondent has been making payments to the appellant for the supply of the lubri tars. The respondent is not entitled to claim any damages for the period during which the lubranc e remained idle. [821F G] 1.2 The respondent company is not entitled for any relief against the appellant company for the period prior to the filing of the writ petition. [822G H] 1.3 The respondent company cannot be allowed to take advantage of its own wrong. [823A] 1.4 The
929: The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of certain properties mortgaged to him by the respondent, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 2,51,904 8 6 as interest on the mortgage money and for costs. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the amount due on the basis of a loan which had been the subject of a decree was Rs. 2.51,900 8 6; (ii) the decree passed by the Special Judge was not inconsistent with section 14 of the Encumbered Estates Act and so the Special Judge could not have acted under section 15 of the Act. HELD: (i) Section 14 of the Act is not applicable to proceedings before the Special Judge because the Special Judge has no power to determine the amount due from the mortgagor on the basis that the mortgage money was not recoverable from the mortgagor. [123F] (ii) The Special Judge was bound by section 14 of Act II of 1934 and so he was bound to accept the finding of the Court which passed the decree except in so far as they were inconsistent with section 15. [124A] (iii) The Special judge was entitled to take into account the amount due to the mortgagor on his application under the Encumbered Estate Act, if he thought fit. [124B] (iv) The Special Court was competent to pass an order under section 15(2). [124C] (v) The Special court was bound by the provisions of section 14 of Usurious Loans Act, 1918. [124D]
5347: The respondent No. 1 filed an application for transfer of the case from the court of the First Additional Sessions Judge to any other court. The learned Judge, however, made observations that the trial should be concluded expeditiously and if necessary the Court should hold day to day trial to conclude the same at an early date. The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the High Court setting aside the conviction of the appellant was not proper inasmuch as the trial had been commenced within three months from the date of the order of remand passed by the High Court. It was further contended that the High Court erred in holding that the trial must be concluded before the expiry of three months from June 23, 1986. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The order of the high Court setting aside acquittal of the accused persons was not correct. [835E] (2) The High Court has committed a manifest error in passing the impugned order. [836A] (3) The High court could have recalled its earlier order dated March 24, 1986 for reasons known to him only when the bail application was listed before Justice Kamleshwar Nath on March 24,1986. But the fact remains that the order was passed after the order of bail was passed by the high Court. [837B] (4) The High Courts were wrong in observing that the trial ought to have been completed within three months. [838D]
4083: The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala, was arrested on the basis of a search warrant issued by the Magistrate under section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. He moved an application before the learned Magistrate to recall the warrant and return the books and documents seized under the authority of the search warrant. The Magistrate ordered that anything recovered pursuant to the search warrant could be returned to the person from whom the same were recovered. The petitioner challenged the correctness of the decision of the Magistrate and the claim to constitutional immunity of the accused from search and seizure of books, documents etc. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant (a) that the power conferred on the Magistrate under Section 91(1)(new Code) is not limited or circumscribed by the words "any court" occurring in the latter part of the said section; and that the word "person" used in the latter provision has been deliberately used in order to cover up the mischief sought to be remedied thereby. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "person" in section 91(1) (new Code) does not take within its sweep a person accused of an offence which would mean that a summons issued to him to produce certain documents or things in his possession irrespective of the fact whether those documents contained some statement of the accused made of his personal knowledge and accordingly the summons issued to the accused to produce certain document or thing considered necessary or desirable for the purpose of an investigation, inquiry or trial. [766A B] 2. The expression 'person ' in section 91 (new Code), means a person accused either of an offence or of an offence as defined in section 2(c) of the Act. It includes a person who is alleged to have committed an offence. [767C D] 3. The expression `person ' in Section 91(new Code) takes within its sweeping meaning a person accused or suspected of committing an offence. The expression is used in order that it may be possible to comprehend a person who can be tried with reference to the provisions of the Code. If the Legislature intended to give such wide powers to the Magistrate to issue summons to persons accused of an offense under the
1992: The mortgagee in possession of the land mortgaged to him by the mortgagor was a tenant under the mortgagee. He obtained a decree for arrears of rent and at the rent sale held on June 18, 1934, the mortgagee purchased the land in the farzi name of the mortgagee. The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee would pay Rs. 33 14 9 pies, whereas the mortgagors consistently defaulted in payment of the rent. The mortgagee sold the land to the mortgagee and the mortgagor filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The mortgagee contended that the sale was not binding on the mortgagor and that he had no right to redeem the mortgage. He also contended that the mortgage was void as it was not executed by the mortgagor himself. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal in part. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The mortgagee was entitled to redeem the mortgaged property on payment of the mortgage money. [166 G] (2) The mortgagee could not be said to have paid the amount due to the mortgagee. It is only when the mortgagor has made default in payment of rent for several years that the mortgagee can get back the amount deposited with interest. [167 A B] (3) The mortgagee had agreed to pay the rent of the entire holding to the mortgagor. The mortgagee was not bound to pay the rents of the entire holdings. The mortgagee had no right or title to redeem the property. [168 D] (4) The mortgagee did not sell the land to him nor did he execute any lease deed in respect thereof. The mortgagee did neither sell the land nor gave any permission to the mortgagor to sell the land. The mortgagee could only sell the land if he wanted to do so. [169 E F] (5) The mortgagee 's right to redeem was not affected by the mortgage. [170 C] (6) The mortgagee in his capacity as a mortgagee was not entitled to redeem his mortgage. [167 H] (7) The mortgagee having failed to pay the mortgage money within the period prescribed by law, the mortgagor was entitled to recover the amount due from him. [165 D]
6522: The appellant was granted nautor land measuring about 4 bighas biswas in village Kanal for cultivation. He applied for the grant of nautor on June 29, 1974. The Forest Department filed an appeal against the said order before the Deputy Commissioner who accepted the same and vide his order dated September 9, 1983 set aside the order sanctioning nautor. The Financial Commissioner accepted the revision petition and set aside the grant of Nazarana to Gopinder Singh. The Forest Depart ment filed a revision petition before the Financial Commis sioner (Revenue Appeals) Himachal Pradesh who accepted the revision peti tion and set aside that order. The Financial Com missioner (Revenue Appeal) Himachal Pradesh rejected the revision petition. The Forest department filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court which was dismissed in limine. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was having less than 10 bighas of land but as he had not been able to produce any evidence to show that he had more than 10 bighas. The Financial Commi ssioner has rightly held that the appellant was eligible for the grant. [799C] 1.2 The appellant was not entitled to the grant of khair wood because he did not have the minimum area of 10 bighas. He could not be considered eligible for the allotment of khaira wood. The Forest Officer was not competent to sanction the nautor lands. The Forest authorities were not justified in rejecting the application of the appellant. [701E F] 1.3 The appellant was entitled to the benefit of Rule 7(1)(b) of the Rules. The Financial Commission erred in holding that the appellant had less than 10 biswas of land. The Financial commissioner ought to have given reasons why he came to the conclusion that the appellant is not eligible for the benefit of the rule. [702B C] 1.4 In the instant case, the Financial Commissioner wrongly assumed that the appellant would be eligible for the nauthari khaira land. The Forest Authorities were not justified either in refusing the na utari or in granting the nautors land. [703D] 1.

3068: The respondent was employed as a clerk in the appellant company. He filed an application under section 78 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, before the Labour Court for relief under section 7 8 (1) D. The Labour Court took the view that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under Section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order should be set aside on that ground alone. The Industrial Court allowed the appeal holding that the order was passed by the Labour Court in accordance with the provisions contained in section 78(1)D. The High Court confirmed the order of the Industrial Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the third Respondent had failed to apply under section 42(4), and that the order dismissing him was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Labour Courts have jurisdiction to consider whether the order is legal or just. If they find that there has been a breach of the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder, then they can pass appropriate orders according to law. [511C] 2. The Labour Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Labour Courts unless they are perverse or contrary to material on record. [512E] 3. The Labour courts have jurisdiction to examine whether the order of discharge or dismissal was properly passed or whether the procedure prescribed in the statute has been followed. [513F] 4. The Labour Tribunals have jurisdiction to enquire into the legality or propriety of the order of termination of service of a workman. [514A] 5. The Labour Cour t could not go behind the order of punishment. [515B]
1423: The appellant, a guarantor of a loan advanced by the respondent Bank to the principal debtor, filed an application under section 19(1) (b) of the . The High Court held that the letter of guarantee was not signed by the appellant and that it could be enforced only against the principal debtor. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court erred in holding that there was no contract between the appellant and the Bank on the question of guarantee. The letter of guarantee is not signed by any person other than the principal debtor but it is signed by the guarantor himself. It is not necessary for the guarantor to sign the letter of bank 's guarantee. [754 B] The letter of indemnity does not require the principal debtor to sign the document as a whole. The letter merely states that the principal debtor has agreed to pay the amount due to the Bank. There is nothing in the letter of indemnity which requires the principal debtor 's consent to sign the documents as a whole or even to accept the liability of the principal debtor in respect of the amount due. [755 C D]
842: The appellants were employed by the respondent as certifying officers under section 3(1) of the (20 of 1946) (hereinafter called the Act). They submitted to the respondent a draft standing order for certification under section 3 (1) of that Act. Respondent 1 was not satisfied with this draft standing order and, therefore, made an application to the certifying officer for modification in the draft. The appellants objected to the modification on the ground that it amounted to an unfair labour practice within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Act. The certifying officer rejected the objection holding that the draft standing orders were fair and reasonable and that they did not violate any provisions of the Schedule. The appellants then moved the Industrial Court for a declaration that the alteration made by respondent 1 was arbitrary and illegal and that the modifications made by respondent were invalid. The appellants contended that the modification made by respondent was not fair or reasonable and that the modification was not justified. The Industrial Court held that the modification in question was valid and that the appellants ' petition was maintainable. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The object of the Act is to require the employers to provide for conditions of service in respect of all the matters covered by the Schedule. It does not forbid the employer from enquiring whether any of the provisions made in the draft standing order are fair or reasonable. The object of enacting the Act is not to prohibit the employer from making the modification in the Standing Orders but to make them fair and reasonable. [978 E F] The object of section 3(2) is to require a copy of the draft standing Orders to be sent to the certifying office and to the employer so that the certifying officer may consider the same before he makes his report. Section 15(2)(b) provides that the certifying office shall forward to the certifying authority a copy of such draft standing orders together with the reasons therefor. If the certifying officer finds that the draft Standing Orders have been prepared in contravention of the provisions of the Act, he can pass suitable orders according to law. [977 G H; 979 A B] The object behind the enactment of section 3 is to enable the certifying officer to satisfy himself that the draft of the standing orders has been properly drawn up and that they conform
6762: The petitioners, who were the owners of a petrol tanker, were injured in an accident on 10.3.1989 and they filed claim petitions under section 92A of the Act claiming compensation for the death of one of their drivers. The Claims Tribunal held that the death was due to explosion and fire and that the tanker was carrying petrol which was a highly combustible material and volatile material and after the collision of the petrol tanker it had fallen on one of its sides on sloping ground resulting in escape of highly inflammable petrol and there was grave risk of explosion and fire in the tanker and that the accident occurred due to the use of a motor vehicle. [39E F] 1.3 The expression 'acture of use of a transport vehicle ' includes all those cases where the use of motor vehicle results in death or serious bodily injury to the person concerned. 4861: The appellant, a partnership firm, filed a suit for the recovery of certain amounts due to it from the respondent. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the decree was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit was not maintainable as it was barred under section 34 of the Arbitration Act; (ii) the suit is barred by limitation; and (iii) the suit being one for enforcement of an agreement between the parties, the stay sought for by the appellant could not be granted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the suit is "in respect of any matter agreed to be referred" as required by s.3 of the Foreign Awards Act or not is essentially a question of fact which has to be determined on the basis of evidence adduced before the Court. [832C] 2. The question raised in the suit relating to the effect (scope) of the arbitration agreement does not arise out of the contract entered into by the parties. It is only if the dispute is capable of being settled by way of arbitration that the Court can exercise its power under section 33 of the . [833D E] 3. Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, provides that all questions and disputes relating to the meaning of the said expression shall be decided by the arbitrator who is appointed by the parties and is not a person named or designated in the award. The arbitrator so appointed is a person who is or has been a Judge in his own cause. He is not a judge in his own case but he is a person judicially separated from his original party and has held the proceedings within the competence of the Court. Therefore, the arbitrator cannot act arbitrarily while exercising his functions. [833F G] 4. The question as to whether the suit falls within the scope of section 34 of Arbitration Act depends upon the nature of the relief claimed by the plaintiff and the nature of relief claimed by him. The object of the section is to prevent multiplicity of judicial proceedings and to avoid multiplicity and multiplicity. The object is to avoid multilacing of litigation and to avoid collision of the proceedings. [834G H

The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal by the appellant the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and restored the order of dismissal passed by the Subordinate Judge. The decree does not give any right to the party aggrieved by the decree to file a suit for its enforcement. The decree merely declares what the parties have entered into under the contract. 3065: The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 I.P.C. for causing injuries to the deceased with a knife and for causing her death. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the accused on the ground that the evidence of Kopia (PW 2) did not inspire confidence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The prosecution case was that the accused had caused injuries to the victim with a knife which he was wearing at the time when the incident took place. The accused was given a number of knife blows. He was threatened with knife. The accused then went away towards the place where the dead body was lying. The accused gave a number of sticks blow to the deceased. The accused ran away towards the spot where the dead bodies were lying. The medical evidence showed that there was no injury on the person of the deceased. [818 G H] 1.2. The evidence of K.W. Vaidya (PW 3), who was the brother of the deceased, was corroborated by the statement of the mother of the deceased and the other witnesses. The learned Sessions Judge in convicting the accused relied upon the evidence of P.W. 2, who had stated that the accused stabbed the deceased. According to him, the accused was giving a number of blows to the deceased and that he would go there on the following morning. The High 'Court also found that the evidence was not reliable because the evidence of the mother was not reliable. [819 B C] 1.3. The evidence clearly established that the accused inflicted injuries on the deceased with knife. There is nothing to show that the accused intended to cause such bodily injuries as would be likely to cause death or that he knew that it was likely to cause such injuries as would induce the deceased to commit suicide. [820 D E]
80: The ancestors of the plaintiffs first party and the defendants first party, who were mortga gees of the lands in dispute, made a settlement with the mortgagee of the lands. Under the terms of the settlement, the mortgagor was entitled to take possession of the lands on payment of Rs. 540. Lakhandeo Singh was also entitled to take delivery of possession of the land. The mortgage was redeemed by payment in proceedings under section 83 of the Transfer of Property Act. The mortgagee was not a raiyat within the meaning of section 116 of the Bihar Tenancy Act. He was therefore not a raiyat under section 116 of that Act. The suit for possession against the defendant first party was decreed. In appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the defendant first par ty had no right to take possession as he was a raiyat under the provisions of the Bihar Land Reforms Act. The High Court held that the defendant second party could acquire no rights of occupancy in the lands as the result of the settlement by the mortgagee, Lakhande o f the lands, the plaintiff could acquire no right of occupancy in them. On appeal by special leave it was contended: (1) that the defendant 's title to the lands was not affected by the settlement; (2) that the suit was barred by limitation; (3) that the courts below erred in law in holding that the defendants were not raiyats under section 116 and (4) that the High Court should have remanded the case to the trial court for deciding the question whether the defendants were raiyats within the meaning Of section 116 of Bihar Tenancy Act or not. HELD: (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that there was collusion between the mortgagee and the mortgagee. [778 D] (ii) The High Courts' decision was correct. It is well settled that where a person enters into an agreement with another under which he acquires his interest in the property, he cannot be said to be a raiyat within section 116 of Chotanagpur Tenancy Act. [779 E F] (iii) The High court was wrong in its view that the defendants could acquire no interest in the lands. [780 G H]

In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the constitutional validity of section 133(2)(b) of the Jammu and Kashmir State Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which required consultation with the Commission under section 133(1) of the Act, was not at all attracted; (ii) the State Government 's order dated July 25, 1969, in regard to the appointments of respondents Nos. 3 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of the claims of the writ petitioners who contended that they were senior and more qualified for promotion, was bad; (iii) the Public Service Commissio n has been consulted in accordance with its requirement; and (iv) the Public Services Commission for the State of J & K, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, had not consulted the Commission before making the promotions and transfers from one service to another. This means that the State must have sufficient number of candidates belonging to the backward classes to be eligible for the posts reserved for them. [740G H] 1.3. The State Government has not taken into consideration the provisions of Article 16(4). The word 'rent' is defined in section 2(h) of the Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, to mean "any sum payable by the tenant to the landlord as a condition of re quiring the premises or remitting the rent by instalments together with interest thereon at such rate as may be prescribed". 4919: The petitioners imported newsprint in India from abroad. They were charged with the levy of auxiliary duty under the Finance Act, 1981 on newsprint as modified by notifications issued under section 25 of the . The petitioners contended that the imposition of import duty had the direct effect of crippling the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by the Constitution as it had the direct consequence of cripple the freedom of expression and for the purposes of this section the said duty was not imposed upon them. The petitioners contended (1) that the imposition was unreasonable because the imposition of the import duty had been made without any authority of law; (2) that the impugned notification imposing the import duty was ultra vires the powers of Parliament; (3) that the notification was invalid because it contravened the provisions of article 301 of the Constitution; (4) that the petitioners were entitled to a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to refrain from enforcing the said provision. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief. [347B] 2.1 The petitioners have no fundamental right to carry on business in newsprint. They have no fundamental rights to carry on trade or business. They have only a right to do so. [348C] 2.2 The petitioners cannot be permitted to make a grievance that the imposition is unreasonable because the petitioners have no right to do business in newspritts. [349D] 3.1 The contention that the imposition has the effect of crimping the freedom of the press is misconceived. It is well settled that the freedom of press is not absolute and is subject to restrictions which may be reasonable. The freedom of the Press is subject to reasonable restrictions. [345E]
4426: The appellant was elected to the Assam Legislative Assembly from the constituency of the Manipur Legislative Assembly. He filed a petition in the High Court challenging the election on several grounds including the allegation that he had incurred an expenditure exceeding Rs. 1323.69 in contravention of section 77(6) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court accepted the petition and declared the appellant as having been duly elected. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the appellant had not incurred any expenditure beyond the limit prescribed under section 77(1)(b); (ii) the corrupt practice of hiring or procuring vehicles for the free conveyance of electors to and from certain polling stations within the said Assembly Constituency as defined in section 123(5) of the Act, was not proved; (iii) the returned candidate had incurred an illegal expenditure exceeding the amount fixed by the authorities concerned; (iv) the corrupt practices were committed by the appellant in the course of the election and therefore the declaration of the appellant as being duly elected was absolutely correct and the expenses incurred by him were well below the permissible limit; (v) the corrupt activities alleged against the appellant were not connected with the election but were only with regard to the furtherance of the prospects of the election. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant has not been able to prove either the charge of corrupt practice or of undue influence. [780C] 2. The appellant had not made out a case of undue influence at all. His case is that he had paid Rs. 500 to the voters who had voted for him. The appellant did not produce any evidence to show that he had actually paid Rs. 1000 to the voters. There is no evidence to show how much money he had spent. [773D E] 3. The appellant could not be held guilty of any corrupt practice unless he had incurred any expenditure in excess of the prescribed limit. [774E]
5060: The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Indian Economic Service and were later confirmed in that post. The petitioners contended that the direct recruits who had been holding the posts on ad hoc basis for several years had not been regularly promoted to the said posts and that the direct recruitees who had been working on ad hoc capacity for long years could not be considered for promotion to the posts which were held by them on ad hoc or regular basis. The petitioners also contended that the quota rule prescribed by the Government was not maintained and that the quota of direct recruits was not maintained. The petitioners further contended that the promotees who had been officiating continuously for more than four years without any break in service should have been given the benefit of continuous officiation in the posts. The petitioners therefore prayed for a writ of mandamus directing that the direct recruitment vacancies should be filled up by selection from among the officers serving in the offices under the Government in Economic/Statistics. The petitioners relied upon the decision of this Court in [State of West Bengal vs Dr. N. K. Mitter] (AIR 1970 SC 633) and contended that the ratio of that case would apply only where direct recruitment is made after the initial constitution of the two services was completed and the direct recruits were appointed in accordance with that procedure. The petitioners submitted that the direct appointees who had joined the posts on the basis that they were appointed on ad hoc and temporary basis were entitled to be treated as direct recruits for all purposes including seniority and that the respondents should be directed to treat them as direct recruits in the posts they were holding prior to the appointment of the direct recruits. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. The petitioners are not entitled to claim seniority over the direct recruits because they were not appointed

[307 G H] (3) The expression in section 2 (5) of Act means "all lands which are actually occupied by a tenant, or other person, who holds such land as owner or tenants, as the cases may be". 6373: The appellant along with two others were convicted for murdering Kumari Mangala in furtherance of their common intention and causing disappearance of evidence of the offence. They were sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life under the first count and to pay a fine of Rs.2,500 each with a default clause and directed both the substantive sentences to run concurrently. The High Court enjoys the power of revision under section 397 read with Section 401 Cr.P.C. and also under section 374(1) of the Code. The High court enjoys the powers of a Court of Appeal under Section 386(c) of the Criminal Procedure Code (for short 'the Code') subject to the provisos (1) and (2) to Section 377(1) and also under Section 374(3) of the Cr. P.C. The High Cour t has no inherent jurisdiction to enhance the sentence even if it is not satisfied that the accused person was suffering from any mental infirmity or had been suffering from mental illness which may have prevented him from appearing before the Court. 247: The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for redemption of certain immovable properties. The respondents contended that they had become owners by adverse possession and that the appellants were entitled to redeem the property on payment of the mortgage money. The trial court dismissed the respondents ' application for rendition of accounts but the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court with some modifications. The respondents preferred an appeal to this Court. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that a default had been committed by the mortgagors and ordered rendition. The High Court could not be said to have erred in law in interfering with the order of the lower courts. The High Courts had jurisdiction under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act to determine the appeal and pass orders relating to the properties situated in foreign territories. The High Cour t had no jurisdiction to decide whether the properties were subject matter of the new decree or whether the rights of the parties were affected thereby. The High court had jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the properties in dispute were subject to the provisions of the Act. 6353: The Kerala State Legislature passed the Kerala Sales Tax Act, 1963 (Act No. 9 of 1963) which was enacted in the year 1964. 5087: The appellant assessee was assessed to tax under section 143(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that it had failed to furnish return for the assessment year 1962 63. The Commissioner of Income tax issued a notice to the appellant under section 148 of the Act and called upon it to show cause why the interest charged under sections 139 and 215 of the Act should not be revised. The appellant filed two revision petitions before the Commissioner of Income Tax contending that the interest levied under section 139 and 215 was not appealable but only an enhancement of the penalty imposed by the Income Tax Officer. The Commissioner rejected both the revisions petitions. The appellant then moved the High Court in revision which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Commissioner had no power to revise the orders passed by him under section 264 of the Act; (ii) the order levying interest under section 139 was without jurisdiction as the Commissioner had extended the date for furnishing the return under section 139; (iii) the order imposing interest under section 215 was illegal because the Commissioner had not applied his mind to the question whether the interest levied was payable or not; (iv) the order enhancing the penalty was without jurisdiction; (v) the order reducing the penalty was invalid inasmuch as the Commissioner could not take into account the amount of interest paid by the appellant; (vi) the order of the Commissioner was without jurisdiction and (vii) the order was bad because the Commissioner did not apply his mind to any question of law arising out of the order of assessment. HELD: (i) The Commissioner had no authority to enhance the penalty imposed under section 139. [144 E] (ii) The Commissioner was competent to revise the order of levy of interest under section 214. [145 A] (iii) The order of the Income tax Officer was without jurisdiction. The Commissioner had not exercised his powers under section 263 of the Act. He had merely directed the Income tax officer to file a return of income under section 139(1) or section 215 of the Income 'tax Act, 1961. The Commissioner was not entitled to exercise the powers under section 214 of the Act in respect of the order passed by him. [146 F G]

The Explanation merely says that the goods should have been used for the purposes of manufacturing or production. [997 F] (4) The Explanation is not intended to apply to sales of goods which do not fall under the first category. 4349: The Delhi Development Authority is a statutory body constituted under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The expression "Municipal Committee" in section 3 (31) includes a municipality also. [36A] 2. The expression, 'Municipality ' in section 31(1)(a) means a municipality established or deemed to have been established under the Delhi Municipalities Act, 1959. The expression is not defined in the General Clauses Act. The word 'municipal area ' in section 2(g) is defined in section 2 (h) as meaning the area within the jurisdiction of a
3983: The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for partition of the joint Hindu family properties. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court in appeal, held that the provisions of section 14(1) (a) of the Act had no application to the case and that the sale by her in favour of defendant No. 2 was null and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sale was not binding on the respondent as she did not have any right to alienate the property in execution of the decree passed in her favour. HELD: The High Court erred in holding that the sale in favour of the respondent was null and invalid. [811 D] The provision contained in sub section (2) of section 14 of the Act is intended to provide for a limited interest in the property which may be allotted to the widow at a partition or in lieu of maintenance under an instrument, order or award. It does not prescribe any other interest in the land which may be given to the widow after the death of the husband. [812 E F] The expression "any interest" in sub section 1 of section 14 has reference only to the interest given to the wife in the property and not to the interest of the husband in the property. The expression "interest" in sub sections (1), (2) and (3) of section 13 of the Act are intended to cover all interests of the husband and his heirs including the interest of his wife in the land. [813 G H; 814 A B]

1250: The appellant in Civil Appeal No. 237 of 1960, was a firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of certain goods. The appellant contended that the State legislature having authority to enact a law imposing a tax on the sale of goods it could not impose any tax on the supply of material which was in the course of import from Germany and was therefore outside the purview of the Act. Held, that the State Legislature having authority to legislate on the subject, the State Legislature was competent to enact a taxing statute. The State Legislature having power to enact a tax on sales or purchases of goods, the State legislature could not impose a tax on such transactions. The State legislature having power to levy tax on the transaction of sale or purchase of goods, it could not be said that there was no sale or purchase by the appellants. 5711: The respondent company filed returns for all the quarters covered within the period indicated in section 28(2) of the Punjab Act. The appellants did not accept the award but they moved the High Court by way of a writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the reference made by the Land Acquisition Officer was incompetent because there was no reference at all by the Collector. [766 A] (2) The question whether the reference was competent or not is a mixed question of law and fact depending on the facts of each case. It is not necessary that the decision should have been given by the Land Ac sici ions Officer himself. [764 B C] (3) The High court was wrong in holding that it was open to the Land Acquisition officer to make a reference without making a reference. 4714: The respondent, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation created under the State Act of 1950 was in appeal by special leave. The appellant Corporation came before the High Court challenging the Award. A learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that termination of services while on probation was illegal and invalid. The Corporation filed a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that termination was bad for non compliance with section 25F of the ( 'Disputes ' for short) and set aside the order of discharge. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. Section 2(oo) of the defines retrenchment as meaning "termination of service of a workman for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include (a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or (b) termination of the service of the workman on the ground of continued ill health." [766A] 1.2. In the instant case the services have been terminated on the ground that the services had been terminated on account of unsatisfactory service. The term 'retrenchment' has not been defined in the Act. It is an expression used in the definition clause of the Act. The definition clause in the Act is wider than the definition of retrenchment given in the Industrial Disputes Act. Therefore, the word 'retrenchment ' would mean termination of service of the employee for any reason whatever. [766B C] 1.3. The word 'rettrature ' means 'reckoning ' or 'discharge '. [767C] 1.4. The word `retrenchment ' is not defined in the Industrial disputes Act. It may be possible to describe the word as 'retrenchment'. But it must be remembered that retrenchment connotes some kind of retrenchment which involves some sort of stigma. It also implies a cessation of work or job for a considerable length of time. It is so understood in industrial adjudication. [768D E] 1.5. The word retrenchment is not a technical term. It is a term of art. It is well settled that a person who continues to work after his absorption in the service of a corporation is deemed to be a fresh entrant even though he is not actually working. [769E F
1135: The respondent Sabha had been granted mining leases for the extraction of coal from collieries situated in Chhindwara District. The appellants were called upon to pay the coal tax for the different periods mentioned in the notices issued by the respondent. The appellants challenged the validity of the notices before the High Court and the High Court dismissed the writ petitions. [185 D] (3) The appellants have not been able to show any material to justify their claim that they are entitled to raise the said point at the time when the appeals were filed. [186 E] (4) The appellants could not be allowed to raise this ground at a subsequent stage. [187 F] (5) The appellants were not entitled to raise it subsequently. [188 B]
