2374: The appellant obtained an order for eviction from the premises in execution of which he was evicted. He applied to the Rent Controller for possession under section 3 of the East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948 and the Rent Controller rejected it on the ground that the application had become infructuous because the decree holder had not taken delivery of possession. The High Court held that the Act did not apply to the case and dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that the Act was not intended to cover the cases like the present one where there is no collusion between the decree holder and the judgment debtors and that the Act does not provide for a bar against the execution of the decree. HELD: (i) The Act does not contain any provision for the removal of the obstruction or disconnection of the supply of electricity. It is only in respect of the cases covered by sections 4 and 5 of the Act that the Act has been made applicable to the case. [511 B] (ii) Section 3 of the Act provides that the provisions of the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force. The Act does nothing more than providing for the removal or reconnection of electric lines. The Act is intended to cover cases covered by section 4 and 5. The Act makes it clear that the Act applies to all cases covered by the provisions of sections 4 and5. [512 C D] (iii) The Act is a complete code relating to the procedure for the recovery of arrears of rent and the eviction of tenants. The Act contains no provision for the eviction of the tenant except on the grounds mentioned therein. The Act also does not contain a provision for the payment of compensation for the use and occupation of the premises. The Act therefore cannot be said to be a complete Code dealing with the matters covered by sections 3 and 5 of Act 1 of 1947. [513 E F]

4687: The respondent was detained under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. He made a statement before the Customs Officer admitting that he was a member of the crew but denied any knowledge of the contraband goods. The Customs authorities seized the contraband articles and the trawler. The respondent 's plea was that he had no "full knowledge" about the contraband article and therefore his detention was illegal. The High Court quashed the order of detention on the ground that the respondent at the time of joining the vessel as a member of crew did not know that the vessel was to be used for smuggling activity. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. Section 10 of the Act is mandatory in character. It is not necessary that the person against whom an order of detention is made should have "full knowledge", which means that he must have been aware that the vessel is to be used as a vessel for smuggling activities. [850F] 2. In view of the fact that the maximum period of detention mentioned in section 10 of the Customs act has expired, and as such the appeal has become infructuous. [851G] 3. The High court was wrong in quashing the order of the detention on the basis that the respondent admitted that he was the tindal of the vessel 'Shahe Nagina ' which had been seized by the Customs officer in 1977 for smuggling wrist watches and that a penalty of Rs. 5,000.00 was levied against him. [852A B]
6979: The appellants were the owners of a property in dispute. They filed an application under section 145 Cr. P.C. before the Magistrate for attachment of their property. Against this order, the appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and issued a writ quashing the order of the Sessions Judge. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the appellants have not challenged the order of withdrawal of the attachment and the Sessions Judge has only stayed the operation of the order of attachment, it is not open to the appellants to challenge the order of withdrawing the attachment. It is not necessary that he should pass an order staying the proceeding pending before him before passing any order staying such proceeding. [551G H] 1.3 The Magistrate could not have passed an order staying proceedings pending before the Magistrate. He could not have directed the police to maintain status quo until the Magistrate passed an appropriate order staying proceedings. [552A B] 1.4 The Magistrate could have ordered the police to keep the property in his
7115: The appellant company was ordered to be wound up on the ground that its holding company had failed to pay the subscribers ' share capital of Rs. 10 crores and odd, as directed by the High Court. The High Court set aside the order of winding up and directed the holding company to pay off the subscribers ' contribution to the extent of a sum of Rs.10.40 crores. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have been invested with powers under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956, in cases where there is no scheme for revival or rehabilitation of the company. In such cases, the High Courts are not bound to grant any relief to the depositors. [907 E] 2. The High courts should not interfere with the orders passed by the Tribunals and the High Courts in matters like these. [908 F G] 3. The High court has power to pass interim orders which may be necessary in the interest of justice. It is not necessary to go into the merits of the case. [909 A B] 4. The High Cour ts cannot exercise their jurisdiction under section 394 of the Companies act, 1956 when the company itself is being wound up. [905 D] 5. The High Co urt will not interfere with an order passed by the Company Law Board unless it comes to the conclusion that the Company has committed a breach of the provisions of the Act or has violated the principles of natural justice or has contravened any of the provisions thereof. [906 H; 907 A] 6. The High COurt can only give directions to the Company Law Boards to consider whether the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. [904 D] 7. The High Com missions must take note of the fact that the Company is being woundup because of the failure of the creditors to make payment of their dues. [903 E] 8. The High Commission has to examine the financial position of the company and the circumstances under which the company was unable to pay its debts. The Company Law Board must also examine whether the company has made out a case for winding up of the company on just
472: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence of death to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the deceased 's evidence was not reliable as he had been tutored; (ii) the prosecution case was highly improbable because the deceased and the appellant were quite friendly with each other and so were the deceased and Qudrat Ullah; (iii) the prosecution witnesses had a motive to falsely implicate the accused in the crime; (iv) the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt; and (v) the fact that the deceased and his brother had a shop near the shop of the appellant was not sufficient to establish the guilt of the appellant. HELD: (1) There is no reason why the evidence of the eye witnesses should be discarded merely because they are interested witnesses. [464 E] (2) It is well settled that the court can act upon the testimony of a witness if it thinks fit. If the court considers the testimony of such witness as being reliable, it may accept the same. But if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the occurrence, the court would not like to scrutinise the testimony of the witness like the only ritualistic scrutiny about their presence at the time and place perpetrated the crime. [465 F H]
3452: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent Birdhi Lal. He brought a suit in the court of the Assistant Collector, Baran for possession of land comprised in khasra Nos. 513 and 678 situate in village Balakhera under sections 180 and 183 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The suit was decreed by the trial court but on appeal by the State Government, the High Court reversed the judgment of the first appellate court and restored that of the Assistant collector. In the second appeal, the High court held that Birdhi lal being a trespasser was not liable to be ejected from the land. The appellant thereupon moved this Court by means of a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for the issue of appropriate writs or directions restraining the respondents from evicting him. The petition was allowed by this Court and the impugned judgments were set aside. The appellant came up before this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that as the High Court had exercised its appellate jurisdiction and substituted its own opinion for the opinion of the Revenue authorities contrary to the well established principles of law, the impugned judgment cannot be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court has rightly exercised its appellate power and substituted its judgment. [601B] 1.2. The High court has rightly exercised the appellate powers and substituted its decision. The High Courts' interference is justified only when there is an error apparent on the face of the record. [609C D] 1.3. The High courts' interference with the findings of fact is permissible if they are perverse. [607E] 1.4. The High Courl does not interfere with the concurrent finding of fact unless it is shown to be perverse. [608A] 1.5. The High CMJP No. 4/75 Page 6 of 75 Court can interfere with the findings only if the finding is palpably wrong; otherwise, it will be a case of total non application of mind. [608D] 1.6. The High COurt should have taken into account all relevant factors including the fact that the appellate authority had found that the appellant was a trespasser. [605F
3425: The respondent joined the Punjab Education Service in 1933. He was confirmed as a lecturer in the Punjab Education Department on July 1, 1947. In June 1961 he received a copy of letter No. 5137 ED I 60/9269 dated May 2, 1961 addressed by the Secretary to Government, Punjab, Education Department to the Director of Public Instruction, Punjab intimating that in supersession of the aforesaid letter dated May 2. 1961, sanction had been accorded to the grant of pension and death cum retirement gratuity to the respondent under rules 5.27 and 6.13 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Vol. II read with para 9(1) (a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of this order. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order imposing the cut in his superannuation pension and deathcum retirement gratuity was not an administrative order but only a quasi judicial order and therefore it could not be said that the order was an administrative order. It also held that the order did not amount to any punishment within the meaning of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD: The order imposing the penalty of dismissal from service was an administrative act and not a quasi judicial one. [364 D] The order imposing penalty of dismissal was an administrative decision and not a purely executive order. The order was not merely administrative order. The question whether the order was administrative or quasi judicial was essentially a matter for the decision of the authority concerned and if it was not, the question of giving opportunity to show cause would not arise. [365 C D] The State of Punjab vs Gurdas Ram, ; , referred to.
87: The plaintiff alleged that the parties were Sudras and not Dwijas, and that he was in possession of certain properties. He claimed that the parties had been joint and not a Hindu family. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the parties being Sudras and Budparkash were joint and not sepa rate, and that the parties could not sue for partition because the plaintiff 's father had no son. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the parties are Sudras and neither of them was in joint possession of any of the properties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the parties were joint and were not in joint possession; (2) that the parties did not form a joint Hindu family with the plaintiff and the defendant, and (3) that the courts below erred in law in holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to a decree for partition. HELD: (i) The Courts below have rightly held that the plaintiff has failed to prove his case. [875 C] (ii) The Courts have found that the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief. The finding of fact by the Courts below is based upon proper appreciation of evidence. [877 D] (iii) The Courts were wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the parties actually belonged to the family. There was nothing to show that there was any custom or usage which would support the conclusion that the parties belonged to the families of the parties. [878 E] (iv) The Courts had correctly decided that the parties in the present case were joint and the parties were in joint possession. [879 F]

The appellants filed petitions under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of assessment and for restraining them from levying purchase tax on the goods purchased and for refund of the tax illegally collected from them. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 5 of the East Punjab General SalesTax Act, 1948, was void as it conferred only a partial severance of the charging section and that the entire Act was void as the said section was stillborn and that as the said Section was the charging section, the entire Act, was void. HELD : (i) The object of the amending Act 13 of 1959 is to make the levy effective from April 1, 1962. It does not provide for any separate machinery for the collection of tax. The amending Act has been made with retrospective effect. [567 H] (ii) The Act is a self contained code. It is a complete Code. It deals with all matters relating to taxation including the imposition of tax. It is an extension of the Act. It is not a piece of legislation. It is merely a continuation of the Act itself. It is only a piece of delegated legislation. [568 D] (iii) The Act as amended by the Amending Act 13 of 1958 is valid. [569 F] (iv) The Act being a self contained Code, it is not a mere extension of the charging provision. [570 B C] (v) The Act, as amended, is a selfcontained code. [571 E] (vi) The Act was enacted to give effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles specified in clauses (a) to (g). Clause (f) of section 2 defines "tax" to mean "any tax payable under the provisions of the Act". Clause (h) of section 3 provides that the Act shall apply to every dealer who purchases goods from a registered dealer or from a registered dealers other than those specified in cls.(d
1307: The appellant filed a suit for enforcement of the mortgage in the Court of the 2nd Subordinate Judge, Midnapore. He applied for execution of the personal decree passed by the Subordinate Judge. The Subordinate Judge held that the decree was not fully satisfied and dismissed the suit. The District Judge allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the Subordinate Judge and restored the decree of his court. In Second Appeal No. 1442 of 1942, the High Court held that the provisions of section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act were not applicable to the case because the appellant had obtained a decree under section 36 of that Act against the respondent in respect of the property mortgaged to him. [840 F] (iii) The High courts have been adopting a construction which would defeat the purpose of the Act and make it applicable to all proceedings pending before the subordinate courts. 2933: The respondent was a licensee under the appellant. He had been carrying on business in watches and watches. On March 19, 1963, the Rummaging Officer seized watches of the respondent 's business premises and seized watches. The Collector of Customs under section 110(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, extended the period for giving notice under section 124 (a) of the Act either after the initial period of six months or the extended period had already expired. The respondent filed an application before the Collector of Customs claiming that he had no right to resist the extension of time and that he should be given a chance to show cause against the extension of the time. The Collector rejected the application holding that the Collector could not extend the period of six month as the conditions prescribed by section 110(1)(b) were not satisfied. The respondent appealed to the Central Government which dismissed the appeal. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the proviso to section 110(l) did not contemplate any notice to the respondent as the considerations which would weigh with the Collector or which would be relevant for granting extension would be of such a nature that they could not be disclosed; that the proviso did not contemplate a notice to the Collector or to which would be material for granting extension but it did not contemplate an opportunity to the respondent to show cause why the extension should not be granted. [52 F] (ii) The proviso does not contemplate a hearing to the person who has applied for extension of time. The proviso contemplates a notice to him to show cause if he so desires. If he is heard, he can make his representation. If he makes a representation, the authority will consider it and decide whether the extension should be granted or refused. 6019: The appellants instituted a suit in respect of Schedule B land for a declaration that the disputed land formed part of North Bhuggatdih Colliery which had vested in the Central Government and thereafter in the company under the provisions of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. The company resisted the suit on various grounds. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the disputed lan d was part of the North Bhuggata Colliery and that the interest claimed by the plaintiffs stood extinguished with the vesting of the estate of the company in the Central Govern ment. 1488: The appellant, a registered trade union of jute mills, entered into a contract with the respondent for sale and purchase of raw jute. The contract was to be completed within a certain time. 1848: The petitioner, a proprietor of a forest in West Bengal, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the vesting of his right to cut trees in a forest on the ground that the terms of section 5(aa) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, (W.B. Act 1 of 1954), did not include the right to cut the trees and that the provisions of the Act were violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the terms "estate" as defined in section 2(1)(a) of the Act included the right to the trees in a forests and that the word "personal" was wide enough to include the right of cutting trees. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the words "land held or other rights possessed by an intermediary" in section 5(4) of the W. B. Act, 1953 must be construed in the light of the context in which they occur. The word "personally" is used in the sense of property or personal rights. It includes all persons who are entitled to the possession of such land whether such possession has been taken or not. In the present case, the right to trees in a village vested in the State and the right to fell trees in a private forest vested in the Government. The right to cut and remove trees in a plot of land cannot be said to have been acquired by the Government under the Act. The word 'personal' does not necessarily mean the right to hold property. The right of the Government to cut trees is not a right to property but is a right to the property. The word is used in a wider sense to include both the right to possession and the right of the owner to cut and carry away the trees. The word has been used in the context in its widest sense and it means the right to use the soil for the purpose of raising a loan for raising a loan. The word does not necessarily imply the right to acquire the land. The right is not merely the right to take or possess a thing or right to raise a loan. It is a right in the land itself and not a right in any other person. The word in the context means the right of taking or acquiring a thing
3105: The respondent company paid bonus for the year 1964 at the rates mentioned in the agreement exhibit A.5. The appellants claimed that they should be paid the profit bonus as per the Act in addition to what has been paid as per exhibit A. 5. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim and held that the payment of bonus under the agreement was not a profit sharing bonus but an amount paid as production bonus or incentive wages. The Company appealed to this Court by special leave. It contended that the payment made under the agreement exhibit 'A.5 was an ex gratia payment made out of charity and as such, it was not a payment of bonus linked with production or productivity. HELD: (i) The payment of bonus is an ex grafit given to the employees who are employed on a permanent basis. The payment of Bonus is an additional benefit which is available to all the employees irrespective of the fact whether they have completed six months ' approved service or not. [454 E] (ii) The payment under the agreement exhibits 'A. 5 is an ex gromate payment made out to the employees. The payment under this agreement is an ex post facto payment made out from the funds of the employer. The payment is an ex mertia payment made to the employee during his employment. The payment does not depend upon any contract between the parties. The payment may be made in consideration of past services rendered by the employee. In the present case, the payment is an ad hoc payment made out on behalf of the employer and is not a profit shared by the employees. [453 B C]
931: The respondent firm which is not a licensed dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, was assessed to sales tax for the year ending 31st March, 1956 under the provisions of the Madras General Sale Tax Act, 1930. The contention that r.16(5) was ultra vires was rejected by the High Court. The appellant had no right to claim exemption from taxation on hides andkins under the provisions contained in the Turnover & Assessment Rules, 1938, and the Explanation thereto. The appellant could not claim exemption from tax under the provisions relating to hides, skins and hides made under the said two Acts.

5898: The respondent retired as Superintendent, Directorate of Industries, Punjab on September 30, 1983. He filed a complaint against the appellant under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act alleging that he had purchased sign boards in 1979 and that he had not been able to purchase such sign boards from the appellant. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. On appeal, the Sessions Judge acquitted the respondent holding that the proviso was not applicable because the same had not been included in the main rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Volume II. The High Court allowed the petition by its order dated September 4, 1985. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 2.2 is not applicable since the respondent had already retired as Superintendent on September 30. 1983 and that the bar contained in the proviso would be attracted only if the cause of action arose after his retirement and before the sanction for prosecution of the appellant was obtained. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The proviso cannot be read in isolation but has to be given full effect. [923F] 1.2 The proviso does not take away the right of the Government servant to move any court for quashing the charge-sheet or the First Information Report at any stage of the proceeding. It merely provides that no judicial proceedings shall lie except with the previous sanction of the competent authority. [924G H] 1.3 The object of the proviso is to save the concerned officer from being prosecuted for the offences referred to therein. The language employed in the proviso clearly indicates that the intention of the legislature was to save the officer who was sought to be proceeded against from being prosecuted. [925A B] 1.4 If the interpretation canvassed by the appellant is accepted, the very purpose of enacting the proviso would get defeated. [926C D]
2885: The appellant was a dealer in food grains. He manufactured two packets of the same article and sold it to the respondent who was the wholesale dealer of the said article. The respondent purchased the said packets from the appellant for sale and delivered them to the appellant. The appellant contended that the respondent had no authority to sell the said packets at the price fixed by the Food (Health) Authority under the Act, and that the appellant was not liable to be prosecuted for selling the said packets. Held, that the appellant did not fall within the definition of 'consumer ' in section 2(1)(d) of the , and was not liable for prosecution. The appellant was not a manufacturer or a seller of the said articles. The appellant did not manufacture any article of food but only used the said articles for manufacturing the said articles and sold them to the respondent. The appellant could not be prosecuted for sale of the said products as he was not a consumer within the meaning of section 2(i)(d). The appellant was neither a manufacturer nor a seller of articles of food. The appellant had no authority either to sell or to sell the articles of food to the respondent at the price determined by the Food Inspector. The appellant, therefore, was not a person aggrieved by the order of the Food Inspector and was not entitled to maintain an appeal against such order. The appellant 's case was covered by section 7 of the Act. The appellant failed to prove that he was a manufacturer or seller of the articles of Food. The appellant also failed to establish that he was not guilty of any offence under the Act.

44: The appellant was a salesman in a retail shop in Pulbazar in the district of Darjeeling. The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal of the accused. In this appeal, by special leave, it was contended for the appellant (1) that the trial court and the Sessions Judge were wrong in holding that the facts established by the prosecution did not constitute any offence, and (2) that the evidence showed no more than that the accused could have been convicted on the basis of the circumstantial evidence. The fact, therefore, that the accused have not been able to establish that they were carrying the silver in contravention does not mean that they were not dealers. [1165 F H] 4. 5886: The petitioner filed an application under section 11 A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for making a reference to the Civil Court on the ground that the award was not made within two years from the date of the commencement of the Act. The Land Acquisition Officer, after hearing the parties, passed an order dated 23.9.1986 holding that the award had been made beyond the period of two years from 24.9.1984 and directed that the land acquisition proceeding should be declared as lapsed. The petitioner challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it by its judgment dated 30.4.1987. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The proviso to section 11 A(2) of the Act is mandatory and not directory. It is only when the Collector has not made an award within the time prescribed therein that the provisions of section 11A are attracted. [780C] 1.2 Section 11A of the Act provides that if the Collector does not make an award within a period of two yeas from the date on which he receives notice of the award, he shall proceed with the acquisition proceedings in accordance with the provisions of the Act to the extent provided for in sub section (3). Sub section (3) of section 11B provides that if no award is made within two yea from the date when the notice of the Award was served on the owner of the land, the entire proceedings for the acquisition of the land shall lapse. In other words, the Collector must have knowledge of the award within the meaning of section 11 A. [771E F] 1.3 The proviso to sub section (2) of section11A makes it clear that where the award is made more than one year after the date of publication of the declaration under section 6 of the Act, the award shall be made within a period oi two years from such date. The proviso further makes it clear in case of urgency that the Collector may extend the period for making the award. The proviso also makes it clear beyond doubt that the period of limitation would commence from the date the Collector takes possession of the land. [772F G] 1.4

The appellants accepted Rs. 2.400 as premium and paid the same to the complainant. The complainant was not entitled to receive any amount by way of premium. The appellants filed an appeal to the High Court against their conviction. The High Court held that the appellants had accepted Rs.2,400 as the premium and paid it to the complainant on 23rd November, 1950, and therefore, they could not be said to have committed an offence under section 18 (1) of Bombay Act LVII of 1947. 2932: The appellant was appointed as a member of the Bihar Civil Service (Executive Branch) in the State of Bihar. It only empowers the appointing authority or any other authority empowered in that behalf to place an Officer under suspension if the circumstances so warrant. [718 E F] (ii) The order of the Disciplinary Authority is not vitiated either on the ground of mala fides or on the ground the evidence collected during investigation is not sufficient to sustain the order of dismissal. [719 C D] (iii) The order is not vitiated merely because some other view is possible. 6937: The appellant moved the High Court for a writ of Habeas Corpus directing the respondents to produce the records relating to the criminal contempt committed by him. The High court has rightly held that the contempt jurisdiction is discretionary in nature and the Court should be loath to exercise its discretion in favour of a party who moves the Court with clean hands. [766F] 2.1. It is well settled that the power conferred on the Court under Article 215 of the Constitution is of wide amplitude and can be exercised suo moto or on an application made by any person or authority. The High courts are empowered to take action against the contemnor for committing contempt of court. [769E F] 3.3. 6141: The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, established an industrial unit in the State of Rajasthan. 1705: The respondent was charged with an offence under section 348, I.P.C., and section 420, I. P.C. for having committed the offence of cheating. He pleaded not guilty to the charge but was convicted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate on a charge under section 120B, I.p.C. and section 420 I.P,.C. On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent had been wrongly acquitted by the trial court; (ii) the order of acquittal could not be sustained because the evidence showed that the respondent had made a confession before the police officer in his office at Calcutta and that he had given the same to the police officer who recorded his statement; (iii) the High Court erred in quashing the process issued against the respondent by the Magistrate without giving any reasons for doing so. HELD : (1) The High Court has rightly quashed the process issued by the Magistrate. [880 A] (2) It is true that the High Court should have given reasons for quashing the process. But it must be remembered that the High Courts are not powerless to issue directions or writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. It is a matter of great public policy to respect the liberty of citizens. The power to issue writs is a very wide one. It may be exercised where some special circumstances exist, e.g., where there is no material to support the allegations, or where the allegations are wholly arbitrary or where theIDA has been able to rebut the presumption arising from the existence of facts which point to the commission of a criminal offence. [877 B C] (3) The High Courts should not interfere with the exercise of discretion of the High Courts in issuing prerogative writs except when they are satisfied that the exercise of the discretion itself is contrary to law or is vitiated by mala fides. [878 D E]

2791: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 147, 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to those charges but were convicted by the trial court. On appeal the High Court acquitted them on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the action of the appellants in conducting the search outside the limits of their police station house was bona fide because they knew that it was a police officer and could have easily asked the police station house officer to conduct the search under section 166(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was further contended that the evidence of the witnesses did not establish that the appellants had been carrying arms and ammunition at the time when the incident took place. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) There is no reason why the police should be held to be guilty for an offence under section 147 of the Indian penal code even though the act of the appellants might have been committed within the limits of his police station. [447C] (2) The police party had come to the house of Gopi and Munshi and they had gone there. The police party was armed with guns and lathis. 1559: The appellants were the owners of sugar and were selling sugar at a price higher than the price fixed by the Controller under the Sugar and Sugar Products Control Order, 1948. The appellants contended that the sale was not in compliance with the directions issued by the Controller in exercise of authority under the Sugar & Sugar Products Control order, 1948, but was in violation of the provisions of section 3(1) of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947, as amended by the Bihar Finance Act, 1949. Held, that the appellants were not liable to pay sales tax on their sales. The expression "sale" in the two Acts at all material times was used in the sense of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of contract but the word "transfer" was used in section 2(g) of the Act in the sense that the transfer of property is for consideration. The word "sale" has been defined in section 2 (g) of Bihar Sales Tax, Act, 1947. The definition of sale in the two enactments at all material time was: "Sale" means, with all its grammatical variations and cognate expressions any transfer of property from one person to another."

2297: The appellant was appointed a Commission of Enquiry by the Chief Justice of Assam High Court. The High Court rejected the petition holding that the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction to pass the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Chief justice could not act as a Judge when he was working as a Commission of Inquiry and that the order of stay granted by the High Court on November 3 was without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The Chief Justice was not competent to sit at Sibsagar and hear matters of public importance. The power conferred on the Central Government by section 5 of the Telegraphs Act, 1885 is a judicial power and it cannot be delegated to any other authority except the Central Government. [523C] 2. 2435: The petitioner was detained under section 3(3) of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. 1748: The petitioners who were members of the Ruling Family filed a suit against respondent No. 2 for appropriate reliefs. They alleged that the Ruler when so chosen and installed held the State and Zamindari as life tenant subject to the usual charges for maintenance of the members of the family, had failed to obtain the sanction of the Union Government under section 87B(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The petitioners contended that the said section is ultra vires, because it contravenes articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and as such, the condition precedent prescribed by it which requires previous sanction of the Central Government before filing a suit against the Ruler of an Indian State, was not fulfilled. Held, that the provisions of section 87B (2) are ultra vires, and the condition precedent laid down in section 87B must be satisfied. The words "as they think fit" in section 87 B(2) have been used in the same sense in which it has been used in section 87C(3). The expression "as they thinks fit" in the context means "the conditions precedent to the institution of a suit against a Ruler of a former Indian State". The word "as he thinks fit" does not mean "the conditions precedents" but only those which would justify the grant of sanction to the suit. The sanction given by the Central Government under section 86(1) and (3) of the Act is a condition precedent to the maintainability of the suit.

1277: The respondent K. Rangachari was appointed as a Clerk in the Southern Railway on April 1, 1957 and he was promoted to the post of Assistant Station Master on May 31, 1960. He was further promoted to the selection grade on October 1, 1961. In respect of non selection posts seniority in service is the qualification but in respect of non promotion to the selection post one of the qualifications for promotion to such posts is that the candidate should have passed the examination held by the Railway Board for recruitment to the post. The respondent applied for and obtained a certificate from the said High Court under article 132(1) of the Constitution as it involved a substantial question of law, namely, whether reservation of posts at the stage of appointment and not for reservation of posts for promotion after appointment and so the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus directing the Railway authorities to give effect to the directions of the Railway Board. Held, that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of article 16(4) of the constitution and the High Court was right in holding that the respondent could claim the benefit of that article. The object of Article 16(4), in view of the wide language employed therein, is to provide equality of opportunity to all citizens who enter service on the basis of any scheme of public employment and to make appointments to posts in the public services 'and to enable them to exercise their right of consideration for promotion. It is not necessary that each and every person who comes into the service must be appointed to the post according to the rules applicable generally or to a particular post. It is sufficient if each and everyone concerned has his own knowledge and experience of the matters relating to employment and it cannot be denied that there is nothing which makes it obligatory that the State or its instrumentalities should act fairly and in public interest. If the State Government considers that a particular post should be filled in by direct recruitment, then the procedure prescribed by the said rules should be followed and the result thereof should be made known to everyone concerned. The State Government should therefore take steps to fill up the vacancies and fill up the same expeditiously. 1910: The appellant, a local board of Barpeta, was assessed to property tax by the respondent. In 1953, the local board imposed a tax on the Kharma market at Rs. 1000/ for holding the market. 6204: The appellant was appointed to the Indian Police Service in 1955. 1892: The respondent was a cinema house owner. It had been granted licence for its cinema house and had been paying a licence fee calculated on the basis of annual valuation of the cinema houses made by a method which does not appear on the record. The appellant Corporation, however, fixed the scale of fees on the basis that the cinema house was situated in a municipal area and that the rate was Rs. 400 per year. The respondent challenged the levy on the ground that it was unreasonable and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the fixation of the scale of fee under section 548(2) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, was a tax and not a fee. The word 'tax ' has been used in the same sense in section 443 of the Act and the word 'fee ' in section 548 (2) must be construed as including a tax. The word "tax" is defined in section 2(1)(a) to mean "any tax imposed or authorised by this Act or by any other law". The word "cess" means a tax levied or authorised by the Act or by a rule or regulation made under it. The word tax is also defined in section 3(4) to include a tax on advertisement. The word `cess' includes a tax on advertisements. The word cess means a tax on the entry of goods into a local area for consumption, use or sale therein. The word fee is therefore, a tax on a commodity like tobacco within the meaning of the Act. The word fees is not a tax on an activity but a fee.

992: The appellant was a shopkeeper and the Inspector of Shops and Commercial Establishments, Ferozepore Circle, visited the appellant 's shop on February 29, 1954. He found that he had been engaged in the business of selling articles to customers and that he had not paid any wages for the period of his employment. The Inspector of Shops & Commercial Establishments, however, refused to give him a certificate of fitness under section 7(1) of the Punjab Trade Employees Act, 1940 (hereinafter called the Act). The appellant pleaded that the Act would not apply to his shop but that the entire work in the shop was being done by himself and by the members of his family, and that to hold that section 7(I) of the Act would apply to his shops would be unconstitutional as violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of the Act were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution because the Act did not provide for the closure of an establishment or for the payment of wages for such closure. The Act was intended to regulate the working hours of the shop and to make provision for the regulation of the hours of work of the employees employed therein. The Act did not deal with the question of fixing hours of work or the conditions of service of the employees who were employed on any day in a factory. The Act is not concerned with the management of the shop or the commercial establishment. It does not deal with any particular class of persons employed in the shop or commercial establishment. The Act deals with the employment of certain classes of persons and provides for the control of the hours o f work of such persons employed by the employer. Section 7(1), therefore, cannot be said to have any application to the facts of the case.

1049: The petitioners, who were registered as bulls and bullocks for the year 1958, were issued a certificate under sub section (1) of section 3 of the U.P. Prevention of Cow Slaughter (Amendment) Act, 1958, by the State Government. They challenged the validity of this order on the ground that it was passed without giving them an opportunity to show cause against the said order. Held, that the petitioners had no fundamental right to carry on their trade or business guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and they could not be asked to pay any fee for the use of the bulls and buffaloes which they had been carrying on in pursuance of the orders of the State Government under section 3 of Act. 2728: The appellant tenant filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he had sub let out the shop to one Alladia. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant tenant that the tenant had not been in possession of the shop since he had vacated it and that he had no right to remain in possession. HELD: (1) The order under section 7A(2) of the Act is not an order of ejectment but only an order directing the eviction of the tenant from the premises. [859 E] (a) Section 7A(3)(b) provides that where in pursuance of an order of the District Magistrate under sub section (2) of section 7, the vacancy of any accommodation is required to be reported and is not reported, or where an order requiring any accommodation to be let or not to be let has been duly passed under sub section(2)of section 7, and the District Magistrate appears to have satisfied himself about the fact that the tenant has not sub let the premises, the District Magistrate may declare that the premises shall be vacant. [860 A B] (b) The District Magistrate must be satisfied that the tenant is in possession of a building in which he is carrying on business as a commission agent. If he finds that the tenant was in possession of such building, he can make an order directing him to put the landlord in possession of that building. [861 C D] (c) The District Judge was wrong in holding that the District Magistrate could not go into the question whether the tenant had sub let the building to a person who was not a member of the family of the landlord. 2302: The petitioners were the owners of a Union Territory. They continued to be the owners of the territory of India until they became the owners of certain other territories. On August 16, 1962, Pondicherry became a Union Territory and was brought into existence under the provisions of the Constitution. The President promulgated the impugned Regulation No. 3 of 1963 which provided that all taxes, duties, cesses or fees levied by the Union Territory would continue to be levied in Pondicherry and to be applied for the same purposes until other provision was made by a competent legislature or other competent authority. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned Regulation on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution as it infringed their fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution and also on the ground of violation of article 14 of Constitution. Held: (i) Article 14 does not forbid reasonable classification for the purpose of legislation but permits reasonable classification based on some rational and substantial distinction between persons within the class and those outside. In order that a law may be valid, it must satisfy two conditions namely, (i) that it is beyond the competence of the Legislature; and (ii) that it can be struck down only if these three conditions are satisfied. The test of reasonableness is not whether the impugned law falls foul of article 14 because there is no such clear policy or objective in the Act which could justify it. The test is whether the classification made for the purpose is based upon an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group. If the nexus test is applied to the impugned legislation, then the classification made is free from any infirmity. [446 F] (ii)The impugned regulation cannot be said to offend article 14 because the object of the impugned regulation is to prevent evasion of tax and to ensure that the income derived by the citizens of the Union Territory should not be subjected to tax. The impugned regulation has been passed with a view to provide fair and reasonable opportunity to the citizens to make their representation against the proposed levy. It is not necessary that the opportunity should be given to the persons affected by the impugned regulation before making a representation. [447 C D]

The notification further provided that where the duty of Excise levi ered on the specified goods for the first time before the date of notification was less than Rs. 10,000, then the exemption would be available to the extent of the duty payable on such goods. The notification also provided that where any manufacturer or producer of tyres or tubes had been allowed exemption from duty under the notification, he shall not be entitled to claim refund of the duty paid on the said inputs. The appellant assessee claimed that it was entitled to set off the entire duty paid on inputs against the duty determined as payable after applying the notification dated July 4, 1978. The Assistant Collector rejected this claim. On appeal the Collector (Appeals) held that the notification dated August 1, 1975 was applicable only to the extent that the duty was paid on the goods manufactured by the appellant and not to the extent the duty was not paid on the raw material purchased by it. 4772: The appellant, a candidate of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) contested the election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Kerala from the Communists Party of India. He was declared elected. The first respondent challenged the election by filing an Election Petition under article 324 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Commission had no power to make any law in respect of matters relating to or in connection with elections to the Parliament and State Legislatures. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the manner of voting was a matter coming within the ambit of articles 324 and 327 which empowered the Parliament to make laws in respect of the matters relating to the elections to the Legislature and that the Commission could not be said to have been entrusted with the task of making a law for regulating the conduct of elections to the House of People and Legislative Assembly. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. Article 324 does not confer any power upon the Commission to make any legislation. It only confers the power of making laws in respect to matters relating to elections to the legislature and the legislative bodies. [639E] 2. The Commission is a body created under article 324 and its functions are quasi judicial in nature. The powers conferred on the Commission are not merely those conferred on the Executive but also those which are incidental and ancillary thereto. The Commission has to act within the limits of its authority and in such manner as may be provided for by or under the Act. The Commission can also regulate its own procedure. Therefore, the Commission is not necessarily a court nor is it required to decide questions of fact or law correctly. [640F G]

Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellant is not sustainable in law. [103 B] 2.1 The death penalty imposed on the appellant is a very harsh punishment. It is not only harsh but also cruel. Therefore, it would be appropriate if the court imposes the extreme penalty of death or imprisonment for life. [104 C] 3.2 The appellant has undergone incarceration for about two years. He must have suffered incarcerated for a period of more than one year. In the circumstances of this case, the sentence of death imposed on him may be modified as imprisonment for life and the fine may be enhanced from Rs. 5,000/ to Rs. 10,000/. [104 D E] 3.3 The appellant shall pay a fine of Rs. 5 lacs. [105 F] 4.1 The appellant shall serve out the remaining part of his sentence. [106 H]
1543: The assessee company was a private limited company carrying on business as directors of a company. In the year 1941 43, the company held shares and debentures in its name. At a General Meeting of the shareholders of the company held on July 10, 1943, it was resolved to declare dividend at 60 per cent on the shares. The resolution was passed by the company with the approval of the shareholders. The company declared dividends at 60 per centum on the shares, but the company did not pay any dividend for the three years in question. The Income Tax Officer treated the dividends as paid out of capital and taxed them accordingly. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. The Tribunal held that the dividends were paid out of the capital of the company and therefore they could not be included in the profits of the year 1941 42. The High Court dismissed the reference. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The dividend income received by the company is taxable under section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The dividend income is not liable to be taxed in the hands of the company. [847 C] (ii)The dividend income is taxable only when it is paid out of funds of the company, and not when it is not paid out of income. [848 E] (iii)In the present case, the dividend income was paid out of profit and was not paid out or paid out of profits. [849 F] (iv)The dividend is not paid from the profits of a company but is paid out out of profits of the company; and the dividend income is chargeable to tax. [850 B] (v)Therefore, the dividend is not taxable in the hands or the assessee 's own account. [851 A] (vi)The dividend was paid out out and paid out of business. [852 D]

Rathore, IAS, Principal, H.U.M. College, Bhatinda as Chairman of Haryana Board of Secondary Education. The appellant was holding the office as Chairman of Board till 11 1285 when he resigned. 150: The petitioners were arrested on the 6th March, 1953, and they were being prosecuted for defiance of an order prohibiting meetings and processions in the area in question. They were subsequently released on bail by the Magistrate on the 9th March, but their detention was not stayed by him until the 11th March, and the trial was adjourned to some other day. On the 10th March, the petitioners moved this Court under article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus contending that the order of remand passed by Mr. Dhillon, Additional District Magistrate, Delhi, at about 8 p. m., on the 6 th March, was illegal and should be quashed. Held, that the order directing the production of the petitioners ' records before the Magistrate was not made in accordance with section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code and therefore the order of the Magistrate dated the 9th of March, was without jurisdiction. The order of remand was not made by the Magistrate in accordance with the directions contained in his order of remand. The order was not made as required by section 344(1) of the Criminal procedure Code and therefore it could not be said that the Magistrate had no power to pass such an order.
2643: The respondent was the owner of a firm M/s. Seth Brothers and the appellant was its partner. On March 14, 1961, the Income tax Officer, Meerut issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, intimating M/s Seth Brother 's firm that M/s seth Brothers had been found to be guilty of an offence under section 13(1)(e) read with section 13(2) of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that it was not issued by the Director of Inspection or the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., on the basis of information received from the Directorate of Inspection and that the Director of inspection did not have any knowledge of the facts constituting the belief that the instructions were being issued by the Directorate of Investigation for a general raid and seizure of all accounts books and papers which may be found at the premises of the firm. The High Court held that the Director 's report could not be relied upon as evidence against the appellant and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Director of Inspection and the Commissioner of Incometax, U. P., were not competent to issue the notice under section 147 of the Income tax Act, 1961. [601 B] (ii) The Director was not authorised to issue the notices under section 148. He was not entitled to issue the same. [603 C] (iii) The Director had no power to issue the show cause notice under section 142 of the Income 'tax Act, 1961 and the proceedings taken by him were without jurisdiction. [604 D] (iv) The Director 's reports cannot be looked into because he is not a person who has made the statements in his report. [605 E] (v) The Director could not be said to be a person who had merely passed the orders of assessment but had only acted as an agent of the Department. [607 F]
5431: The appellant was the owner of a house in which he had been residing. On March 25, 1975, the respondent State issued a notice under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to the appellant requiring him to deposit certain amounts with interest thereon. The appellant deposited the amount on June 30, 1975 and thereafter filed an application for payment of interest on the amount. The respondent State did not pay the interest. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court praying that the interest be paid to him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to interest only from the date when possession was taken by the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the application of the rule was intended to exclude the application of this general rule in the matter of the payment of interest. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule is applicable where there is a statutory provision providing for payment of compensation or interest. [1048E] 2. Section 23(1) does not contemplate any such provision. It merely provides for payment of the compensation. The question whether the application of section 23(1)(a) is intended to be excluded by the Act of 1948, and as we have already observed, the mere fact that section 5(3) of the Act makes section 23(I) of the land Acquisition Act,1894 applicable, it cannot reasonably infer that the Act intends to exclude the applica tion of this general Rule in the matter. [1049F G] Satinder Singh vs Amrao Singh & Ors., ; , followed.

3306: The appellant was charged for an offence under section 379 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for snatching two sarees from one Govind, while he was carrying them from the show of his master to that of a washer and dyer. The learned Presidency Magistrate found him guilty of the offence under section 374 read with section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since he was a young boy of about seventeen years and three months old at the date of the offence and the offence was not punishable with imprisonment for life, the attention of the learned Presidency Magistrate and the High Court was invited to the provisions of section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, and the appellant preferred an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence to the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 6 of the Act does not require that the court should consider the circumstances of the case including the nature of the offence, and the character of the offender as well as the circumstances of his employment in the society. [12 G] (2) The object of the Act is to provide a speedy trial and to ensure that the criminal justice system does not fail. It is only when the offences are serious that the legislature has made provision for the imposition of appropriate punishment. [13 E F] (3) The object and purpose of the Act clearly appears to be to give a speedy trial to the accused who may be convicted of the offences with which they were charged. [14 D E] (4) The object behind the Act is not to punish the offenders but to make the law workable. The object of providing a speedy trial is to do justice between the parties so that the accused may get a fair opportunity of defending himself. [15 C] (5) The object underlying the Act is that the accused should be tried speedily and the accused should not be subjected to undue harassment or torture. 6210: The plaintiff, a Hindu widow of a Hindu male who died intestate on June 6, 1949, filed the present suit for possession of certain properties. She challenged the power of her grand mother to adopt the first defendant on the ground that her right to adopt was lost on the death of her husband 's widow. The trial court decreed the suit and passed a decree for possession of the properties along with mesne profits. On appeal the High Court held that the right of the mother in law to adopt was revived on the death in question by her remarriage, the right of her mother in law was extinguished and could never be revived. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the mother 's power to adopt a son was revived when there was nobody to continue the line, and since the widow did not succeed to the estate after the death of the father, she could not have adopted a son to her husband ' 's widow ' 's estate. HELD: (i) A Hindu widow 's power of adoption is revived on her death. The widow 's powers of adoption are revived when the widow dies leaving a widow. The widow has an absolute right to adopt a daughter if she is able to maintain herself or her children. [527 F] (ii)The widow 's right to adopt is revived when her husband ' s life becomes extinct. The widow does not lose her right to take the property by survivorship. It is only when the widow's right to adopt subsists that the widow can validly adopt a son to the extent of her own entitlement. [528 H]
3921: The appellant was working as a Deputy Director in the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and was charged with offences under section 161, IPC and under sub section (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted by the Special Judge on the ground that he had committed an offence punishable under section 161 IPC and under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the sanction given by the President to prosecute him was not valid because the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 6 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, and therefore, the prosecution against him was bad. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 6 are mandatory and they must be strictly complied with before any action can be taken against a public servant. [355F] 2.1 The question whether the sanction is valid or not has to be decided in each case on its own facts. If the sanctioning authority does not apply his mind to the relevant facts then it would be open to the court to examine the matter in detail and come to a conclusion whether the sanction was valid or not. [356B C] 2.2 It is not necessary that the sanction should have been obtained before the accused could be prosecuted. [354E] 3.1 The sanction order cannot be challenged on the ground of mala fides. [353A B]
2711: The appellants, who were operating their stage carriages on the route applied for a permit to run a bus service on the ground that the route for which they applied was one of the routes mentioned in the application. The Regional Transport Authority rejected their applications and granted them permits. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the R.T.A. on the ground, inter alia, that the route proposed by the appellants and others should be opened and that it was not necessary in public interest to grant permits. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that no appeal against the order of. the R. T.A. could lie under section 64(a) of the Bihar Amendment Act, 1952. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 47(3) of the Act provides that an appeal shall lie from every order passed under section 48 or section 49 to the State Government or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be. The power of the R,.T.A., under section 48 is subject to section 47(3). [247 B] (2) The power of revision conferred upon the State Government under section 47(1) is not subject to any other provision of the Act. It is only after the decision of the Appellate Tribunal that the R.I.A. becomes entitled to exercise revisional powers under section 47. [248 C D] (3) The power to decide whether a proposed route should be opened or not is not subject either to section 47 or section 48. The power to determine whether a particular route should be operated or not is vested in the R.M.O. under section 48(1), and the R.F.A. has no authority to decide whether the route proposed is suitable for a particular route. [249 E F] (4) The R.T..A. cannot refuse to grant a permit on the ground of non availability of permits. [240 G H; 241 A] (5) The R,T.A.'s order does not suffer from any error of law apparent on the face of the record. [241 B]
1429: The respondents were the employees of the appellant company. They claimed that they should be treated on par with the other workmen in the same industry and that their wage structure etc. should be taken into account for fixing the wage structure etc., and that the wage structure should be adopted by the appellant. The appellant contended that the chemical works was an integral part of the Company and therefore the wage structure, etc. should have been fixed on the basis of the over all position of the Company; (iv)The tribunal had not given any reasons as to why the appellant should be directed to pay the respondents a minimum wage which would meet the requirements of the industry. Held, that the appellant could not be directed to give the same minimum wages to the respondents as are being given to other workers in the same factory. The appellant was not entitled to make any claim for the higher wage structure or for the lower wage structure. The appellant could not claim the higher wage structures or the lower wage scales. The appellant had no right to claim the higher wages. The appellant 's case that the chemical work should be treated as an independent unit was not correct. The appellant did not raise any dispute about the wage structure or the scale of pay but raised only a dispute regarding the wage structure. It was not open to the appellant to raise such a dispute. The appellant failed to prove that the chemical Works was an independent unit. The appellant also failed to establish that the chemical industries were separate units. The appellant merely relied upon the fact that the chemical industry was one unit. The question whether the chemical industry is one unit or more than one unit was not decided by the Tribunal.
3051: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Under the terms of the Deed of Conveyance, the appellant company was to convey the entire property including the building and the site on which it had been constructed. The appellant company agreed to assign the right of occupation in those flats, shops and offices to certain persons. The appellant Company assigned the right of occupancy in those flats and shops and offices. The appellant 's case is that the assignment was not valid as it was made without consideration and without notice to the other shareholders of the Company. The appellant contended that the assignment of the right of possession in the said properties was not binding on the appellant company and that the assignment did not confer any title on the appellant. Held: (i) The assignment was not invalid because the assignment was made without notice to all the shareholders of the company. (ii)The assignment was not a mere transfer of the right to enjoy the property but was merely an assignment of the rights of the company to the exclusion of all other shareholders. (iii)The assignment could be only by way of sale or mortgage of the property and not by way of lease. (iv)The assignment of the lease was not a transfer of the property. (v)The assignment in favour of the appellant company is not a transfer for valuable consideration. (vi)The assignment is not a mere transaction of transfer of the title of the assignee to the property. [339 D]

In the course of its business, it manufactured paper and packing material. The excise duty was payable at the rate of 12% on the value of the goods under Item 68(4) of the old Tariff. The appellant claimed that the excise duty should be calculated at the rate applicable to the goods manufactured by it. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the appellant was liable to pay central excise duty at the rate prevailing on the date of manufacture. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the duty was payable only at the rate prevalent on the date when the goods were manufactured. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. The appellant is entitled to exemption from payment of excise duty. [328G] 3.3. The appellant was required to pay central Excise Duty at the rate prescribed for the goods manufactured and cleared from its unit during the period of six months prior to the notice dated May 4, 1984. The appellant has paid the excise duty on the goods. The appellant cannot be said to have paid the excise duties on the goods after the expiry of six months from the date of the notice. [329A B] 3.4. The appellant could not be said to be entitled to exemption. [330C] 3.5. The appellant had produced a certificate issued by the Director General of Foreign Trade certifying that the goods manufactured were classifiable under Item 68 of the old tariff. The certificate also stated that the goods were classified under Item 17(4). The certificate further stated that the products falling under sub heading (4) were classifiably classified under Item 17 (4
1506: The appellants were charged with having committed the murder of Arjan Singh and Sukhjit Singh. They pleaded that they had been falsely involved in this case, but the prosecution evidence was not accepted by the trial Judge who convicted them of the offence under section 302/34 I.P.C. The High Court held that the charge under section 302 read with section 34 I.P., C.I. Act, against the appellants was proved beyond a reasonable doubt and so, according to it, the prosecution case under section 148 I.P,.C. had not been proved beyond a reasonably doubt. Held, that the conviction of the appellants for the said offence was justified and the appeal must be dismissed. It is well settled that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in a case, one pointing out towards the guilt of the accused and the other pointing towards his innocence, the view which favours the accused should be adopted. In the present case, the High Court did not take into account the fact that Gurcharan Singh and Ajit Singh were not examined as witnesses. The High 'Court could not have taken into account the facts that Gurcharans were injured and that they were not examined. The High court was wrong in taking into account the circumstances that Gurcharank Singh and Ajit singh were not examined and that the prosecution case was not supported by the eye-witnesses.

862: The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of sugar. In 1947, the appellant decided to close down its factory at Bombay. On October 30, 1951, the Government issued an order under section 6A(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, which provided that the Company should work for 40 hours per week during a period of 30 weeks from November 1, 1951. The appellant thereupon filed a petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order on the ground that it had been passed without jurisdiction and that the award was vitiated by fraud. Held, that the order was not vitiated by fraud but was based upon a misunderstanding of the true scope of the order. The order did not amount to a direction or order made under section 6 A(1), because, as soon as the order was made, the workmen were entitled to work for the whole period of the day. The order was therefore bad. The order could be challenged only if it was made after the date of the order, but before the expiry of the time allowed by the order. It was not necessary to make such an order because the order was passed after the expiry of time allowed by section 6A (1). The order was not one of dismissal within the meaning of section 11(2)(b) of the Act. The order being one of dismissal, it was not necessary for the appellant to challenge the validity of it.
1882: The appellant was convicted in four cases of an offence under section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted in two other cases of offences under section 467 read with section 471 and section 477A I.P,C. The sentences imposed for these offences were to run concurrently with the sentence awarded in the first case on January 17, 1962. The Sessions Judge ordered the sentences to run concurrently but did not order them to run concurrently. In each of the other two cases, the appellant was sentenced to 3 years ' rigorous imprisonments. The sentences were directed to run concurrently and the sentences were to run consecutively as no order had been made by the Sessions Judge for the sentence in the second case on January 20, 1962. On appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court held that the sentences were excessive and set aside the convictions and sentences passed against the appellant. It was contended for the appellant that the sentences in the two cases were not concurrent and could not be considered excessive. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The sentences imposed in the two criminal trials were not excessive. [447E] (2) The High Court was right in holding that the sentences imposed in one case were excessive. [443G] (a) There is no illegality in the sentences awarded in the other case. [444B] (b) The sentence in the other two case was not excessive. The sentence in both the cases was not excessive and the appellant was entitled to have his sentence reduced. [445D] (c) The sentence of fine in the other three cases was not disproportionate. [441F] (d) The sentence was not excessive because the appellant was a public servant. [442H]
